title: Early Scottish records
standfirst: The early Scottish records anchor the search for one extended Glasgow family. The next task is to connect its oldest documented households, retaining tentative joins with their evidence and open questions.
question: How can the earliest Glasgow branches be joined into the shared paternal family?
answer: Start with the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess, the Stirling John of 1475–1480, Alan in the late-fifteenth-century justice record, and the Saltmarket family. The Saltmarket John-to-William property succession is the leading father hypothesis, followed by a proved father–son generation. These working connections guide a single-family reconstruction while the missing identities and generations are tested. The local working tree now selects the Stirling John as an uncertain father of the Saltmarket candidate and, more tentatively, Alan Glasgw. The imported John profile’s identity and Alan’s exact collateral degree remain open.

chapters.title: Stichill: Patrick’s court records and James’s confident father link
body: Research question: is [James](/people/glasgow-1238.html), the 1712 child of [Patrick](/people/glasgow-1440.html) and Helen Fairbarn, the later husband of Elizabath Tait? The combined household argument supports 92% confident, from 86% probable.

The 1712 Stichill James, explicitly indexed as Patrick Glasow and Helen Fairbarn’s son, is confidently inferred to be the James who married Elizabath Tait in the same parish in January 1740. An age of about 28, continuity in this small local surname family and the later household’s son Patrick (1742) and daughter Helen (1750), repeating both proposed paternal grandparents’ names, form a combined identity argument. Naming is supporting evidence rather than a mandatory rule or independent proof of each step. The specific Patrick/Helen household is independently established by their 1707 marriage entries and 1708–1716 children. Newly inspected printed court minutes place Patrick at Stichill in 1712 and appoint him a burlaw man in 1715; these add local continuity, not a father clause. The unsupported Uphall field is not a competing contemporary record. No concrete rival Stichill James family has been identified in the held material; this is not an exhaustive population search.

Newly checked printed court records: 8 November 1712, Patrick Glasgow in Stitchill was fined one shilling sterling for reclaiming his impounded horse; 10 December 1715, he was appointed one of five burlaw men. The 13 November 1739 body names Peter Glasgow, fined with two other men over carrying teind peas; the edition’s index groups this under Patrick. Retain that last identification as a compatible continuation, not a certain death/survival boundary. The manuscript court book was not inspected. These records concern the local Stichill adult, not independent identification of the 1667 Gordon child.

92% is a subjective confident inference for James’s father Patrick in the Stichill Patrick/Helen household, including the 1712-child/1740-husband identification. The underlying parish images and the FamilySearch 1742 page were not newly inspected; a security challenge blocked the latter. Patrick’s identification with the 1667 Gordon child, the 1765 Swinton couple, the Leitholm Robert hypothesis and all mothers retain their separate assessments. No birth, death, place, spouse, parent selection or identity merge changes. The new court pages establish recorded acts, not biological kinship. WikiTree’s father control was checked on 22 October 2026 and was already confident; no new live certainty mark is pending.

Next useful test: Check the original 1712 child and 1740 marriage for residence, relatives or occupation; test the 1765 Swinton household separately. Seek a title or probate link for the older Gordon identity rather than repeating this now-confident local father inference.

chapters.title: Hugh of Kilwinning: a probable father from the reported family
body: Family comparison: [Hugh Glasgow](/people/glasgow-1056.html), [John Glasgow](/people/glasgow-1057.html), [William Glasgow](/people/glasgow-1055.html) and [George Glasgow](/people/glasgow-1058.html). The family account attributed to Elaine Comes identifies Hugh, husband of Janet Kilpatrick, as William Glasgow’s brother and names their parents John Glasgow and Agnes Spark. William’s held Stevenston child citation names that same parental couple, also recorded with George at Kilwinning in 1687. Hugh’s Kilwinning family from 1710 belongs to the same local generation. These specific people, spouse and household make John-1057 the probable father. The incorrect Glasgow-1080 hyperlink in John’s duplicate quotation is an editorial inconsistency: Hugh’s own captured account links John-1057 correctly and both texts name John and Agnes Spark. It is not evidence for a competing parent. The household records corroborate the named couple, while Hugh’s siblinghood and transfer of that fatherhood still depend on the single secondary account; duplicated quotations are not independent testimony.

74% assesses the complete Hugh-to-John/Agnes-household father identification, from 58% possible. The sibling relationship is reported, not independently proved. No Hugh childhood record or underlying evidence for Elaine’s statement was inspected. John’s own 1661 Edinburgh-child identification, the unrelated 1685 testament comparison, other ancestry and all mothers retain separate assessments. The circa-1692/1700 estimates are not birth records; no dates are changed.

The prior 58% review treated a mistaken profile hyperlink as a bar to probable confidence. That is an editorial problem, while the unverified secondary sibling attribution is the real evidential limit. The exact 74% is a subjective judgment, not a measured frequency. No new father, mother, identity merge or confident link is added.

Next useful test: Find the underlying evidence for Elaine’s specific brother/parent statement, or an identifying marriage, apprenticeship or inheritance record for Hugh. Rechecking the broken hyperlink alone cannot resolve the historical relationship.

chapters.title: Irvine and Dundonald: a possible shared William household
body: Research rationale: connect the earliest remaining multi-child working head through a ranked existing adult identity, preserving its competing child and wife questions.

Prefer the Irvine father account William Glasgow-1055 as the same adult as the Dundonald weaver William Glasgow-3586, at 56% subjective identity confidence. The Irvine entries name Wm or William as father of Grizell in 1724, Agnes in 1725, Katherine in 1727 and Margaret in 1729. The Dundonald entry names William Glasgow, weaver at Achenyeards, as Jean’s father on 1 October 1732. An existing adult household in the adjoining Irvine parish followed by the 1732 Dundonald household is a specific chronological and local fit, and is preferred to matching an otherwise untraced childhood profile alone. This is an inferred adult identity: the Irvine transcripts do not state the father’s trade or Achenyeards residence.

Select John Glasgow-1057 as the Dundonald William’s possible working father at 46%. This is an assessment of the complete father proposition, including both the 56% adult identity and the further identification of the Irvine adult with the Stevenston child cited as born or baptised on 30 November 1700 to John Glasgow and Agnas Spark (OPR615,10/3,frame11). The current William-1055 account estimates 1701; the citation and estimate are not silently harmonised. John-1057 is the existing account for that named parent. Its separate identification with an Edinburgh child baptised in1661, and its own earlier ancestry, retain their existing qualifications. The percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies or independent values to multiply.

No record names the Dundonald father’s own parents, connects the two adult households, or supplies an occupation for the Irvine father. William Glasgow-3288, baptised at Kilbirnie on20August1704, remains a compatible alternative. William Glasgow-1061, whose maintained transcript gives birth25June1715 and baptism26June1715 at Byres,Kilwinning, could have been a father at seventeen in1732; this is a weaker generation fit, not an exclusion. An unrepresented William remains possible. No wife’s death, remarriage, exact migration or craft inheritance is invented. Katherine’s1727 transcript names Mary Monfodd, while the other three Irvine entries name Margaret with Monfood/Montford/Montfod variants; this maternal distinction remains unresolved. The undated Mary Montfort marriage attached to William-1061 cannot identify the1727 mother merely by her name. No maternity is transferred from either William account.

The two William profiles remain separate accounts, with no merge and no claim of two proved William sons. Jean’s existing father link stays ungraded. The1733 child’s selected father remains possible52%, and Barbara Stevenson’s maternity remains99%; neither is strengthened by this upstream hypothesis. Jean’s mother remains unknown. Barbara’s existing pairing with the Dundonald father is ungraded and does not establish a remarriage after the Irvine household. Preserve all vital fields and previously selected relatives. Resolve the possible duplicate before a live attachment or merger. This is one new possible father proposal based on reassessment of held transcripts and profile citations; no original parish register was newly inspected and no live edit is made.

James Richmond’s Irvine account in the Old Statistical Account,volume7,printedpp169–170 (PDFpages1–2), describes the part of the settlement south of the river as belonging to Dundonald parish. The inspected printed page supports close geographical context, not this man’s residence in that part of Irvine or an individual migration in1732.

Inspect the original Irvine1724–1729 and Dundonald1732–1733 entries for the father’s occupation, residence and witnesses, and compare the Stevenston1700 entry with the adult’s later household. Seek a marriage, tenancy or kirk-session record distinguishing the Irvine father from William-3288 and William-1061. Test Mary versus Margaret independently; do not create a wife’s death to explain a later pairing.

chapters.title: Edinburgh: the Duffe father probably is the older weaver
body: Research rationale: connect the Duffe family to the earlier Duddingston weaver family by assessing the entire craft, civic-status and successive-wife sequence, rather than preferring a younger generation merely because of a guessed birth year.

James Glasgow-2682, father of the Edinburgh Duffe household, probably represents the same adult as James Glasgow-1150, the weaver apprenticed on 16 June 1641 and admitted burgess on 20 June 1649: 70% subjective identity confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 youngest-son Thomas apprenticeships name a father James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. Thomas’s maintained 1684 baptismal identification and the Duffe household’s James children of 1679 and 1680 fit those apprenticeship ages and the youngest-son order. The older craftsman independently has that specific craft and civic status, with an exact master/date cross-reference between his 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 admission. The maintained admission review found one matching admission, although this does not establish uniqueness. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Successive marriages explain the wife sequence without requiring another same-name weaver and burgess.

Select Robert Glasgow-1156 as James-2682’s probable working father at 61%, conditional on that preferred adult identity and the then-86% identification (reassessed at 91% for the older James only on 23 October 2026) of the 1641 apprentice’s named father Robert with the Duddingston account buried in 1647. This replaces only the former local Johnne Glasgow-1151 hypothesis, retained unselected at 26%. The live father was blank in the public check on 21 October 2026: the outstanding WikiTree action is a new probable father addition, not replacement of a live father. The 61% and 70% are subjective assessments of nested propositions, not independent confirmations or statistically calculated probabilities.

The main weaknesses are a very long working life and late fatherhood through 1691, together with the absence of a marriage, prior-wife clause, address, witness or admission-date reference directly joining the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. The 1693 same-name weaver master is an inferred identification, not an independently dated identity bridge. Another younger Edinburgh weaver and burgess remains possible. The cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship could concern the 1696 son, but its deceased father would conflict with assigning that father to the living 1693 master; resolve this before a merge. Retain both James profiles as accounts of potentially one adult, not two proved sons of Robert. Johnne-1151 remains an unselected younger-family alternative at 26%, alongside the James-3076/James-3077 and Annapill Glessie childhood route, John-1084’s Gordon family, and an unrecorded father. Those alternatives are conditional on the Duffe husband being a distinct younger man, not equally compatible with the preferred pre-1641 adult.

The circa-1655 birth, previously inferred from the first known child in 1677, is a creation estimate rather than an age or birth record. The preferred older-adult identity independently supports birth before 16 June 1641, uncertain and conditional on that identity. Replace the local preferred estimate with that boundary, retaining the old circa-1655 and “by about 1657” reasoning as superseded history. This is a separate vital/identity correction, not a date altered solely to fit Robert’s 1647 burial. No exact birth year is established; retain the broad Midlothian birthplace without claiming a new birthplace record.

No mother is selected for James-2682; do not transfer Deborah Ivey or any wife of Robert from the older profile. Robert’s own 28% Corsoun father hypothesis remains unchanged. The older James’s Robert link was 86% in that dated review and is now 91% (23 October 2026); the Duffe father link remains 61%. The 1696 apprentice’s selected father James-2682 remains 82%, probable mother Duffe-18 remains 72%, and brother comparison remains 79%. The two childhood James accounts stay separate. This is a reassessment of held evidence, with no new source discovery, original inspection, profile merger, live edit or confident upgrade. Connectivity counts still describe retained profile accounts and cannot establish their distinctness.

The most useful test is an Edinburgh marriage, guild, property, witness or prior-wife clause linking the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. Check the original 1690 cancelled indenture against the 1693 master before identifying that son or merging either James account; inspect the original Duffe baptisms for residence and witnesses. These are targeted next tests, not prerequisites to representing the preferred probable family.

New1733connection,30October2026: James Glasgow-4124, the Saltoun naval surgeon of Swift of Sheerness, is confidently identified with the surgeon son of James Glasgow, Edinburgh weaver/burgess, and Isobel Duff in Grant’s testament index, printed p.106/PDF p.116, entry3February1733. Father Glasgow-2682 and mother Duffe-18 are each95%, newly added from a checked absent-parent state. Printed Surf and Dobson’s Swift remain unresolved variants. Isobel’s separate4April1733relict entry is printed p.81/PDF p.91. Originals not inspected; dates are register dates. This does not identify the surgeon with apprentice4114 or settle the older-weaver identity70% or upstream father61%.

chapters.title: Kilwinning George: select a possible Leith father, 43%
body: Research rationale: connect an unattached seventeenth-century Kilwinning household through its existing Leith-child comparison, keeping record-defined fatherhood distinct from adult identity.

Findmypast’s inspected Leith transcript gives George’s baptism on 16 May 1658, father “Ard Glasgow” and mother Agnes Watsone, OPR 692/2/2, item 2, register range 1643–1666. The Kilwinning transcript gives Marie’s baptism on 29 July 1688, father George Glasgow and mother Jannet Willie. A third transcript gives Gorg Glasgow and Jean Gardiner, Kilwinning, 8 November 1678. All three transcripts were inspected on 18 October 2026; no original register image was inspected. Baptism dates are not established birth dates.

Select Archibald Glasgow-3078 as George Glasgow-3120’s possible working father at 43% subjective confidence, through possible identity with the Leith child George Glasgow-2714. The unattached George is the record-defined father with Jannet Willie at Kilwinning in 1688. His own biography cross-references George-2714, and Marie’s biography already links that other George as her father while her structured field names George-3120. These are dependent inherited identity suggestions, not independent historical witnesses. The 1658 child would be about twenty at the recorded 1678 Kilwinning marriage and thirty at Marie’s 1688 baptism. The latter George account’s circa-1660 birth is only an estimate and does not exclude the 1658 child. Prefer this already identified childhood/father route to inventing a new parent or treating the two George accounts as demonstrably unrelated.

The 43% rates the whole proposed father link to the 1688 adult, including the unresolved childhood and household identities. No record names that adult’s parents or carries the Leith child to Kilwinning. Jean Gardiner, Isobell/Jonet Young and Jannet Willie remain separately recorded women; no remarriage, alias or combined household is established. Another local George or another father remains possible. George-1082 of Mid Calder, George-1090 of Glasgow, George-1560 of Linlithgow and George-3100 of Campbeltown remain weaker chronological comparisons; different recorded settings and missing later records are not exclusions. Keep George-3120 and George-2714 as separate accounts and retain all spouses and children; the added son account does not establish two distinct George sons of Archibald. Agnes Watsone is named as the 1658 child’s mother, but no maternal attachment is selected for George-3120 in this paternal working comparison. Existing mothers, all vital fields and the uncertainty of Archibald’s own wider identity are preserved.

The record-defined father of the 1658 child George-2714 is assessed at 98%; the record-defined father George-3120 of Marie-3090 is assessed at 98%. These named record roles do not establish the childhood or migration identity of the 1688 adult. George-2714’s live father is already marked certain; no pending father-certainty upgrade is counted for him. Marie’s attached father is currently unmarked, so her proposed confident mark is separate from George-3120’s new possible father.

The useful next test is a household or occupational identifier in the original 1678 marriage and 1688 baptism, followed by Leith/Kilwinning apprenticeship, property or testament evidence. Check the two 1683 maternal index readings before combining Gardiner and Young. The original 1662 Archibald testament names a lawful son George, but does not identify his later adult residence.

chapters.title: Easter Newtoun: prefer the James father route, 40%
body: Research rationale: compare the competing childhood and father routes at the head of the largest Calder descendant branch; prefer the route with fewer unsupported identity steps while retaining compatible alternatives.

Prefer James Glasgow-991 as the possible working father of the Easter Newtoun adult John Glasgow-3610 at 40% subjective confidence, through the adult’s possible identity with John Glasgow-1084, the Mid Calder child of 1616. The 1616 index names James as father. The existing 1616-child account already carries the specific later-family attribution to Annah and the proposed 1642 Porteous marriage and 1643 Edinburgh child. The inspected 1649 and 1652 transcripts now place the named father Johne at Easter Newtoune/Easter Newtoun, supporting one adult household. This makes the existing 1616-family comparison a more economical preferred reconstruction than the 1608 route: the latter requires both the 1608 child’s identification with this adult and the identification of his named Mid Calder father with the Quothquan testator John-3296. Neither route is proved. The inherited Annah attribution is not independent corroboration of the new residence reading.

Retain John Glasgow-3296 as an unselected uncertain father alternative at 28%, through the compatible 1608 Mid Calder child. The original name, neighbouring-parish and generation argument remains viable, but its two unproved identity steps are less economical than the preferred 1616-child/James-991 route. The omission of children from the 1650 testament does not exclude him. No new record disproves the alternative.

The 40% is a combined judgement about James’s fatherhood of the later adult, not the 98% record-defined fatherhood of the 1616 child. The existing 42% childhood-to-adult comparison remains a distinct scoped assessment; these values are not independent measurements and are not mechanically multiplied. Both childhood dates fit an adult father in 1649: about 33 if baptised near birth in 1616, about 41 if in 1608. Neither childhood transcript supplies a residence, occupation or mother. The retained published Edinburgh marriage entry calls the 1642 groom a whipman but supplies no parents or residence to distinguish the candidates. The 1643 child names John and Issobell Porteous; the 1652 Annah transcript names no mother. A household, property, occupation or witness bridge to either childhood is still missing. Another local John, including the retained Linlithgow comparisons, or an unrepresented family remains possible. Robert-4006 remains a father-generation alternative. William-1087 remains a removed unsupported father, not biologically excluded merely by a 1609 baptism. John-1084 and John-3610 may be duplicate accounts, not two proved distinct sons named John; no merge is performed. Mothers remain separately assessed.

This reassessment reuses held evidence; it adds no newly inspected source. The retained Findmypast 1616 transcript reads “10 ?1616”, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.13; the supplied ScotlandsPeople index gives 18 February 1616, OPR 694/10/28. Preserve that discrepancy pending original comparison. The 1608 transcript gives 26 June, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.5. The 1649/1652 Findmypast pages, inspected on 18 October, give OPR 689/20 item 1 pp.5 and 13; supplied ScotlandsPeople references are 690/10/14 and 690/10/32. No original register was newly inspected. Repeated indexes of an event are not independent witnesses.

The selected local father changes from John-3296, uncertain 28%, to James-991, possible 40%. The previous selection and its sources remain available as an alternative. Fresh public WikiTree capture has no father attached to John-3610, so the outstanding live proposal is a new possible father, not replacement of a live father. No live edit is made. This revises the ancestry route above 309 fixed pre-1850 profile accounts (253,689 connected pairs depend on the old edge); those overlapping accounts are not 309 proved unique people. It adds no component join. Confident and supported connectivity do not increase. James’s own probable Mureistoun father, 82%, John-1084’s recorded father, 98%, Annah’s record-defined father, 96%, and John-3012’s father, 98%, retain their grades. John-3610’s before-1629 birth bound and all other vital fields and mothers are preserved.

Prioritise a discriminating household link for the Easter Newtoun adult: compare original 1649/1652 entries and their neighbours, then any 1642 marriage details, kirk-session, land or inheritance evidence tying him to James’s Mid Calder family. Test the 1608/Quothquan route in parallel. A mother or a precise holding would be more useful than another generic name match.

chapters.title: Easter Newtoun: Annah and John share the same father
body: Research rationale: test the identity alternatives in the largest Calder branch using precise household details, separating the adult father from his uncertain childhood and ancestry.

Prefer John Glasgow-3610, the adult father in the 1649 Kirknewton baptism, as Annah Glasgow-1439’s father at 96% subjective confidence. Findmypast’s transcript of John’s 22 April 1649 baptism names father Johne Glasgow and residence Easter Newtoune. Its transcript of Annah’s 20 June 1652 baptism names father Johne Glasgow and residence Easter Newtoun. The matching uncommon full paternal name, specific residence, parish and three-year interval strongly support one household. This is a combined identity inference across two child records, not a literal statement that the children were siblings. A different Johne in the same settlement or a transcription error remains possible.

The 96% concerns the record-defined father of the 1652 child and his identification with the adult father of the 1649 child. It does not identify that adult with the John baptised at Mid Calder in 1616, prove his own father, or establish Annah’s later identity as the 1676 bride. The transcripts name no mother. Issobell Porteous’s existing maternal attachment remains separately unproved; no maternity is transferred to other children. The earlier John-1084 account may represent the same adult, but its 1616-child-to-adult identity remains possible at 42%, rather than established. These are overlapping profile-identity propositions, not mutually exclusive biological fathers; the percentages must not be added or treated as independent evidence. Retain that account as an alternative and resolve the possible duplicate before any live family change. No profiles are merged.

The Findmypast transcript pages were inspected on 18 October 2026; the parish originals were not inspected. The provider gives archive OPR 689/20, item 1, pages 5 and 13, while the supplied ScotlandsPeople index gives parish 690, references 10/14 and 10/32. Preserve that reference discrepancy for original comparison. Both Findmypast pages label the place Kirknewton and East Calder. The extra indexed version of Annah’s baptism, R_686208660, also names Johne and leaves the mother blank; it is another derivative of the same event, not independent corroboration. The September daily-limit responses are historical access failures; these targeted transcript retries now succeeded, without completing the wider Findmypast audit.

The earlier household batch changed Annah’s father-profile assignment at 96%, without itself settling the adult’s ancestry. The subsequent working-ancestry review selects James-991 as possible father of John-3610 at 40%, retaining John-3296 as an unselected28% alternative; this is a separate combined inference, not an upgrade of the household evidence. John-3012’s existing 98% father role remains unchanged. All birth and death fields, mothers and saved WikiTree family fields are preserved. Margaret-3112’s competing 1646/1649 readings are unresolved: her 26 November 1649 Findmypast transcript names John and Kirknewton/East Calder, but gives no residence. It does not independently place her in the Easter Newtoun household.

Compare the original 1649 and 1652 entries, their register references and neighbouring households; look for a recorded mother, occupation or witness tying the Easter Newtoun adult to the 1642 Porteous marriage and 1616 baptism. Shared residence alone does not choose his grandparents.

chapters.title: Irvine: John is James’s possible father, 58%
body: Research rationale: connect the earliest remaining sizeable unattached Irvine household using an explicit combined identity inference, with competing models retained.

Select John Glasgow-2475 of the Irvine Isabell Kyle/Kelle household as the possible working father of James Glasgow-4157, Helen Nasmith’s partner, at 58% subjective confidence. The leading explanation identifies the later James with John and Isabell’s James, baptised at Irvine on 19 August 1711 (Glasgow-4100). This joins a specific recorded birth family to a specific later household in the same parish. Assuming infant baptism, that James would be about thirty when John was born in August 1741 and about thirty-five at Susanna’s 1747 birth. The later household’s first known son is John, agreeing with the proposed paternal grandfather. Same-parish continuity, a comfortable adult chronology and this modest naming clue together favour this family over the younger 1721 comparison. None independently proves the identification.

The 58% assesses the complete father proposition, including the uncertain baptism-to-adult identity. No source names the 1741–1747 father’s own parents, and no residence, trade or witness links the households. Baptism is not necessarily near birth, John is a common forename, and the first known child is not necessarily the eldest child. The 1711 and 1721 ages are illustrative infant-baptism assumptions, not recorded ages. James Glasgow-4157’s before-1722 birth is an inherited adult-age estimate, not a 1722 birth or a hard biological boundary. Do not use that estimate to prefer or exclude a candidate. All dates and identities remain unchanged. The original registers are uninspected; maintained Findmypast transcripts are being reassessed, not newly discovered.

Retain James Glasgow-4158 as an unselected alternative father at 26%, through possible identification of Helen Nasmith’s partner with his son James Glasgow-4129, baptised at Irvine on 11 April 1721 to James and Margaret Rae. If baptised as an infant, he would be about twenty at the 1741 child’s birth: young but fully possible, not excluded. The Rae household and its Margaret/Marion distinction remain as previously assessed. James Glasgow-1932, baptised at Kilwinning in 1707 to John Glasgow and Mary Gemill, and James Glasgow-1131, indexed at Kilbirnie in 1718 to John Glasgow and Agnes Ferguson, remain broader compatible comparisons; their father’s name could also explain a John child, so naming is not unique. An unrepresented family is also possible. No new individual percentages are assigned to these unselected broader identity comparisons. Another compatible model identifies Helen Nasmith’s partner with the older Rae-household James Glasgow-4158 himself, after a different partnership. His inherited age estimate would make him at least about thirty-nine in 1741, which does not exclude this model. No spouse death or remarriage is established. This is distinct from the 26% model making the later man a son of James Glasgow-4158; neither identity is merged. Hugh Glasgow-3109’s existing uncertain attachment belongs to the elder account and is not transferred to James Glasgow-4157.

This is one newly selected possible father, not a confident relationship or a source discovery. The Irvine James, John, Allan and Susanna household provisionally joins the larger working component; supported and confident connectivity do not gain this 58% edge. James’s documented fatherhood of the three children remains separately 98%. His identification with the Prosperity shipmaster in 1740 remains unresolved and supplies no family bridge. John Glasgow-2475’s own uncertain upstream pedigree is not strengthened. Isabell Kyle is not selected as James Glasgow-4157’s mother. Glasgow-4100 and Glasgow-4157 may be two accounts of one person: no merge is performed and the working profile count is not a count of distinct proved people or two independently established James brothers. Resolve the possible duplicate before any live attachment or merger.

Compare the original Irvine 1711 and 1721 baptism entries with the 1741, 1743 and 1747 entries for occupations, addresses and witnesses; seek a James–Helen marriage or earlier child. Those details could distinguish the birth identities without relying on naming. Reassess the 58% and 26% together when a discriminating record appears.

James Glasgow-4157 is the documented father of Allan Glasgow-4110 at 98% subjective confidence. Allan’s maintained Findmypast baptism transcript explicitly names James Glasgow and Helen Nasmith at Irvine on 22 May 1743, with birth on 15 May. James-4157 is the existing adult account defined by this same three-child household, not a name-only match to a separately known shipmaster. The shared parish, father, maternal forename and compatible sequence support one household, with Macsmith retained as the indexed maternal variant. The 98% applies to the father of these record-defined children, allowing for derivative transcription and an uninspected original. The saved Findmypast transcripts were captured on 3 September 2026 and are reused here; no original or new source is claimed inspected today. This neither identifies James with the Prosperity shipmaster in 1740 nor gives him a named father. Other Irvine James profiles remain compatible comparisons for those distinct identity questions. No birth, death, occupation, marriage, mother or upstream parent is inferred from this decision.

The anonymous public WikiTree check on 18 October 2026 confirms Allan has no attached father, although his existing biography already names James. Add James-4157 as his confident father: this is a genuine outstanding family-field amendment, based on previously held evidence. John-4116 and Susanna-4128 already have James attached with blank certainty flags; their 98% assessments are confidence changes, not new fathers. Their omitted public father rows are publication reconciliation. Do not count restored old rows as new genealogical connections or call this a new source discovery.

chapters.title: Andrew of Kirknewton: Alexander is the possible father, 58%
body: Findmypast transcripts inspected on 20 October 2026 give Andrew Glasgow and Christian/Chtian Cook in banns dated 18 May and 14 June 1700, both OPR 689/20, item 1, p.39. The earlier entry gives both residences only as Kirk Newton and East Calder. Neither names parents or an occupation; no separate solemnization date is supplied. The already cited FamilySearch marriage index gives 14 June. Retain that indexed association with the new banns qualification, without changing a structured date, the record-defined intended-couple grade of 99%, or Andrew’s possible Alexander-3118 father at 58%. The two entries concern one proposed union, not two wives or independent proofs of parentage.

Prefer Alexander Glasgow-3118 as Andrew Glasgow-1546’s father at 58% subjective confidence, possible. The particular Alexander household is established at Kirknewton by the 1667 Margaret Smith marriage and the father-named Alexander and Agnes entries in 1673 and 1677. Andrew’s 1700 Christian Cook marriage and fatherhood of James in 1702 place his own adult household in the same parish, one generation later. The sustained parish setting and feasible household succession together favour this existing family. Andrew, Alexander and Agnes recur in the descendant branches, providing modest supporting context rather than an independent naming rule. This weighs a specific family against alternatives, rather than inferring fatherhood from surname and estimated ages alone.

The checked 1702 christening index explicitly names Andreu Glasgou as father of James Glasgou at Kirknewton and East Calder on 20 September 1702. Andrew-1546’s original cited source is this same named-father entry, and James-1547 is the child account. Their record-defined father–son relationship is assessed as documented at 99% subjective confidence. This does not identify the child with a later adult or strengthen Andrew’s own possible father. The checked marriage index names Andreu Glasgou and Christian Cook at Kirknewton and East Calder on 14 June 1700. The existing Andrew-1546 and Cook-36136 accounts carry this exact couple, parish and date. Their record-defined spouse relationship is assessed as documented at 99% subjective confidence. The 1702 child index does not name a mother; no maternal relationship is upgraded. These are newly graded existing relationships, previously unmarked, rather than new parent attachments or new source discoveries. FamilySearch transcripts were inspected 18 October 2026; original images are unavailable there. The 1702 displayed birth field contains only “9”, which does not independently establish the full 9 September date retained on James’s profile. James’s possible later-life identities and his descendants’ parent questions remain separate.

The 1685 birth is an unsourced estimate. Taken literally it makes Andrew about fifteen at the indexed 1700 marriage and seventeen at the 1702 christening. Those ages are possible, but they cannot independently support the pedigree. A birth earlier in the 1670s or early 1680s would also fit the adult events and Alexander’s family chronology; no replacement birth year is adopted. Alexander’s own circa-1650 birth is likewise an estimate. The argument rests chiefly on the recorded adult households, not on moving either birth date to fit.

No checked source names Andrew’s father. Another Kirknewton father remains possible: the older Andro account Glasgow-1319, or one of the local John or William households, cannot be excluded merely because no Andrew baptism has been identified. John Glasgow-1057 of Kilwinning/Stevenston remains a weaker comparison because his documented household is elsewhere. Common forenames and the inherited father attachment must not be counted as independent confirmation. The complete sibling and child sequences are not established. Margaret Smith is not assigned as Andrew’s mother.

This reviews an existing uncertain father attachment, previously without an individual percentage; it is not a new father, a newly confident relationship or a new source discovery. The selected parent remains the same and the 52-profile pre-1850 child side retains its earlier identity qualifications. The 58% ancestry review alone changes no connectivity measure. The separately checked 1702 father role is now documented at 99%, contributing independently to the supported and confident views; the working topology remains unchanged. No profile is merged, no vital field is changed and no live WikiTree edit is made.

Check the Kirknewton register around the 1667 marriage and the known 1673/1677 children for an earlier Andrew, and compare residences, witnesses and occupations with the 1700 Cook household. Inspect the original marriage and 1702 child entry when available. These could distinguish Alexander from the surviving local alternatives.

chapters.title: James the ropemaker: Hugh preferred as father, possible 52%
body: Research rationale: choose the strongest existing parent hypothesis for a substantial Larne/Inishrush branch rather than leaving the recorded Hugh comparison outside the working family.

Select Hugh Glasgow-1499 as the preferred possible father of James Glasgow-1509, the older Belfast/Larne ropemaker, at 52% subjective confidence, replacing William Glasgow-1505 in the local working tree. The archived chronology explicitly places a James, son of Hugh, at New Town/Larne in 1737 and identifies its reported 1762 Janet Shutter groom with that James. Hugh is an independently documented Larne merchant and elder, jointly leasing Newtown property in1736 and dealing with Hugh Shutter in the original1749 mortgage. The later James/Janet account and the distinctive Jane Shutter name in the younger William’s monument fit a recurring Glasgow–Shutter network. These combined named-parent, locality, generation and family-association clues favour Hugh over retaining a William father without a named-son record.

This is a preferred working identification, not a proved father clause for the adult ropemaker. The chronology is one derivative reconstruction: its1737 child,1762 groom and reported1737–1802 stone must not be counted as three independent confirmations. The adult’s1737 birth may itself derive from that reconstruction; the independent1773 affidavit establishes only birth before27 October1743. The original1737 entry,1762 marriage and alleged James/Janet stone remain uninspected. Hugh Shutter’s relationship to Janet is unknown, and a business association does not identify a father-in-law. A different Hugh remains possible. No mother is selected: Ann is not established as the1737 child’s mother by the reviewed account.

The monument’s separately recorded James Glasgow-3991, son of Hugh and Ann, died in1812 aged64 and belongs to the younger1747/48 generation. That is a serious rival explanation: the reported1737 child could have died and the name been used again. It is not a recorded death of that earlier child. Withdraw the categorical earlier inference that the1737 James must have died young. Do not equate the two James profiles, invent a second wife, or infer surviving brothers with the same forename as an established fact. The older ropemaker was already an adult in1760–1761 and over thirty in1773, so he remains distinct from the younger monument/tanner comparison.

Retain William Glasgow-1505 as an unselected uncertain father alternative at27%, preserving his earlier possible but individually unrated placement. A William Glasgow, Larne merchant, witnessed the1760 ropewalk lease, which is genuine positive association with James; the witness is not expressly called his father and may be the older William or another adult namesake. William and Hugh’s joint1736/1757 property activity makes a wider family or business relationship plausible without choosing its degree. William could be father, uncle or another associate. The specific reported Hugh-son identification and Hugh–Shutter connection now favour Hugh, but do not exclude William. The percentages express comparative research judgment, not a measured frequency or independent-source calculation.

One selected father is replaced locally. The child-side working branch contains49 retained pre-1850 profile accounts, including James and uncertain descendants; their own grades are unchanged. This is not49 new or proved relationships. The men were already in the same working component, so no component merger or new genealogical connection is claimed. No vital date, place, spouse, mother, identity merge or live WikiTree field changes. Hugh’s own uncertain ancestry and James’s Inishrush descendants retain their prior assessments.

The next discriminators are the original1737 entry,1762 marriage, full James/Janet monument and any surviving1737-child death or later household recital. The1760 William witness must be identified separately rather than silently assigned to the older William. A document naming a parent, sibling or inherited holding would test the preferred model; its absence is not an automatic exclusion.

chapters.title: Two taxable Daniels in Currituck, 1718–1719
body: Research rationale: test the Daniel–William join supporting 51 retained pre-1850 profiles, without confusing two contemporary taxpayers or treating an inherited birth estimate as an age.

New original,25October2026: The original deed calls Daniel junior the eldest lawful son and heir apparent of Daniel senior and Mary, expressly his father and mother. They were of Moyock in North Carolina; the land lay above the Southern Branch Great Bridge in Norfolk County, Virginia. The80-acre tract is explicitly the property granted to Daniel senior and Mary by John Gamon’s will of4October1693, recorded15March1693/4, with remainder to Daniel’s bodily heirs by Mary, Gamon’s daughter. Daniel senior, Mary and Daniel junior acknowledged the deed in Norfolk court on17September1714. This completes the1693→1714 Richford Swamp title bridge and establishes the parent–child relationship. The later1733 and1752 dates are contingent redemption/lease endpoints, not execution dates. The documentary son is distinct from his father. Glasgow-3322 represents the1693 Mary Gamon husband and is therefore the98% confident father identification for this record-defined son. Glasgow-1158 also carries Mary Gammon as wife and may duplicate the senior account; assigning it to junior would turn that wife into his mother without resolving the identity conflict. Keep both current profiles and their existing parents; do not merge or reparent them. The1718–1719 Currituck Senior/Junior taxpayers are probably this Moyock father and son (85% identity assessment), supported by the close locality, same unusual names and four-to-five-year continuity, but the tax lists alone do not identify their land. The1729 Slade100-acre tract remains separate; William-428’s father remains42%, Daniel-1158→Robert-1157 remains12%, and Daniel-3322→Robert-1157 remains34%. No Scottish ancestry, exact birth or maternal maiden name beyond the explicit Gamon daughter identification is inferred.

A second original transaction identifies Daniel Glasgow as a planter of Moyock, Albemarle County, North Carolina. By a lease dated 15 September 1714 and release dated 16 September, he conveyed 100 acres to Thomas Miller. The release names Daniel senior; Mary joined it and acknowledged her consent in court on 17 September. Daniel Glasgow junior witnessed both instruments with John Nicholls and G. Halliday. The deeds recite Thomas Miller’s 800-acre patent of 20 April 1689 and his conveyance of this 100-acre parcel to Daniel on 16 May 1692, acknowledged on 17 May. Thus this 1714 original supplies a specific 1692 acquisition to follow; the original 1692 deed was located and inspected on 30 October 2026, completing this acquisition test. The 100-acre Miller parcel is distinct from the 80 acres inherited through John Gamon and from the 100-acre Henry Slade parcel sold in 1729. Shared acreage alone does not join those titles. The same court day, Moyock residence, Mary, Daniel junior and John Nicholls strongly identify the senior as the father in the separately proved Gamon deed. This adds chronology and a witness network, without naming William Glasgow-428 as a son or resolving junior’s later identity. Father ratings remain junior→Glasgow-3322 98%, William-428→Daniel-1158 42%, Daniel-1158→Robert-1157 12%, and Daniel-3322→Robert-1157 34%.

The published Currituck tax transcriptions distinguish two contemporary Daniels. The 1718 levy list separately enters Daniell Glasco Ser. and Daniel Glasco Jur., each assessed for one tithable and 15 shillings. The 1719 return repeats the distinction: Senior has one tract of 250 acres and land tax of 6s 3d; Junior’s land columns are blank. Blank columns are not proof that Junior owned no land. The 1715 land-tax return separately records Daniell Glasco paying 6s 6d on one 260-acre tract on 27 March.

These are newly reviewed published transcriptions attributed to NCSA Colonial Court Records, Taxes & Accounts, CCR 190; manuscript images were not inspected. Senior and Junior distinguish the two entries and suggest relative age, but do not state father and son. The two years support retaining at least two record-defined Daniels, without supplying their exact ages, wives, children or a physical household arrangement. The similar 1715 and 1719 acreages are a possible continuity clue, not proof of the same tract or man.

The existing profiles Daniel Glasgow-1158 and Daniel Glasgow-3322 are compatible comparison accounts, not automatic matches to Senior and Junior respectively. Both are attached to Robert-1157 in the current tree and may themselves duplicate one adult; the fact that the returns contain two Daniels does not prove that these two profiles represent those two men. Daniel-3322’s account represents the Mary Gamon husband named in 1693. The 1729 Norfolk Daniel/Mary deed is a further compatible identity, not a proved continuation into either Currituck taxpayer. Daniel-1158’s inherited 1712 death remains unverified: it cannot establish which later Daniel is excluded, nor should a later same-name entry automatically extend his life. Preserve both profiles and their vital fields while testing these identities.

Retain Daniel Glasgow-1158 as William Glasgow-428’s possible working father at 42% subjective confidence. The established early Daniel name in the Norfolk–Currituck region, the 1693 Daniel/Mary Gamon household and the later Currituck Daniel tax entries provide a plausible older local family for William’s 1738 and 1746 household. William’s inherited circa-1685 birth is an estimate, not a recorded age. The existing older Daniel account is a useful provisional choice, but the evidence does not identify the taxpayer as that profile or name William as his son. The two contemporary Daniels make the adult identification materially less specific than a single-name reconstruction suggests.

42% is the first individual assessment of this existing father placement, not an increase from a previous numerical probability or a newly discovered father. A younger local Daniel, another Glasgow father, or a collateral relationship remains possible; the two modern Daniel accounts could also duplicate the same man. William’s 1746 will names his children and an unnamed grandfather of Sarah, but does not identify that grandfather as paternal or as Daniel. No mother, Scottish origin, Robert ancestry, father replacement, merge or vital-date change is selected. The tax suffixes alone are not a basis for connecting the two Daniels as father and son.

Title-clause review, 20 October 2026: the enlarged original 1729 deed describes Daniel Glasco’s tenure and occupation, rather than naming William as a predecessor. Withdraw the provisional William reading. Mary remains the named wife; the Gamon-to-Slade title chain and Daniel’s modern-profile identity are unresolved. Keep the selected Daniel-1158 → William-428 hypothesis at 42%. [Current account and corrected reading](/people/glasgow-428.html#research-findings).

Trace the 260/250-acre Currituck property separately from the 80 acres at Richford Swamp in the 1693 Gamon will and the 100-acre 1729 Norfolk/Princess Anne conveyance. An acreage resemblance is not a title chain. Compare deeds, cattle marks and associated people for the two Daniels before allocating either taxpayer to a modern profile or treating the unnamed grandfather in William’s will as Daniel.

**30October2026 — original1692acquisition located.** The original conveyance of 16 May 1692, acknowledged in Norfolk court on 17 May, names Daniel Glascock of Norfolk County as purchaser of 100 acres from Thomas Miller and Elizabeth his wife. It identifies Miller’s 800-acre patent of 20 April 1689 and land on the Northwest River between the two Indian Creeks. The inspected 1714 lease repeats that patent, acreage, deed date, acknowledgment and particular land description for Daniel Glasgow’s earlier acquisition. These linked title particulars identify the 1692 Glascock purchaser with the 1714 Glasgow senior, rather than relying on surname resemblance alone. Reinspection of the 1714 original also confirms Thomas Miller: the earlier Willson reading is corrected. Elizabeth is Miller’s wife, not Daniel’s. The 1692 deed names neither Daniel’s father nor a wife or son of Daniel. It does not connect the separate Gamon 80-acre tract or Slade 100-acre tract, identify junior’s later family, establish Scottish origin or resolve whether Glasgow-1158 duplicates the senior account Glasgow-3322. Existing father ratings and all vital fields remain unchanged. [Original1692deed](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9TX-J3KL) · [Daniel senior’s current account](/people/glasgow-3322.html).

chapters.title: Edinburgh apprentice brothers: James and Thomas, probable 79%
body: Current maternal assessment, 21 October 2026: Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) is now the selected probable mother of the 1696 apprentice James-4114 at 72%, through the qualified Duffe household. This supersedes the earlier decision below to leave his mother unselected. The 1679 Elizabeth and 1680 Issobell entries may name different women, and neither child is identified as the apprentice. Father82% and brother79% are unchanged; this is one new maternal hypothesis, not a new paternal join. See the full argument and original index locators in the linked maternal account.
Research rationale: link the late Edinburgh apprentice families while testing whether their father has two profile accounts.

James Glasgow-4114, apprenticed to William Adam, apothecary, on 22 April 1696, and Thomas Glasgow-3285, assigned to the baxter apprenticeship of 11 October 1699, are selected as probable brothers at 79% subjective confidence. Both entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. The matching personal name, craft and civic status, in the same register only three years apart, favour one father. Thomas is expressly the youngest son. His 13 November 1684 baptism fits entry at almost fifteen, while the Duffe household has sons James baptised in 1679 and 1680, fitting the 1696 entry at about seventeen or sixteen. This is a coherent sibling group rather than a name-only regional comparison.

The 79% assesses the profile-to-profile sibling inference, not a literal brother clause or measured frequency. The apprentice entries do not name a mother, address or the father’s admission date; two matching craftsmen remain possible. Thomas’s apprenticeship-to-baptism identity is a maintained assignment, supported by age and locality rather than a repeated birth date. Do not choose between the 1679 and 1680 James children, merge either with James-4114, or transfer Isobell Duffe as his mother. The 1690 Lindsayland apprentice James-4131 remains a compatible comparison, including the possibility of a cancelled first apprenticeship. If that identity is established, its deceased father must be reconciled with the master appearing in 1693.

The printed Greyfriars register records Agnes Duncan, wife of James Glasgow, weaver, buried on 21 January 1674 (printed pp.196 and 252; PDF pp.212 and 268, visually checked). This fits the wife married in 1653 and removes a supposed overlapping-wife obstacle to identifying the older weaver James-1150 with the Duffe husband James-2682, whose known children begin in 1677. Different wives alone do not exclude successive marriages. The same surname page records an unnamed stillborn child of James the weaver on 16 January 1687 and another unnamed child on 18 March 1690. Neither is assigned to a named baptismal child or mother.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: James-1150 and James-2682 remain compatible accounts of possibly one adult. James-2682’s circa-1655 birth is an estimate from his first known child, not an age record excluding the older man. The older craftsman’s long career and the late Duffe family are compatible, though fatherhood continuing to 1691 would be late. No marriage, wife clause or address ties the Duffe household directly to the 1649 burgess. Retain both accounts and recorded families while testing that identity. The 20 October review prefers the Duffe father account for James-4114 at82%, with James-1150’s earlier76% selection retained as a compatible same-adult alternative; James-2682’s Johnne-1151 placement stays speculative 26%, conditional on a distinct younger identity. These are different propositions, not independent corroboration. No live parent replacement, new mother, vital change or identity merger is selected; the local father preference is revised. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

The useful next discriminator is a weavers’ incorporation, testament or baptismal original giving the Duffe husband’s trade, address or prior marriage. A further same-name hit without such detail will not distinguish the adult accounts. The 1701–1760 burgess PDF at Trades House starts with Hepburn and cannot establish absence under Glasgow. The maintained 30 September ScotsFind transcript review covers that missing surname section, but the original Part I page remains uninspected.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: 20 October 2026: Prefer James Glasgow-2682, the father account defined by the Edinburgh Duffe household, as the 1696 apothecary apprentice James Glasgow-4114’s probable father at 82% subjective confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 Thomas entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 13 November 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe gives an entry age of almost fifteen. The household’s James children of 16 March 1679 and 18 April 1680 fit the 1696 entry at seventeen or sixteen. Thomas is the youngest recorded son in this family, consistent with the 1699 indenture’s youngest-son description; the later recorded child, Margaret in 1691, is a daughter. This household-specific age and sibling order gives a better father-profile fit than selecting the older craftsman solely through the repeated occupational description. The James-1150 account remains compatible as another account of this same adult, not an excluded or necessarily different biological father. The 82% assesses the complete father-profile proposition, including Thomas’s inferred apprentice-to-baptism identity and the inferred common father. These clues are related and are considered together, not multiplied as independent confirmations. Neither apprentice entry names a mother, address, father’s admission date or birth date. Another matching family remains possible. The 1679 mother’s Elizabeth/Isobell attribution is retained with its existing qualification. The 1679 and 1680 James profiles remain separate, and neither is selected as the apprentice or Jean Dobie’s husband. Isobell Duffe is not assigned as James-4114’s mother. The possible cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remains unresolved; its father was deceased, while a same-name Edinburgh master appears in 1693. The 1691 baptism alone does not prove its father alive. James-2682’s speculative Johnne-1151 ancestry at 26%, James-1150’s probable Robert-1156 ancestry at 86%, and all vital fields are unchanged. This is a revised local selection; the live father remains blank, so the pending WikiTree action is a new father addition, not replacement of a live parent. The sibling assessment remains 79%. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

chapters.title: Edinburgh: the Duffe household is the preferred father account, 82%
body: Current maternal assessment, 21 October 2026: Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) is now the selected probable mother of the 1696 apprentice James-4114 at 72%, through the qualified Duffe household. This supersedes the earlier decision below to leave his mother unselected. The 1679 Elizabeth and 1680 Issobell entries may name different women, and neither child is identified as the apprentice. Father82% and brother79% are unchanged; this is one new maternal hypothesis, not a new paternal join. See the full argument and original index locators in the linked maternal account.
Research rationale: identify the apprentice’s father through the known sibling household before selecting between possible accounts of the adult.

Prefer James Glasgow-2682, the father account defined by the Edinburgh Duffe household, as the 1696 apothecary apprentice James Glasgow-4114’s probable father at 82% subjective confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 Thomas entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 13 November 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe gives an entry age of almost fifteen. The household’s James children of 16 March 1679 and 18 April 1680 fit the 1696 entry at seventeen or sixteen. Thomas is the youngest recorded son in this family, consistent with the 1699 indenture’s youngest-son description; the later recorded child, Margaret in 1691, is a daughter. This household-specific age and sibling order gives a better father-profile fit than selecting the older craftsman solely through the repeated occupational description. The James-1150 account remains compatible as another account of this same adult, not an excluded or necessarily different biological father.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: The 82% assesses the complete father-profile proposition, including Thomas’s inferred apprentice-to-baptism identity and the inferred common father. These clues are related and are considered together, not multiplied as independent confirmations. Neither apprentice entry names a mother, address, father’s admission date or birth date. Another matching family remains possible. The 1679 mother’s Elizabeth/Isobell attribution is retained with its existing qualification. The 1679 and 1680 James profiles remain separate, and neither is selected as the apprentice or Jean Dobie’s husband. Isobell Duffe is not assigned as James-4114’s mother. The possible cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remains unresolved; its father was deceased, while a same-name Edinburgh master appears in 1693. The 1691 baptism alone does not prove its father alive. James-2682’s speculative Johnne-1151 ancestry at 26%, James-1150’s probable Robert-1156 ancestry at 86%, and all vital fields are unchanged. This is a revised local selection; the live father remains blank, so the pending WikiTree action is a new father addition, not replacement of a live parent. The sibling assessment remains 79%. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

chapters.title: Dublin: Philip is the preferred father of Thomas, 67%
body: Research rationale: use the combined Dublin family and trade evidence to select a useful working parent, with its unresolved identities explicit.

Select Philip Glasco-146, the provisional elder Dublin watchmaker account, as the probable working father of Thomas Glasco-144 at 67% subjective confidence. The maintained reading of the 1773 advertisement explicitly says that Thomas served his apprenticeship to his father Philip Glasco and subsequently practised in London before returning to his father’s Christ-Church-lane house. Thomas’s 12 December 1773 marriage to Margaret Duffy at neighbouring St Audoen’s supplies a particular same-name adult, same year and immediate locality, rather than a Scotland-wide name comparison. A young tradesman returning to the family business and marrying later that year is the preferred explanation. The later Christ-Church-lane to 20 Ormond Quay sequence supports continuity of the watchmaking business. The separate marriage and apprenticeship evidence together justify preferring Philip to the unsupported Thomas-173 father attachment.

The 67% rates the complete profile-level father proposition, including identification of the 1773 groom with the advertised watchmaker and of the named Philip with the elder account. Neither the marriage index nor the Duffy pedigree gives Thomas’s trade, address or father’s forename. The advertisement is reused from the 7 October full-page OCR reading; its original image was not newly inspected. The older Philip account contains some junior events, so the elder/junior distinction remains material. Thomas’s circa 1753 birth is an estimate: age twenty would make completed apprenticeship plus several years in London compressed, favouring a somewhat older adult without establishing a replacement birth year. No date is changed. The rare surname, close locality and year are correlated clues, not independent parent statements.

Retain Thomas Glasco-173 as an unselected, previously ungraded father alternative, and retain a distinct unrepresented Thomas watchmaker as an identity alternative. Thomas-173, father with Catherine of Sarah in 1760, is chronologically compatible with the trade cluster, but connecting that household to the 1773 groom adds an unsupported generation, whereas the advertisement names Philip. Thomas-143 could represent the tradesman only if his very weak circa 1766 estimate is revised; the date is not a hard exclusion. The 1779 Miss Hynes marriage and the 1785 Mary King licence may concern remarriages, but no spouse death or identity bridge establishes that sequence. No merge, new wife or new child follows.

The current Catherine Mangan mother attachment and Thomas-143 child attachment remain separately ungraded; Philip’s spouse is not thereby proved to be Thomas’s mother. The selected father replaces one existing local working attachment. Two already-catalogued descendants move into the main working component; the old Thomas-173 account remains separate. No new person, live WikiTree edit or confidence-only upgrade is claimed. The earlier Scottish ancestry assigned to Philip remains uncertain and does not become probable through this change.

Check the original 1773 advertisement and marriage entry, the Duffy 1774/1775 probate papers, and Thomas’s London apprenticeship/freedom records for trade, address or named kin. Seek the 1777 Margaret Glasco grant and the full 1777 Philip/Thomas chancery bill before accepting a Duffy–Hynes remarriage or a precise Philip generation.

chapters.title: Torryburn: John, James and Jean Mitchell
body: Research rationale: restore the complete named baptism household before testing its earlier ancestry.

The maintained Findmypast transcript of the 15 October 1689 Torryburn baptism names John Glasgow, father James Glasgow and mother Jean Mitchell. James-4176 and Mitchell-58830 were created specifically for those named adults and their current public biographies define them by this same event. No later adult identity or guessed parent generation is needed to identify these record roles. Assess each parent–child relationship as documented, 98% subjective confidence, allowing for an uninspected original and derivative transcription.

This is one register entry, not several independent sources or a recurring series. The transcript was captured on 3 September 2026 and is reused; the original OPR 458/2 image has not been inspected. The parents’ before-1670 dates are inherited age estimates, not recorded ages or hard biological bounds; Torryburn is event context, not a proved birthplace. No marriage date, further child, occupation, parent of James or Jean, or link to another Glasgow family is established. John’s later life remains unknown. The existing live family links are retained; no live edits, mergers or new people are made.

The existing public links were omitted locally because both named parents were outside the One-Tree export. This is a restored documented family, not a newly inferred connection to the early surname trunk.

Search the exact James Glasgow/Jean Mitchell pair and literal surname variants before selecting a birth family. chapters.title: Dalziel to Cambusnethan: a possible James father
body: Research rationale: compare two neighbouring Lanarkshire families using their actual recorded household settings, generation and the James/Samuel name sequence.

The Findmypast transcript records Samuel Glasgow and Janet Broun, both resident in Dalziel, in banns dated 23 June 1716: OPR 639/1, item 2, p.71. It gives marriage year 1716 but no separate ceremony date, ages, occupations or parents. The transcript was inspected on 18 October 2026; the original register was not inspected. Prefer the 1716 Dalziel groom as Samuel Glasgow-3166, the father named in James’s 1719 Dalziel baptism index. The same full name, exact parish and three-year interval make one household more likely than two contemporaneous Samuel Glasgows. The selected working couple is assessed as probable at 88% subjective confidence, including the groom-to-profile identity. This rates the proposed couple identified by banns, not proof of a completed wedding. The record-defined intended couple is explicit; the link to the later father is inferred, without a residence below parish level or a named parent. Janet is a possible maternal lead for James Glasgow-3523, not his assigned mother: banns alone neither prove a completed marriage nor establish the mother of a later child. Samuel’s own parents remain unknown. The existing James-to-John Glasgow-3094 working father proposal remains possible at 41%; the new banns do not bridge the seventy-year identity gap. All birth/death fields, mothers and existing father grades are preserved. No new paternal component is joined and no certainty upgrade is counted.

Select James Glasgow of the 1719 Dalziel record (Glasgow-3523) as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father, at 41% subjective confidence. This joins the Cambusnethan John-and-Ann family provisionally to the adjacent Dalziel James-and-Samuel family. The positive comparison combines a particular nearby surname household, a viable parent generation, and John’s two currently listed sons James and Samuel repeating the older two given names. Samuel is a more discriminating comparison than John or James alone. The proposed sequence is Samuel to James to John to the later James and Samuel; only the first and last household roles have cited baptismal support. No record names the adult John’s father or shows the 1719 child’s later life. The 41% rates that whole immediate-father proposition, including the child-to-adult identity gap; it is comparative judgment, not a measured frequency or a probability for the complete pedigree.

John’s saved family association supplies the precise place missing from his broad Scotland birth field: the Ann Clerk marriage is dated 23 October 1790 at Cambusnethan. The maintained child accounts place James Glasgow-3095 there on 11 May 1793 and Samuel Glasgow-3096 there on 17 February 1798, with John named as father in their cited indexes. James Glasgow-3523 represents the Dalziel child indexed 15 March 1719 as son of Samuel Glasgow-3166, under OPR 639,10/28. These are reused family and index citations, not newly inspected register pages; the original entries still need checking. A fresh reading of the printed Dalziel parish account, p. 443, confirms that Cambusnethan bounded Dalziel on the east. That establishes neighbouring parishes, not an individual’s movement or kinship.

John’s 1770 birth is an uncertain profile estimate, not a baptism or recorded age. If taken literally with 1719 it implies fatherhood at about 51, which is possible and supplies no maternity information. An illustrative John birth in 1750–1770 would give a James age of about 31–51 and a 1790 groom aged 20–40; neither range is adopted as a new date. The 15 March 1719 index date is not independently established as a birthday. The named James may have died young or belonged to another later household. Adjacency does not prove continuity, and an interval of roughly seventy years separates the two parish events. James and Samuel are the currently attached children, not a proved complete or birth-ordered family. Samuel could come from Ann Clerk’s family or another relative; no Scottish naming rule determines the father. The family names and the existing father assignment to Samuel are not independent demonstrations of John’s ancestry.

Retain another local James or another unrepresented father, and a collateral relationship to the Dalziel family. Samuel Glasgow-3166 is an alternative direct father if John was substantially older than the 1770 estimate; the ordinary younger-groom generation favours an intervening James, but the absent age cannot exclude an older groom. The earlier Calder Alexander/Clerk-marriage comparison remains a possible wider ancestry route, not a proved direct father: repeated Clerk marriages do not identify Ann’s family or establish a two-century pedigree. Other Scottish James households are not excluded for missing fields, but no comparably specific Cambusnethan–Dalziel and James/Samuel sequence was found in the bounded local catalogue comparison. James’s mother and wife remain unknown. No mother is selected for John, and no relationship is inferred between Ann Clerk and the earlier Clerk women. Preserve the existing ungraded Samuel-to-James father mark and all current child-parent grades, without a confidence upgrade or live save. The 1690s–1794 London pen-cutter comparison for Samuel remains very weak and separate; it supplies no evidence for this family. No person is merged, created or redated.

Inspect John and Ann’s original1790 marriage and the 1793/1798 child entries for residence, occupation, witnesses and further children. Inspect the 1719 Dalziel entry and search Dalziel, Cambusnethan, Shotts and Carluke registers for a John born broadly 1750–1775 and for the 1719 James’s later household or early death. Test maternal Clerk naming separately. Seek tenancy, kirk-session or testament material joining the two generations; keep the alternative older John/Samuel model open until an age or parent is recovered.

chapters.title: An original will identifies the Sinking Valley children
body: Research rationale: identify the existing central Pennsylvania branches through John’s named children, while keeping the testator’s earlier Scottish ancestry separate.

The original will names wife Margaret, sons Richard, William, John, Samuel, Matthew, James and Taylor, and daughters Hannah and Jane. James and Taylor receive the 322-acre, 72-perch home tract jointly, subject to Margaret’s support and the legacies, and are appointed executors. The register records probate and the grant to both executors on 12 March 1825. The will names no mother for the children, no Hunter maiden surname, and no Scottish father for its testator. The widow Margaret is not automatically each child’s mother. The original will and probate have now been inspected. The original will names wife Margaret, sons Richard, William, John, Samuel, Matthew, James and Taylor, and daughters Hannah and Jane. James and Taylor receive the 322-acre, 72-perch home tract jointly, subject to Margaret’s support and the legacies, and are appointed executors. The register records probate and the grant to both executors on 12 March 1825. The will names no mother for the children, no Hunter maiden surname, and no Scottish father for its testator. The widow Margaret is not automatically each child’s mother. Richard’s father confidence rises 72%→97%, William’s 65%→96%, Matthew’s 64%→96%, Taylor’s 64%→98%, and the Cambria John’s 57%→86%. Select Samuel-1984 as a new probable son at 88% and James-2577 as a new probable son at 80%. The Missouri James-45 is a surviving alternative to the preferred James-2577 identification, but the will gives no age, wife, residence or other feature tying the executor to the drummer. Do not treat them as an established identity. The testator’s own Richard father remains 21%; no Hunter mother is newly assigned. Earlier statements that the will was uninspected, or that Samuel had only a census-age slot, are superseded by this original reading.

The original will now proves that the Antis/Sinking Valley John had a son John. This independently supports the previously compiled report of a young emigrant son John. The Cambria adult’s reported 1777 Scottish generation, 1820 Allegheny Township household and central Pennsylvania continuity make him the leading checked identity for that son. The will supplies no residence, wife or age for its John, so identification with the Cambria adult remains a probable inference. Daill and Glasgow birthplace claims are not equated or verified.

The original will explicitly names a son Samuel and gives him a $50 legacy. Samuel Glasgow-1984’s reported circa-1786 Antis birth and 1829 Huntingdon death fit the testator’s Antis household and father generation. The previously suggested John family is now supported by an actual named-son clause and a specific locality match. The bounded catalogue comparison found no stronger same-generation Antis Samuel. The will gives no Samuel residence, age or spouse, and his profile dates remain derivative, so the complete identity and father proposition is probable at 88%, not certain. Samuel’s reported death before the legacy’s 1832 due date is not a contradiction: the will provides for a deceased child’s issue.

The original will names James as a son, joint devisee of the Antis home tract and executor with Taylor. James Glasgow-2577 is the strongest checked adult match: reported born in Blair County on 4 October 1793, with a daughter Mary Ellen reported born there in 1829 and eventual Logan Valley Cemetery burial. His age about31 at probate fits. These profile and daughter details are derivative and their memorial originals were not inspected. The bounded public-catalogue comparison found no closer local same-generation James. The Missouri James-45 remains a compatible alternative by name, generation and broad Pennsylvania origin, but his probable Downington birth and later Missouri household are a weaker locality match. The will supplies no age, wife or residence for its James; select2577 as an80% probable working father connection, retaining the alternative and all vital fields.

The Missouri James45 remains a compatible alternative to the preferred local James2577. Hannah and Jane are named daughters whose later identities are unresolved; the will supplies no married surnames. The claimed migration dates, exact vital fields and the widow’s Hunter surname are not verified by this will. Earlier census slots do not independently identify the named children.

Trace the son John’s estate receipt to Cambria, Samuel’s representatives and executorJames’s deed/signature to the HannahTurner household. Keep MissouriJames45 as an alternative and test John1549’s earlier Scottish ancestry separately.
