chapters.title: Drumearn to Martinsburg: testing a reported John father
body: The Geneanet entry already cited in Robert’s saved biography was inspected directly. It represents the man reported born in 1769 in Ireland and dead at Martinsburg on 26 November 1858, with the same wife and children. It explicitly attaches John Glasgow, born 1745 in Ireland, and Margaret, entered under the surname Nee, as parents. John’s own page cites only Ancestry Family Trees. This verifies what the contributed tree says; it does not verify historical paternity, either parent’s birth, or Margaret’s surname. The page gives Ireland, not County Tyrone. Robert’s more specific Tyrone origin remains an inherited local-profile claim.

Select John Glasco of Drumearn (Glasgow-2990) as Robert Glasgow-1189’s possible working father, at 31% subjective confidence. The specific reported father name John favours a John comparison over the automated leading candidate James Glasgow-1970. The actual 1766 Derryloran return places John at Drumearn beside two James Glasco households, three years before Robert’s estimated birth. That supplies a real Tyrone father-generation account compatible with the reported origin. John’s circa-1750 local estimate and the contributed father’s 1745 year are both unproved; either permits fatherhood around 1769, and no date is changed to fit. The estimate assesses the whole proposition that the documented householder was the reported father. It is not a rating of the census record, a statistical probability, or a product of the uncertain ancestry above John.

There are two unresolved steps: whether the contributed John/Margaret parentage is correct, and whether that John was the Drumearn householder. A common given name, estimated generation and claimed county cannot establish identity. The 1766 return supplies no wife, child, age or parent; the nearby James entries do not identify John’s father. Robert’s Tyrone birthplace is not independently established by the inspected Geneanet page. John’s existing uncertain James Glasgow-2988 father is preserved, with no new support. The Cookstown reward subscriber of 1796 is an unresolved namesake comparison, with Robert Glasgow-3941 the stronger maintained candidate; that notice supplies no parent and is not used as proof that the Martinsburg man lived at Cookstown. The single Geneanet/Ancestry family-tree chain and its repetition in WikiTree are not independent witnesses.

Retain another unidentified Irish John as a serious alternative. John Glasgow-3314, associated with Margaret Mill and the West Calder children of 1762–1770, matches both reported parental given names and a viable generation, but has no inspected Robert or Irish-origin bridge. His Scottish baptism and actual West Calder household are distinct facts; an unproved Irish birthplace is not a categorical exclusion. John Glasgow-4179 of Larne also fits the estimated generation; his known Rose Allan marriage does not prove there was no earlier Margaret, but no record connects him with Robert or Drumearn. James Glasgow-1970 has a Cookstown family tradition and a rare Julia/Julia Ann descendant-name resemblance; those are useful regional clues, but do not outweigh the specific reported John father name. If that report is wrong, James or another local man remains possible. No competing candidate is rejected merely for missing fields. No mother is selected: the reported Margaret is not identified with Margaret Mill, Rose Allan or any existing profile, and Nee is not adopted as a verified birth surname. Robert’s wife Elizabeth and every existing child remain unchanged. No merge, vital-field change, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.

Trace the source of the John/Margaret attachment behind the contributed tree. Inspect the 1803 Caughnawaga baptism and Robert’s American naturalisation, land, probate or family papers for an actual Irish locality or named parent. Compare Drumearn estate/tenancy records and collateral emigrants with the West Calder and Larne alternatives. Keep the eighteenth-century parent question distinct from later descendant record work.

chapters.title: Leitholm: a working route into the Stichill family
body: The inspected FamilySearch marriage index names Robert Glasgow and Agnes Whitehead at Eccles on 4 April 1779. A separately inspected baptism index names them as parents of James Glasgow, christened at Eccles on 30 December 1779. Its birth field contains only “12”, which is not a complete birthday. The source supports an earlier James child; John, born in 1786 in the captured family account, is not the first known son. The index pages are derivative records; no original register image was inspected.

Select James Glasgow (Glasgow-1238), the father recorded with Elizabath/Elizabeth Tait at Stichill, as Robert Glasgow’s possible working father, at 34%. The couple’s maintained marriage citation is dated 25 January 1740; their David and James children are indexed in June 1744 and July 1746. Robert’s estimated 1745 birth fits that family generation and could fall between those events; it is not a dated baptism. Stichill and Eccles/Leitholm belong to the same small Borders district, and the later Swinton entry attributed to the James/Tait couple offers a further local comparison. Robert’s earlier son James supplies a modest naming clue consistent with this father; a common forename cannot establish paternity. The combination favours this existing, record-defined family over the catalogue’s distant Kirknewton candidates, whose apparent proximity came from mapping Leitholm to South Leith. No inspected record names Robert as James’s son.

This is a preferred, revisable hypothesis, with 34% subjective confidence, not a measured probability or a confident connection. Robert’s 1745 birth and 8 August 1800 death each have zero attached sources on the inspected FamilySearch tree. Neither date establishes an age or place of birth. The local 1745 estimate is retained unchanged. FamilySearch attaches John Glasgow (1720–1785, GFNP-FS8) and Agnes Spark (1722–deceased, K8CD-HCW) as parents; retain that alternative without treating a contributed tree as documentary proof. The evidential basis of that parent attachment has not yet been reviewed. Do not equate that John with the much older John Glasgow-1057, husband of Agnes Spark-330, from the matching names alone. James’s brother John Glasgow-1444, christened at Stichill in 1708, is another compatible local father-generation alternative with no presently inspected Robert link. An unrecorded local father or another kinship degree remains possible. The Swinton/1740 couple continuity and Robert’s own early life need testing. Elizabeth Tait is not selected as Robert’s mother: her marriage and maternity of other children do not identify his mother. Robert is not merged with an earlier child, and James’s existing older ancestry retains its own uncertainty.

Inspect Robert’s 1779 marriage and children’s original Eccles entries for residence, occupation and witnesses, then check Leitholm feu/tenancy and joiner apprenticeship records for a named father or master. Test the contributed John/Agnes Spark account against actual records before identifying it with any local person. Recheck the 1765 Swinton household independently. James Glasgow-1222 (1777 Kelso, attributed to David Glasgow and Janet Hood) is a nearby child-name comparison for the 1779 James, not a selected identity; retain both record accounts unless a record resolves the different parents.

chapters.title: Whitecastle James: a Clydesdale setting and provisional Quothquan family
body: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments.

The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale.

Select [John of Quothquan](/people/glasgow-1086.html) of Quothquan as the uncertain local working father of [James of Whitecastle](/people/glasgow-1376.html). The choice is conditional on the Whitecastle man’s possible identity with [James, the possible Lindsaylands weaver](/people/glasgow-3332.html), provisionally compared with the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The newly supported probable Clydesdale setting supplies a positive regional bridge that the earlier review lacked. The same name, neighbouring Libberton/Biggar households and compatible adult dates favour that existing local account as the leading identity comparison. The 1690 apprentice entry names a deceased James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland, as father of the apprentice; that trade and place probably identify the 1680 testator, not the Whitecastle man directly. John is already the uncertain father attached to [the possible Lindsaylands weaver](/people/glasgow-3332.html). Carry that family placement across the possible identity at its actual uncertainty, rather than inventing another father. John’s possible 1608 childhood would fit a son born in the 1630s–1650s; neither James birth estimate is a recorded age. This is a selected, revisable family hypothesis, not a parent clause in the 1672 decree.

There are two dependent gaps: Whitecastle James is not proved to be the Lindsaylands weaver, and John’s paternity of [the possible Lindsaylands weaver](/people/glasgow-3332.html) is itself unproved. John’s 1685 Quothquan testament names his widow but no child; the absence of James, if dead by 1680, would not exclude this model. [the possible Lindsaylands weaver](/people/glasgow-3332.html)’s possible identity with the 1624 weaver would invalidate this particular later-life route, because the 1624 decedent cannot be the man present in 1672. [James of Edinburgh](/people/glasgow-1150.html), the Edinburgh weaver, remains an alternative adult identification for the later weaver rather than being excluded from an unsupported birth estimate; another local James or a different kinship degree remains possible. The old Marion-baptism role error supplies no positive parentage for [the Whitecastle man](/people/glasgow-1376.html), and the Duffe household [James, husband of Isobell Duffe](/people/glasgow-2682.html) is not merged. The 1738 Edinburgh Castle lead is unselected and incompatible with a death by 1680 if this weaver identity is right. No 1680 original was newly read: the maintained case has only the supplied wills index, and no linked manuscript or transcription. Neither a marriage nor a mother is supplied. Jonet Kinnie, John’s widow, is not automatically James’s mother. Keep both James profiles separate; they may represent one man, not two proved brothers.

The fixed historical cohort and all names, dates, places, spouses, existing father choices and live WikiTree fields are preserved. The circa-1650 birth on [the Whitecastle man](/people/glasgow-1376.html) is an estimate; the newly checked occurrence is in 1672, not a pre-1650 record. One selected uncertain father connects this previously isolated account locally. Supported and confident paternal measurements remain unchanged. Working counts concern retained profile accounts and may include the unresolved duplicate represented by the two James profiles; a gained connection is not another proved person or a proved pedigree. The 27/24 July discrepancy and imprisonment-versus-fine correction remain visible beside the family hypothesis.

chapters.period: 1663–1702 · documented father roles; probable household and maternity
chapters.title: Polwarth and Gordon: one probable James–Agnes household
body: Prefer one household: James Glasgow, indexed with Agnes Waitte at Polwarth on 18 June 1663, is probably the James who fathered the Gordon children John (1666), Patrike (1667), Jean (1671), Robert (1673), Agnes (1676) and Margrat (1679). The father’s repeated full name, the neighbouring Berwickshire parishes, the first child three years after marriage and the orderly thirteen-year child sequence form a coherent family. The daughter Agnes supplies modest naming support; it is not the deciding evidence. The maintained 1702 Gordon marriage citation for Jean also names father James, adding a compatible adult continuation for her. Read together, these favour a single local family over six isolated fathers or an unrelated Polwarth couple. No concrete competing contemporary Gordon James household has been identified in the maintained material. That is the scope of this comparison, not a claim to have exhausted the population.

The child indexes explicitly name James as father but omit the mother. Their named-father roles are documented for the record-defined children; identifying that father with the 1663 Polwarth husband is probable. Agnes Watt is separately assessed as probable mother of all six children on the marriage, locality and sustained family sequence. This is an inference, not literal maternity in the indexes; a later marriage or another local James remains possible. Jean’s later marriage and the later adult identities of John and Patrick remain separately assessed. Patrick’s proposed Kilclone son and migration, James’s own John Glasgow-1084 ancestry and the unrelated Kilwaughter James are not strengthened. No original register image was newly inspected: this review combines the previously accepted index entries and maintained citations.

The unchanged paternal working branch below James contains 43 pre-1850 retained profile accounts. This count includes uncertain later identities and the speculative Gordon–Kilclone join; it is not 43 proved descendants. The 1666 John account lacked Agnes as a mother; the local tree now adds her as probable, extending the same assessed household across all six children. The other five maternal attachments are retained and explicitly graded. One saved maternal flag was already confident, but the reviewed source does not name a mother: the local assessment is probable and the saved flag remains separately visible. Three father flags were already confident and are confirmations, not new certainty upgrades. Date/place conflicts are preserved for source checking: John’s structured Duns location versus the cited Gordon baptism; Patrick’s 8 April field versus the 4 August index; Robert’s 4 January field versus the 1 April index. No birth date, place, father attachment, spouse, merge or live WikiTree flag changes. The named-parent conclusion must not silently certify those conflicting vital fields or any later migration.

chapters.period: 1722 · documented Scottish parents; American identity unproved
chapters.title: Libberton 1722: John’s recorded parents are documented
body: The accepted Findmypast transcript for John Glasgow’s Libberton baptism on 23 September 1722 explicitly names father Robert Glasgow and mother Katherin Wilson, with residence Sandyburgh: OPR 650/1, page 17, item 3, SCOT/OPR/BAP/4033399. The existing John profile is already assigned to this exact record by the completed person-level audit. Robert Glasgow-3407 is the maintained Wilson-household father account and Katherine Wilson-127539 its mother account. Both recorded parent roles should therefore be documented locally, rather than left as unassessed tree fields. These are two explicit parental names in one baptism transcript, not a mother inferred from a husband’s surname. The existing Carnwath 1713 Robert–Katherine Wilson marriage citation is compatible household context; it is not needed to invent the 1722 parents or to treat every local Robert as the same man.

The documented assessment applies to the Scottish child and parents in the 1722 baptism. The later American identity attributed to John—Nottingham, Chester County, and a May 1769 death—remains unproved. The profile’s Bible and burial citations have not supplied an inspected migration, household or parent bridge from Libberton. No American newspaper attribution is reinstated. This does not establish that the American John had these parents. The source supplies a baptism date, not an independently proved birth date. Katherin in Findmypast and Katharin in the retained MyHeritage index are provider spelling variants of the record’s Wilson mother, not two independent maternal confirmations. This review reuses the captured transcript of 3 September 2026; no fresh register-image inspection is claimed.

The existing working branch below John contains 14 retained pre-1850 profile accounts. That is a measure of the current topology and includes the unresolved Scottish-to-American identity; the baptism does not prove the entire descendant chain. No person, parent attachment, identity merge, spouse or changed vital field is added. Robert’s own selected James Glasgow-3332 father, his competing Johne route and his birth estimate remain uncertain. The separate Gibson/Watson Robert family remains separate; neither woman is equated with Wilson. Local record-parent assessments and reciprocal child descriptions are synchronized in both viewers. The raw WikiTree parent fields and saved certainty flags remain unchanged. Any live certainty change requires resolving its profile-identity scope; the prepared amendment adds the baptism evidence and that limit. Working connectivity is unchanged. The supported and confident paternal measures gain the existing Scottish father edge only; this is classification of previously ungraded record parentage, not a new ancestor or a proved American connection.

chapters.title: Kilwaughter: James’s 1669–1726 continuity is probable
body: The preferred identification is one James Glasgow from the Kilwaughter Demesne hearth household of 1669 to the Kilwaughter overseer of probably 29 May 1701 and the later elder marked deceased in 1726. Assess that continuity as probable rather than unresolved. The hearth roll places Jo and James Glascho consecutively in the same demesne, records 5347–5348. The later congregational extracts again contain both names acting for Kilwaughter: John senior in 1700 and an unmarked John in 1700/01, whose individual identity remains open, and James as overseer in probably 1701. John’s already-probable continuity supplies a coherent parallel ageing household, rather than leaving James’s later occurrence as an isolated name match. James’s later elder, 1722 commissioner and 1727 Kilwater probate-index accounts were already assessed as probably one man. The repeated local pairing, the particular district served and an ordinary adult generation in 1700/01 together favour continuity over an otherwise unattested replacement James. The preference uses the combined local sequence; no literal same-man clause is required.

The inference is not documented identity. The later men never occur together in the same reviewed minute, the 1669 roll does not state a kin relationship, and similar spellings are not independent identifiers. Kilwaughter Demesne and the later Kilwaughter district are compatible but not identical address statements. A father-and-son succession or another local James remains possible. Assuming an adult aged at least 21 in 1669 would make James at least about 74 in 1722 and 78 in 1726; those are conditional age calculations, not recorded ages or a new birth bound. His local commission in 1722 is compatible with advanced age, but the long career is the strongest reason for caution. No age at death, occupation, holding or named relative equates the occurrences. The missing 1701–1721 session sequence leaves a real gap. Porter’s 1699–1701 extracts are a printed transcription of a manuscript copy; the later extracts and lost probate index do not independently prove the earlier identity. The probable grade is an overall inference across the groups, not the product of independent probabilities. Neither the 1726 death annotation nor the 1727 probate is newly assigned to a separate earlier James; they remain events of the later elder whose identification with the 1669 man is now probable.

This strengthens the identity at the head of James’s existing 104-profile pre-1850 working branch. The number describes retained profile accounts, including uncertain descendants and unresolved identities. John’s 1669-to-1700 identity was already probable and is not counted as a new upgrade. Exact kinship between John and James remains possible: brother, father and son, uncle and nephew or cousin are not distinguished. Glasgow-3970 of Larne remains their uncertain proposed father. The Scottish Robert and James comparisons, the later South Side family represented by Glasgow-1502 and all mothers retain their separate assessments. No father or mother is regraded, no profile is merged, and no birth, death or place field is changed. Working, supported and confidently marked paternal connectivity are unchanged. This is a re-evaluation of the maintained source readings, not a newly found record or fresh original inspection. Nothing is saved to live WikiTree.

chapters.title: Hugh’s 137-profile branch: prefer the local Corsankell family
body: Prefer John Glasgow-3193 of the Corsankell/Kilwinning family as Hugh Glasgow-1603’s uncertain working father. This materializes the leading Ayrshire placement already argued in the maintained five-generation map. The 1571 Corsinkell deed expressly names John as James elder’s son; the earlier Kilwinning tenant appearances are attributed to him as probable. Hugh’s surviving profile account describes an Ayrshire progenitor, his son’s account is centred on Kilwinning, and the following households lie in Kilwinning, Ayr and Kilbirnie. These successive local settings favour the documented nearby family over the existing Mid Calder/Inveresk father attachment, which depends on an online tree and has no movement, household or property bridge. A John-to-Hugh-to-John sequence is compatible supporting context, not a naming rule. Father is selected as a revisable one-generation model, rather than leaving the previously preferred local route only in prose.

Hugh remains a tree-derived generation: no inspected contemporary record securely identifies him, names his father or establishes his own c.1600 birth. John’s before-1540 boundary means a birth for Hugh near 1600 would make him an older father, around 60 or more; a grandson or collateral position may fit better. Neither date is changed to fit. An earlier Hugh birth is possible but is not adopted as a new estimate, and no missing person is invented. The 1571 John is documented as a son, while his additional Kilwinning identity is only probable. John’s brother James Glasgow-3921, another local Glasgow family, an omitted generation and the former James Glasgow-991 placement remain alternatives. This is stronger locality reasoning, not a probable or proved father assessment. The 1677 deed-index Hugh, preacher of the gospel, remains an unresolved identity comparison and supplies no evidence for this father choice.

The existing 137-profile pre-1850 working child side is rerouted from James of Mid Calder to John of Corsankell; descendants retain every earlier identity and relationship qualification. No mother, spouse, merge, new person or changed vital field is selected. Hugh-to-John-1604 and the minister’s separate father and duplicate questions are unchanged. Shared Y-DNA can motivate the extended-family model but cannot identify this father. Both proposed fathers already belong to the same working component: cohort membership, working component and pair coverage, supported connectivity and confidently marked connectivity remain unchanged. This is a better-supported placement within the working tree, not a newly connected component or confidence upgrade. No new source inspection or live WikiTree save is claimed.

The earlier Murieston father-review impact was 216 profiles below James. Rerouting Hugh’s 137-profile branch leaves 79 below James in the current pre-1850 working model; these are dated profile-impact counts, not changes in population or proofs of descent.

chapters.title: Murieston: a probable George father for James’s large branch
body: Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule.

The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William.

The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

James’s former selected Andrew father becomes an uncertain alternative; George of Mureistoun becomes the preferred probable father. A separately uncertain William upstream link keeps the family model inspectable. The record-only George uses the existing complete sourced public subject account and is not a new WikiTree profile or an independently counted extra surname person. The 216-profile pre-1850 child side below James retains all its downstream uncertainty and possible duplicates. The working cohort’s connected components and connected pairs do not improve merely because this named intermediary is displayed. No live WikiTree save, new original inspection, mother, birth/death change or certainty upgrade is claimed.

chapters.title: Killybegs James: a tax balance and a working Donegal father
body: The inspected printed return identifies James Glasgow under Killybegs, opposite the year 1728, with a balance of £34 5s 6d. Its full heading is an account of deceased and dismissed tax collectors’ balances in Ireland as at 5 January 1826, under Land and Assessed Taxes. The entry is therefore retrospective. It is not a customs-collector appointment, an assertion that James lived in 1826, or a recorded birth or death in 1728. The precise meaning of the unlabelled year column is not stated on the inspected pages. Printed p.198 supplies the return heading and p.201 the James entry; Internet Archive leaves 216 and 219 were visually checked on 17 October 2026. The item’s inconsistent catalogue date is not used as the document’s date.

Select Thomas Glasgow-3556 of Lifford/Raphoe as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3001. Thomas is an established Donegal legal/property actor from the 1684 Raphoe-linked court occurrence through the 1692–1695 Shannon/Ballindrait deeds and the 1701 Exchequer continuation. James belongs to a later dated Donegal account under 1728. The same uncommon surname, regional continuity and compatible succession of legal/property and revenue roles make Thomas a useful preferred existing father account. This extends the recorded Ramelton–Lifford family into the otherwise unattached collector account without inventing an intermediary. It is a regional and generational inference: none of these records names James as Thomas’s son.

The record dates are not measured ages. The 1728 entry may carry an earlier deceased or dismissed officer’s balance, so it cannot select a generation precisely. Archibald Glasgow-1101, Thomas’s probable father, remains a concrete older-family alternative: James might be Thomas’s younger brother or another kinsman rather than his son. An unrelated Donegal or wider Ulster Glasgow family remains possible. The Tyrone James Glasgow-1025 and Belfast Captain James Glasgow-3172 are not merged with this collector or excluded solely by their unproved birth estimates and parent fields. No Scottish-to-Irish migration, exact age, mother, spouse or child of James is inferred. Thomas’s existing probable Archibald father and his other children keep their separate assessments.

Replace the unsupported circa-1650 birth display with Unknown. Use 1728 only as the retrospective account-reference year for research grouping, with birth year unknown. The unlabelled year column does not supply an age or a firm birth boundary; birth could have been substantially earlier. Scotland remains an inherited uncertain birthplace claim; no Irish birthplace is substituted. This correction is independent of the proposed father: the same chronology applies if Thomas is rejected. The old circa-1650 value remains in the imported/current-profile comparison, and all live WikiTree fields are unchanged.

One uncertain local father is newly selected; no confidence upgrade or documentary parentage is claimed. The new link joins the collector’s one-profile component to the existing working family before 1850. Removing the unsupported 1650 chronology changes membership of the current pre-1650/pre-1700 cohorts; that denominator correction is not a family connection. The immutable baseline and separately reported fixed-cohort results are preserved. No mother or identity merge is added.

chapters.title: Glasgow to Donegal: Archibald’s parents, wife and eldest son
body: Prefer the Glasgow child baptised on 19 June 1614 and the Archibaldus Glasgua who graduated M.A. in 1635 as the earlier identity of the Donegal cleric. The uncommon full name, compatible age at graduation, clerical career and 1639 Irish clerk occurrence form a coherent Scottish-to-Irish career. A baptism in 1614 places him at about 21 in 1635 and 25 in 1639. These are conditional ages, not separately recorded ages. No incompatible parentage or simultaneous Scottish household is identified for this proposed cleric. The other known same-generation Scottish Archibald, the Leith man Glasgow-3078, has a separately traced craft career: apprentice to cordiner Thomas Park in October 1639 and shoemaker/heir in May 1647. That positive career sequence makes him a weaker fit to the 1635 graduate and Irish clerk than the 1614 Glasgow child. It is a ranking argument, not an absolute exclusion or an assertion that a man could never change occupation. The Irish testator is securely the Ramelton/Rathmalton cleric by exact name, residence and profession. Assess his existing George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart parent links as probable, reflecting the probable Scottish childhood identification. The baptism explicitly names both parents, so maternity has its own record basis rather than being inferred from George’s spouse field.

No Irish record reviewed names Archibald’s Scottish parents or university. The graduation and 1639 clerk entry do not themselves state the 1614 baptism date. Another Archibald remains possible. This is a preferred combined identity, not documented migration or proof that every early Scottish and Irish occurrence is one man. The quoted baptism witnesses are reused from the maintained reading, not newly checked against an image. Margaret’s own Stewart ancestry, George’s wider family, and the 1647–1661 ministry chronology retain their existing grades.

Betham’s inspected abstract of the April 1673 will of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton, explicitly identifies Thomas Glasgow as his eldest son. Prefer the existing Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe account for that son: the exact uncommon name, the adjacent Donegal setting and the next adult generation fit the independently documented Raphoe-linked court case of 1684, Lifford occurrence of 1689 and Ballindrait/Shannon deeds of 1692–1695. The 1692 Creighton court association and later estate material strengthen the continuity of that adult Thomas account; they are not independent statements of his parentage. The full local and generational fit warrants a probable father link to Archibald. A further unique estate or household identifier would strengthen it, but its absence does not require leaving this coherent family at merely uncertain.

Betham gives the son no age, residence, spouse or estate. He could be another Thomas, so the Lifford identification remains inferred rather than documented. The profile’s before-1671/circa-1670 birth estimates are not ages supplied by the abstract or court records and are not used as proof of either identity or exclusion. No maternity is assigned to Thomas from Elizabeth’s status as Archibald’s wife. Nathaniel and George remain Thomas’s separately assessed children; the later Killybegs James and Belfast Captain James are not made relatives by this review.

Betham’s inspected pre-destruction abstract explicitly identifies Elizabeth as wife of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton. The existing Elizabeth account represents that record-defined wife, while Archibald’s Irish identity is secured by exact name, clerical designation and residence. The spouse relationship is documented independently of the probable Scottish baptism and Thomas-to-Lifford identifications. The provisionally read M’Auley surname is retained as a reading, not installed as a certain surname.

The abstract is not the complete will; April 1673 is the will date and 1677 the separate probate index date. It does not establish a wedding date, Elizabeth’s birth or parents, or her maternity of every named child. Her existing profile name and estimates are preserved.

Four existing assessments change: two probable Scottish parent links for Archibald, a probable Archibald–Thomas father link, and a documented Archibald–Elizabeth marriage. This is a confidence review of existing attachments, not four new relatives. No live WikiTree save, identity merge, new mother for Thomas or new manuscript inspection is claimed. chapters.title: Fisherrow: two linked couples and the Inveresk children
body: Prefer the existing [James Glasgow](/people/glasgow-991.html) and [Christina Bie](/people/bie-55.html) family account for the Fisherrow James and Christina Bye. The printed 1624–1625 index explicitly groups James, tailor in Fisherrow and burgess of Musselburgh, his son Alexander and wife Christina Bye; it separately names Alexander’s wife Janet Clerk. Those are the same named family roles already represented by these profiles. The local James account also includes the Inveresk father sequence of 1609–1618, which can continue into the Fisherrow household. The ordinary Bye/Bie spelling and the full family fit make the identification probable, rather than a match resting only on James’s forename. This is an assessment of the preferred existing family account, not independent confirmation from its copied tree fields.

The printed sasine index places Janet Clerk with Alexander, while Christina Bye belongs with his father James. The 1637 Inveresk entry explicitly names Alexander Glasgow and Jannet Clerk as parents of their indexed son. The matching named couple and compatible 1624–1637 parish/property sequence document Alexander and Janet’s spouse relationship; no marriage ceremony date is supplied.

The Inveresk entries name Alexander Glasgow as father of Marioune in 1630, Johnne in 1632 and Bessie in 1635. They fall within the 1626–1637 series already represented by the Fisherrow Alexander’s family. The 1624–1625 sasines identify his wife Janet Clerk, and the 1637 child entry repeats that parental pair. The repeated father, parish, ordered child series and independently named couple strongly support this Alexander as the father in all three entries. This is confident family reconstruction from the combined records, not an assertion that each earlier entry names his occupation or wife.

The Mid Calder and Inveresk baptism sequences may still represent one mobile father or two contemporaries; no occupation or property recital joins them. The profile’s birth and death places remain inherited claims. The signed-in FamilySearch record VQ4V-K87 was inspected on 17 October 2026: it names William, father James and the 10 July 1614 Inveresk event, but no mother. It therefore supplies no independent evidence for Christina Bie’s maternity, consistent with the FMP and supplied ScotlandsPeople entries. The earlier citation-based claim that this record named her is withdrawn; the underlying parish image remains uninspected. Christina’s 1589 New Aberdour birth is tree-derived. Naming her as James’s wife in 1624 does not establish her as Alexander’s or William’s mother. The Andrew-3163 and Murieston-George ancestry alternatives retain their grades.

No mother is named in the three reviewed child entries, so their maternal grades stay unchanged. Bessie’s 22 March index date and existing 20 March birth field remain unreconciled; no date is changed. The later identities of these children, James-3923 versus the Edinburgh weaver James-1150, and the Edward property associations remain separate. Existing confident father settings for James-3923, Robert-1149 and Allexander-1152 are retained, not counted as new upgrades. Original sasines and parish images were not newly inspected.

Six existing assessments are strengthened: Alexander’s father and James’s Christina spouse identity become probable; Alexander and Janet’s marriage is documented; three previously ungraded fathers become strongly supported. The four paternal grade changes enter the probable-or-stronger graph, three of them the confident graph. No person, parent ID, maternal grade, date, selected working parent or live certainty flag changes. The existing pre-1850 child side below Alexander contains 24 profile accounts; downstream uncertainty remains explicit.

20October2026: Prefer the recorded George of Mureistoun as Edward Glasgow-1557’s uncertain working father at 26%, replacing the 18% Corsankell James selection. The preferred reconstruction makes Edward and James Glasgow-991 brothers. The 1624 Fisherrow index places Edward at the same RS25 9/135 reference as James the tailor and his son Alexander. Edward-1557 is the preferred 1624 identity at 56%; both Edward and the James family have Inveresk children in 1609, and James’s child Eduard supplies a compatible naming echo. A close local family explains this combined association better than the present unsupported Ayrshire-origin route. George is an already recorded older local candidate and James’s selected probable father at 82%; he is not an invented common ancestor. Brothers are the preferred degree for the two contemporary fathers, rather than a proved relationship. The 26% is an exact subjective assessment of the complete father-and-identity proposition, not a measured probability. Edward’s identity in 1624, James’s Mid Calder–Fisherrow identity, their precise degree of kinship and George’s paternity all remain open. The index gives Edward no capacity or kin clause; shared folio, local births and naming are correlated clues, not independent proofs. Cousins, uncle/nephew, an older Edward as James’s father, and another local father remain alternatives. Eduard-994 and Edward-1558 survive as the indexed Edward. The circa 1570/1575 birth years are estimates; if George is the merchant born 1565–1572, fatherhood requires later births for Edward and James, not those conventional estimates. No dates are changed to force that route. George’s own William-3522 father 26% and possible merchant identity are unchanged. Margaret Smith remains the separately uncertain imported mother; she is not selected as George’s spouse. No biological exclusion of Corsankell James or new Scottish–American proof is claimed.

Findmypast SCOT/OPR/BUR/0189706 reports James Glasgow, writer, died11 October 1716 and buried14 October 1716, aged87; OPR685_1/86, item2, p.318, Edinburgh. Its 1629 birth year is calculated from age, not a recorded birth. Prefer this as a possible later identity of the Inveresk child James-3923 at 45%: the uncommon name, Midlothian setting and a three-year difference from the 1626 baptism make a useful comparison. No occupation is otherwise established for that child. This remains below probable: there is no parent, spouse, residence or career bridge, and another unrepresented James is a substantial possibility. James-1150 is the separately recorded Edinburgh weaver, son of Robert of Wester Duddingston; James-3332 is the unresolved Biggar/Quothquan/Lindsaylands weaver comparison. Their different occupations and age estimates weaken these matches without excluding them. Findmypast’s suggested records are automated leads, not corroboration. chapters.title: Kirknewton and Kilwinning: firmer parent links
body: Alexander’s 1673 Kirknewton birth/baptism index explicitly names father Alexander Glasgow. The existing Alexander-3118 account is the same-parish man indexed marrying Margaret Smith in 1667, six years earlier, with a compatible father generation and a later Agnes child association in 1677. The exact father name, parish and ordered household chronology together favour that existing adult as the named father. Assess the attachment as probable rather than leaving it ungraded. This is an inference identifying the indexed father with the 1667 adult; the child entry alone does not identify that adult by wife, trade or property.

Another Alexander could have fathered the 1673 child. The marriage and baptism supply no inspected cross-reference, and the father’s circa-1650 birth is an estimate, not an age statement. Margaret Smith is not named as mother in the reviewed 1673 entry and receives no maternity upgrade. Andrew-1546 remains an uncertain proposed son of the older Alexander. Alexander-1141 remains an unproved child of the 1673 Alexander; the latter himself remains a possible older father behind the 1721–1732 child series. The 1673 birth/baptism dates, the 1701 and 1705 marriages and the later children’s maternity questions are retained. The older John-3610 father route is not strengthened.

The accepted Kilwinning parish transcripts name Robert Glasgow and Mary Simson as the parents of Hugh in 1716, George in 1719 and Jean in 1722. The existing 1715 Kilwinning marriage index names Robert Glasgow and Mary Simpson; ordinary Simson/Simpson spelling variation, the repeated parental pair and the ordered 1715–1722 family sequence identify one record-defined household. George and Jean also share Byrehill residence. These records document both parents for each indexed child, not merely a spouse inferred as mother. The three child profiles already represent those checked entries, so their father and mother assessments can be marked documented.

These are previously accepted derivative register transcripts and indexes; no fresh original image reading or new record discovery is claimed. The three transcripts derive from one parish register and are not independent sources. Hugh’s transcript has no residence field; Byrehill is not newly assigned to him. The FMP page references and the separately retained ScotlandsPeople references remain literal provider locators. This household proof does not newly identify the adult Robert with the 1678 child, prove ancestry above either parent, or identify any child with a later adult. George’s merchant, Manchester inventor and artillery comparisons remain separate; James-1120 and the later Covington family do not receive a new parentage grade. No date, birthplace, spouse, occupation, live parent field or saved certainty flag changes.

Seven existing local assessments are strengthened: one probable Kirknewton father and six documented Kilwinning parent roles. Four paternal grades enter the probable-or-stronger calculation, of which three enter the confidently marked calculation; mothers do not join paternal surname components. The Kirknewton child side has 33 pre-1850 profile accounts and George’s has 21, but those downstream uncertain links are not upgraded by these parent records. Existing selected working parents, the fixed cohort and all other grades remain unchanged.

The size review still leaves the largest earlier joins uncertain: Stirling John to the provisional Saltmarket John (1,034 profiles on the child side), Stephen to the combined Montfoid/Mid Calder/Quothquan John (316), and John-1093 to Andrew of Corsoun (300). Their existing identity or kinship gaps remain. These overlapping sizes are not additive and cannot justify a higher evidence grade. The parish household upgrades above use named-parent records; they do not certify those older routes.

Household reconciliation,21 October2026. The live Open/non-living profile checked on 21 October 2026 has numeric Father 44215058, Alexander Glasgow-3118, while its biography still links Alexander Glasgow-1152. This is a stale prose reference, not two competing current Father fields. Correct the proposed biography to Glasgow-3118 and state the probable assessment; do not add a new father or merge the Alexander accounts. Agnes’s 28 February 1677 Kirknewton/East Calder index names father Alexander Glasgow. The same-parish Alexander married Margaret Smith on 18 October 1667; Alexander’s 1673 child entry and Agnes’s 1677 entry name the same father four years apart. This favours one local household and extends the existing probable father identification across the two children. Assess Alexander Glasgow-3118 as Agnes’s probable father at 83% subjective confidence. The ten-year marriage-to-Agnes interval leaves somewhat more room for a second household than the six-year interval for Alexander-1314, whose existing 85% is unchanged. Do not treat the stale Glasgow-1152 link as independent evidence that the adults are one man. The 1665 Edinburgh Alexander/Issobell Anderson marriage belongs to the maintained Glasgow-1152 couple. Marie’s 11 October 1674 St Cuthbert’s baptism transcript explicitly names Alexander Glasgow and Issobell Andersone, after the 1667 Kirknewton Margaret Smith marriage and between the 1673 and 1677 Kirknewton children. A simple first-wife-died/remarriage account therefore has an unexplained overlap. The dates are baptism/index dates, so delayed baptism or a more complicated family history cannot be excluded. Prefer separate household accounts pending a record explaining the overlap; no categorical identity exclusion or merge is made. The parish index supplies no mother, occupation, precise residence or explicit link to the 1667 groom. Another Alexander remains possible. The children’s existing tree sibling link is not independent corroboration. The saved confident father flag is retained as capture provenance, not adopted as an independently verified grade. Margaret Smith’s maternity remains unproved and is not upgraded or transferred to another child. No birth/death date, parent identity, sibling topology or upstream father changes. This replaces one inherited confident mark with an explicit probable assessment. It joins no new paternal component and does not increase confident connectivity.

body: Reviewed 23 October 2026: existing father confidence 86% probable→91% confident inference; no new father or original parent record.

The 1641 apprenticeship expressly names Robert as James’s father and supplies the Wester Duddingston association. The 1649 burgess entry repeats William Sclaitter and the exact 16 June 1641 apprenticeship date, securely identifying that son as the Edinburgh weaver James-1150. The indexed Robert Glasgow burial in the same parish on 17 January 1647 is a coherent match to that father six years later. No positively evidenced competing Duddingston Robert has emerged from the held family comparisons. Robert-1027 is a Glasgow cordiner with proved parents but no held Duddingston connection; Robert-4006 is a possible earlier identity of this adult, not evidence of a second local father. Together these positive identity and locality links warrant 91% confident inference rather than retaining a probable ceiling solely for an unattested namesake possibility.

The father’s identification with the burial account remains inferred, not a direct statement joining those records. The burial index supplies no age, occupation, wife, child or precise residence; parish burial alone does not prove residence at Wester Duddingston. The burgess entry corroborates James’s identity, not an independent father statement. The placement of “servitor” in the printed apprenticeship remains ambiguous. No numerical surname-rarity claim is made. A different local Robert remains possible, and the original burial is still uninspected.

This regrades the existing James-1150 to Robert-1156 pair only, from 86% probable to 91% confident inference. It names no new father. The Duffe adult identification remains 70% and James-2682’s conditional Robert father remains 61%; these subjective nested assessments are not recalculated by multiplication. chapters.title: Saltmarket John is William’s probable father
body: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research.

The missing 1527–1529 conveyance has not been found. No inspected instrument calls William the earlier John’s son, and no recorded ages distinguish father from brother. A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

This is a re-evaluation of an existing father attachment, not a new parent or a newly discovered record. The earlier generic uncertain assessment and its 28 September basis are retained in the structured history. All working family membership and confidently marked paternal connectivity remain unchanged. The printed 1528/29 boundary on p.90 and four-shilling rental on p.36 were freshly inspected; the other title steps retain their earlier maintained source reviews. The original manuscript transfer remains uninspected. Review priorities now rank every non-confident paternal link, including older tree attachments, rather than only the 57 selected working hypotheses.

Priority scope corrected: the review now includes older non-confident tree attachments as well as explicitly selected working hypotheses. Dependency counts concern retained profiles through 1850; nested links overlap and these figures must not be summed.

Early priority: Glasgow-3296 → Glasgow-1029; 316 measured profiles on the child’s side and 719 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain, 22%. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

Early priority: Glasgow-3610 → Glasgow-3296; 278 measured profiles on the child’s side and 757 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain, 28%; the secure adult occurrence is the 1649 father entry, not a proved 1646–1650 baptism sequence. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

Early priority: Glasgow-3163 → Glasgow-1093; 236 measured profiles on the child’s side and 799 on the other side. The current grade is uncertain, 25%. These counts set research priority, not evidential confidence.

William’s captured profile leaves birth date, birthplace and death place blank, and the maintained findings already reject the local 1516 birth and High Street death-place claims. No inspected birth record supplies 1516. The local catalogue and both tree views now show these fields as Unknown, with the older import retained for comparison. No replacement birth year or place is invented. His first dated occurrence used for the local chronology is the 20 February 1528/29 boundary in the matched property-title sequence (normalized year 1529); the 1526 remission remains a separately qualified identity. This is a display/chronology correction, not evidence for his father.

Individual father assessments, reviewed 17 October 2026: William Glasgow-1098 remains the probable father of [Robert, the Glasgow burgess and fisher](/people/glasgow-1096.html), at 74%; [Archibald, the 1551 purchaser with Isobell Neulands](/people/glasgow-1097.html), at 68%; and [Isobella, wife of Archibald Herbisoune](/people/glasgow-3916.html), at 79%. These replace the undifferentiated public strongly-supported/confident band with individual probable assessments, preserving the earlier narrative arguments. They are reviews of attached parents, not new fathers or live certainty upgrades. Each mother remains independently assessed.

Robert’s repeated fisher and property associations support a close family, but the Bridgegait John may be John senior, his adult son or Robert’s own son. Archibald bought his 1551 parcel from Elizabeth Beith; that act records neither inheritance from William nor a later transfer to John. Isobella’s husband witnessed John senior’s disposal of the fore tenement inherited from William nineteen days earlier, a closer association with the identified heir. Even there, Isobella’s estimated generation leaves John senior as a possible father and William as a possible grandfather. Repeated boundaries are correlated evidence, not repeated father clauses; collateral family and trusted craft associations remain alternatives.

The older Saltmarket John-to-William hypothesis remains 88%, and the directly recorded William-to-John-1093 relationship remains 99%. The Robert 74% assessment does not also identify the Kilbride man or Carnwath litigant; Archibald’s later Lothian records do not prove his parentage; Isobella’s 79% does not estimate her mother or equate distinct 1563 and 1575 parcels.

chapters.title: Murieston: George’s 1586–1605 identity is probable
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

The witness’s own residence is unstated, and another George in the district remains possible. The residence reading Muirestoun and its identification as Murieston remain probable. Shared spelling and locality are related observations; McCall repeats Maidment’s 1586 act and is not a second muster occurrence. Naming the child George is supporting context, not proof of a naming rule. The 1586 act records an obligation, not attendance. Neither source gives George’s age or states a relationship to James. Father, uncle, brother, other kinsman and neighbour remain alternatives. No father is changed: Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains James’s selected uncertain father, while George is an important competing paternal or collateral explanation. George Glasgow-1099, the merchant, remains compatible but unselected; the 1586 minor’s curatorship and the 1598 marriage contract do not identify him at Murieston. No mother, birth date, identity merge or confidently marked paternal edge is added.

This improves a specific identity assessment within the 216-profile James branch, rather than raising Andrew’s father grade. The earlier possible assessment is retained as history. The working tree, confident paternal graph and fixed cohort are unchanged. The underlying 1605 register page was freshly inspected for this review; the 1586 printed-page verification from 15 October is retained, and the court manuscript remains unread.

chapters.title: Confidence review of the six largest working joins
body: The six highest-impact selected father hypotheses were re-evaluated using their actual source wording and identity assumptions. None has sufficient evidence for an overall certainty upgrade from this review. One existing, previously ungraded named-parent relationship inside the largest branch is newly marked documented locally; no new connection or working family is added. The live WikiTree certainty flag is unchanged and remains a pending amendment. Working and confidently marked connectivity are measured separately.

The existing father relationship from Glasgow-3012 to Glasgow-3610 is now documented locally for the record-defined 1649 child. The supplied Scotland’s People index, Kirknewton and East Calder OPR 690/10/14, FR 15, names JOHNE GLASGOW as parent of the child JOHNE indexed on 22 April 1649. The preserved FamilySearch VQ4K-X6G account agrees on the child, father, parish and date. These are two presentations of the same underlying register, not independent records. Glasgow-3610 is specifically the adult-father account defined by that entry. No inference from age or surname is needed for that parental role.

Earlier argument retained, superseded for the father selection on 18 October: This certainty applies to the child and father in the 1649 record. It does not prove that the child became the 1673 Margaret Currie husband or that the father was the 1608 Mid Calder child, nor does it identify his own parents. The selected Glasgow-3610→Glasgow-3296 link remains uncertain. The profile’s 4 April 1649 birth and the index’s 22 April date remain unreconciled; neither the birth date nor the birth/baptism distinction is changed. The mother is not named in this index. The original register was not newly inspected; the confidence assessment rests on the maintained named-parent index evidence, with those limits explicit. Current selection: James-991, possible40%; John-3296 remains alternative28%. See the current Easter Newtoun working-ancestry comparison.

Earlier argument retained, superseded for the father selection on 18 October: The 278-profile John branch: Glasgow-3610 → Glasgow-3296 remains uncertain at 28%. The earlier measured child-side and other-side counts were 278 and 757 (210,446 dependent connected pairs); these express research priority, not confidence. A child baptised at Mid Calder on 26 June 1608 could be the father named at neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder on 22 April 1649, aged about 40–41. No record equates them. The older Mid Calder father’s identification with the Quothquan testator is also unresolved. Margaret’s 1646/1649 readings conflict, and Alexander-3118’s circa-1650 birth was estimated from his 1667 marriage; neither supplies a proved 1646–1650 baptism sequence. The 1616 child of James-991 is a substantive adult-identity alternative, through the 1642 Porteous marriage, 1643 Edinburgh child and 1652 Kirknewton child, now supported by a supplied index and inspected transcript; the matching Easter Newtoun residence links its father to the 1649 household, without proving the Porteous mother or the 1616 identity. Keep James-991 an unselected, conditional father alternative without a percentage. Re-reading the 1649 father clause alone cannot settle either childhood or grandparent identity. Current selection: James-991, possible40%; John-3296 remains alternative28%. See the current Easter Newtoun working-ancestry comparison.

The 216-profile James branch: Glasgow-991 → Glasgow-3163. Removing this edge separates 216 measured profiles from 819 others (176,904 connected pairs depend on it). Andrew’s 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel; it does not name James. James’s 1605 Murieston household gives no parent clause. Calder locality and age compatibility support a working model, but do not identify Andrew as his father. Retain possible; land succession and the older George witness are the concrete tests. Do not restore the superseded claim that James was named in Andrew’s will.

The 148-profile William branch: Glasgow-1026 → Glasgow-3610. Removing this edge separates 148 measured profiles from 887 others (131,276 connected pairs depend on it). The 1682 William household is in Kirknewton, but no cited record names the 1649 father John as William’s parent. William’s circa 1660 birth is an estimate, and the distinct 1671 William child belongs to Andro. Retain possible; examine the 1682 household’s witnesses and any marriage, testament or sasine naming the older William’s father. No birth estimate can supply this missing parent clause.

The 132-profile Larne branch: Glasgow-3970 → Glasgow-1027. Removing this edge separates 132 measured profiles from 903 others (119,196 connected pairs depend on it). The 1618 Glasgow baptism names Robert and Jonet Cunningham as parents of a child Robert. The 1653 Larne examination names an adult Robert Glaskow without age, birthplace or parent. No identifying Scottish–Irish bridge joins the two. Retain possible; a migration, trade, kinship or property identifier is required. The baptism’s direct parentage is not proof of the Larne adult’s identity.

The 52-profile Kilbirnie minister branch: Glasgow-1073 → Glasgow-1604. Removing this edge separates 52 measured profiles from 983 others (51,116 connected pairs depend on it). The Fasti and university entries establish the minister’s career and approximate generation, but name no parent. Glasgow-1604’s own generation and Ayrshire pedigree are tree-derived. Retain low confidence; seek an original admission, ordination, marriage contract or family property record naming the minister’s father. Locality and an inferred birth year cannot raise the whole link’s grade.

The 48-profile Polwarth–Cavers–Ulster branch: Glasgow-591 → Glasgow-2462. Removing this edge separates 48 measured profiles from 987 others (47,376 connected pairs depend on it). The 1658 Polwarth index names a father William. Identifying that adult with the 1639 Inveresk child requires young fatherhood and an unproved move. Equating the Polwarth child, Cavers Covenanter and later Irish ancestor adds further identity steps; late survivor histories do not independently prove the Irish pedigree. Retain very low confidence. First resolve the named Polwarth father and the Scottish adult before using the later Irish tradition.

chapters.title: West Calder: a possible Kirknewton childhood for John
body: Glasgow-3526 is selected as the uncertain working father of Glasgow-2847, husband of Margaret Anderson and father of the West Calder children recorded from 1745 to 1755. The route provisionally identifies that adult with Glasgow-3525, indexed at neighbouring Kirknewton and East Calder on 31 March 1717 with father James. The parish setting, exact forename and surname, and feasible generation favour this concrete local childhood over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1717, John would have been about 28 in 1745 and 38 in 1755. The later family also contains a James, although a common repeated forename does not independently establish a grandfather. No register entry yet joins the child to Margaret Anderson’s husband. This is a low-confidence identity-based parent model, not a proved father clause for the adult.

The West Calder household is represented by Glasgow-2849 in 1745, Glasgow-2846 in 1747, Glasgow-2848 in 1750, and Glasgow-1922 in 1755, with parents John Glasgow and Margaret Anderson. The 1755 citation is West Calder OPR 701,10/202, FR 142; the other retained citations are parish indexes. No original register image has been newly inspected. The present circa-1730 birth and the former biography’s before-1739 wording are unsupported estimates from a child’s event, not recorded ages or a childhood identification. The 1717 hypothesis requires an earlier birth than circa 1730 but does not contradict a measured date. Those structured fields remain unchanged; the hypothetical date must not be presented as a new birth fact. All four children, their mother, their dates and existing relationship grades are retained.

Glasgow-3526 is the maintained account for the James named in the 1717 record. Its own circa-1688 birth and selected uncertain Glasgow-1026 father remain prior hypotheses. The child’s earlier biography instead names Glasgow-1547. That 1702 Kirknewton childhood, son of Andrew Glasgow-1546, remains an alternative identity for the adult James. If baptised near birth in September 1702, he would have been about fourteen at the March 1717 baptism, making that route less straightforward than the older James account. An older-child baptism or an incorrect age estimate remains possible; neither is asserted as fact. The named father James is distinct from the question of which modern James account represents him. The earlier child-parent grade is not upgraded, and neither James’s ancestry receives new certainty.

A competing childhood is Glasgow-1544, recorded at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. That child has already been used as a possible identity for Glasgow-3481 of the Christian Meek household. The Meek and Anderson households have children in 1755 under different mothers, so the new model keeps those adult accounts distinct; no second household, remarriage or polygamy is invented to equate them. That does not prove the 1702 child could not instead be Margaret Anderson’s husband. The two proposed adult identities for that childhood remain alternatives. Another local John and another James father remain possible; the current shortlist is not exhaustive. The 1717 route is selected weakly because it fits an ordinary adult generation and a specific nearby record without requiring the Meek household identity.

No mother is selected for the West Calder John. The retained 1717 citation names James but supplies no mother in the existing account. Neither Ann McCook from the older William household nor Christian Cook from Glasgow-1547’s childhood is transferred into this generation. John’s new proposed father does not identify the later life of his son Glasgow-2846: that child remains separate from the Larne Rose Allan husband Glasgow-4179 unless their own identity bridge is established. Glasgow-1922’s Kirk marriage and all existing child biographies remain outside the new parent inference.

One uncertain father is newly selected through a possible child-to-adult identity. No mother, original inspection, merge, date change, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The 1717 child and later father remain separate profile accounts and may be duplicates rather than two distinct brothers. Working connectivity counts retained accounts and inherits the uncertainty in their older ancestry; the family-size gain is not identity evidence.

chapters.title: Eight early accounts still need a family connection
body: The unchanged through-1650 cohort has 162 accounts,154 in the largest working paternal family. Its eight remaining accounts are not eight documented Scottish family founders. Some are English burial entries or profiles with estimated dates. They remain visible in the measure; this review adds no edge and removes no one to improve the score.

English entries without a Scottish family bridge: Glascoe-36 is a Berwick burial account whose current citation concerns another person; Glasko-16 is a Norwich burial account without named kin; Glasgow-4063 is the Holkham death/burial account with no recorded age or relatives; Glasgow-3110 is the Flixton burial account with age but no forename or origin. Surname resemblance and an invented Scottish father would not connect their records.

Glasgow-1167 remains in the corrected Edinburgh Glassfuird slater household, with the Glasgow/Glassford index-surname problem unresolved. Glasgow-3357 has a Currie index naming Janet Glasgow but no father; her identity and the date disagreement still need resolution. An unnamed paternal generation is not supplied to make a Y-line.

Glasgow-1376 represents the unresolved Whitecastle comparison and a misread former 1657 citation, which actually concerns Marione. Glasgow-3001 is defined by a 1728 collector account, not a proved circa 1650 birth. Those inherited estimates are retained in the fixed cohort so that changes in membership cannot masquerade as new genealogy.

The next useful evidence is a named relative, residence or occupation continuity, or a supported child-to-adult identity. The hypotheses selected elsewhere in this study remain explicitly uncertain; these eight cases do not currently supply a preferred named parent.

chapters.title: Kilwinning: possible parents of Mary Auld’s husband John
body: Glasgow-1065 is selected as the uncertain working father of Glasgow-2467, the John recorded with Mary Auld at Kilwinning for Andrew’s baptism on 26 October 1746 and James’s on 19 August 1750. The later John’s existing biography already suggests descent from Glasgow-2463, an old parent reference with a 16 September 1683 Kilwinning date. The current captured family fields of the older household’s children point to Glasgow-1065, whose profile carries that same 1683 date and the Jean Wyllie household. This resolves the intended candidate account; it is not a new historical father statement. A specific route is the recorded Glasgow-2464, baptised at Kilwinning on 19 December 1703 to John Glasgow and Jean Wylie, residence Chappell. Treat that child provisionally as the later Mary Auld husband. If baptised in infancy, he would have been about 42 and 46 at the two known children’s baptisms, compatible ages for a father. The later profile’s before-1728 estimate permits this earlier birth. Exact name, parish, an already recorded descent suggestion and a documented child with named parents give a testable family model. No record yet establishes that the child and adult were the same man.

Wyllie-1044 is separately selected as the uncertain working mother through the same possible 1703-child identity. The 1703 index actually names Jean Wylie; she is not supplied merely because she is the selected father’s wife. Her existing profile also cites the 1712 Margaret and 1715 Matthew entries in the same household. The circa-1682 birth is an estimate, and the records cited here do not supply a marriage date or prove her age. Her identification as mother of the Mary Auld husband remains dependent on that adult’s identification with the 1703 child. The two parent fields therefore represent one conditional family connection, not two independent confirmations.

The existing child-record citations are Kilwinning OPR 599, 10/131 for John in 1703, 20/93 for Andrew in 1746, and 20/106 for James in 1750. The retained Findmypast transcript SCOT/OPR/BAP/3625663 names the 1703 parents and residence Chappell. No original register image has been newly inspected. The baptism does not establish an exact birthday. Glasgow-2468 and Glasgow-2469 retain their existing father and Mary Auld retains her existing spouse and maternal links; no new certainty is assigned to them. The 1703 child and later father remain separate profile accounts, possibly duplicates rather than two proved brothers. No merge is performed, and no vital field changes to 1703 follow from this model.

The older John’s profile also represents a Kilwinning baptism on 16 September 1683. If those child and later-father identities are correct, he was about twenty at the 1703 baptism. This is compatible, but not independent proof that the 1683 child became Jean Wyllie’s husband. The competing Jean Gardiner and Jonet Young mother names in the 1683 indexes remain unresolved, as do the older account’s existing ancestral qualifications. A later son of the Wyllie household, a grandson through a different child, or another local Glasgow father remains possible for Glasgow-2467. The already recorded descent suggestion does not specify a generation. The 1703-child route is selected because it provides a named child in the right parish with feasible later fatherhood, without inventing an intermediate ancestor; it is preferred only weakly.

The nearby Stevenston Glasgow-4170 and Mary Auld-2246 household, documented for Margaret in 1717 and Euphan in 1718, is an alternative family to compare, not an established identity with the Kilwinning John and Mary Auld-1724. Matching the mother’s name does not change the father’s recorded forename or prove that the women were the same person. No new half-sibling, remarriage or widowhood is asserted. Missing corroboration does not exclude either childhood or household comparison. Another Kilwinning John could have fathered Andrew and James. The present model should be tested against the original 1703, 1746 and 1750 residences, witnesses and any marriage entry.

One uncertain father and one uncertain mother are selected through one possible child-to-adult identity. No original inspection, merge, new certainty or live WikiTree edit is claimed. Existing dates, recorded family fields and the 1683 mother-name disagreement remain intact. Working connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates; it is not a count of proved distinct people or independent discoveries.
