chapters.title: Irvine’s 1693 father: a very uncertain Kilwinning childhood
body: Glasgow-3375 is the selected very uncertain working father of Glasgow-3018, treating the latter provisionally as the father named with Agnes Martine in the 1693 Irvine child entry. The route adopts the existing comparison with Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679 as child of John and Barbara Alason. Exact forename and surname, the neighbouring Ayrshire parishes, and a specific recorded child/parent pair make this a usable local model. It is not a merge or an identification of all events currently collected under either account. If the 1679 event was an infant baptism, that child would have been only fourteen by the 1693 entry. This is a serious weakness. Baptism of an older child would allow an older father, but no evidence establishes such a baptism; neither an earlier birth nor unusually young fatherhood is asserted as fact. The current circa-1675 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent support for the match.

Allison-6866 is separately selected as the very uncertain working mother through the same proposed 1679-child identity. The indexed 1679 entry actually names Barbara Alason; this is not a mother invented from the father choice or supplied from the surname-only 1689 entry. The existing Allison profile represents that Alason/Allason household and is a compatible account. Her circa-1659 birth is also an estimate, and no date, birthplace or marriage is newly established. The mother identification and the adult John identification remain unproved. These two parent links depend on one child/adult comparison; they are not independent confirmations of the proposed family.

The Irvine source is the supplied Scotland’s People OPR index: JOHN GLASGOW, 08/10/1693, parish 595, reference 10 / 12, FR23, parents JOHN GLASGOW/AGNES MARTINE. The previous review interprets this as 8 October; the structured child field instead says 10 August 1693. Both readings remain visible, and an index from a combined births/baptisms collection does not establish a birthday. Glasgow-1473 is retained as the child-record account. Identification with the John Glasgow younger active as skipper in 1720, the 1719 father of Grizal, or the later bursary recipient remains separate and uncertain. Neither the elder/younger wording nor the new grandparents prove those adult identities or an elder skipper’s paternity. Agnes Martine remains the mother named in the 1693 record; no new spouse or parent-field certainty is assigned to the child account.

The 1725 elder skipper, 1729 Sailors’ Poor Box treasurer, 1734 deceased shipmaster and 1740 living bailie are not newly equated with the 1693 father. The 1734 catalogue describes heirs of a late shipmaster, while the 1740 entry names a living merchant/bailie; those occurrences cannot be one man. Glasgow-1077 remains a compatible candidate for the later bailie, independently of this parent model; the recorded 1690 child is not adopted as the 1693 adult father. The new parent fields are scoped to the 1693 father proposition, not an assertion that the composite biography is one proved life. All later occurrences and original archive references remain available without an invented death date or transfer of records between profiles.

The same 1679 child remains only possibly identical with the Stevenston father of John in 1701 and Adam in 1706. The alleged two-John-sons conflict does not justify excluding the Irvine match when those identities and the survival of the children are unproved. No intervening death, second baptism or remarriage is invented to reconcile the accounts. The already selected West Kilbride Glasgow-3161 route also uses this childhood comparison, so it provides no independent corroboration here. The retained adult accounts may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers. An older Irvine John, another local parent, or identification of the 1693 father with the older Glasgow-3375 rather than his proposed son remain alternatives; the last option would collapse the new father edge as an identity duplicate. The older John’s possible identity with minister Glasgow-1073 and earlier ancestry keep their previous uncertainty; this is not a new proved son of the minister.

One father and one mother are selected, both very uncertain and dependent on the same 1679-child/1693-adult identity. This is one new paternal branch connection, not two independent ancestry discoveries. No original parish image, new contemporary kinship clause, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Vital fields, existing parent grades and the separate later adult identities are preserved. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates, rather than proved distinct people.

chapters.title: Carnwath Robert: a conditional Lindsaylands father
body: Select James Glasgow-3332 as the possible working father of the 1690 apprentice James Glasgow-4131, at 46% subjective confidence. The apprentice’s father is expressly named. His uncommon full name, weaving occupation, specific Lindsayland residence and death before 1690 strongly favour identification with the weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680. Glasgow-3332 is an existing compatible account already compared with that later Biggar weaver; prefer this qualified reuse to creating another same-name father. The overall 46% applies to identifying the named documentary father with that profile, including its unresolved adult identity; it does not express doubt about the explicit father–son wording. The supporting locality and trade are one combined identity argument, not independent proofs. Glasgow-3332’s independent identity is unresolved. Its estimated 1630/1634 birth and Biggar birthplace do not independently prove the 1680 match, and its inherited John-1086 parent and 1648 Johne child attachments cannot be used circularly to establish it. The alternative 1624 Quothquan-weaver identification is retained; that much earlier decedent is a poor father-generation fit for an ordinary 1690 apprenticeship, but the apprentice has no recorded age. Whitecastle James-1376 remains a compatible possible identity of the later weaver, potentially the same man as James-3332, with no merge. The Edinburgh weaver James-1150 remains a weaker comparison: identifying him with the master active in 1693 would conflict with the father being dead in 1690, but that master’s identity is itself inferred. The 1690 apprentice may still be the 1696 apprentice James-4114 after a cancelled first indenture; the different master and the father’s death must be reconciled before merging them. The 1696 father proposal stays unchanged. No mother, spouse or vital field is transferred or altered. James-3332’s 25% father and Robert-3407’s 23% father hypothesis remain unchanged; the two proposed sons are not proved brothers. This adds one selected profile connection, not a newly discovered son, independent source, or proved pedigree. [Current source account](/people/glasgow-4131.html#research-findings).

Glasgow-3332 is the selected uncertain working father of Glasgow-3407, who married Katherine Wilson at Carnwath in 1713 and is associated with son Glasgow-2870 at Libberton in 1722. This is conditional on James representing the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The adjacent Biggar, Libberton and Carnwath family setting supplies a specific local comparison. A James born around the inherited 1630/1634 estimates could father Robert in the 1660s or 1670s; a Robert born in the 1670s could marry in 1713 and father John in 1722 at ordinary adult ages. This provisional older-generation route is preferred to making the two overlapping Libberton Roberts sons of the same Johne. No record names Robert as the weaver’s child. Robert’s current circa-1690 birth estimate would be too late for a father dead by 1680; an earlier birth is required if this hypothesis is right. That estimate is unsupported, but the required revision remains a limitation, not evidence for the proposed father.

The 1680 index describes James as a weaver in the Back of Lindsaylands, parish of Biggar, with indexed testament date 10 November 1680, Lanark Commissary Court CC14/5/10, TD. That is a registration date, not an exact death date. The original has not been read and supplies no reviewed Robert clause. The 1690 Edinburgh apprenticeship names a deceased father James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland; the matching trade and locality make him a probable instance of the indexed weaver, but identification with Glasgow-3332 remains only possible. The apprentice generation is another possible intermediary for the later family, not an additional person invented to complete a pedigree. Glasgow-3332’s existing parentage, the separate 1648 Johne child identity, and the competing 1624 Quothquan-weaver identity retain their previous grades. The new father selection cannot itself prove any of those identities or be used circularly to reject the 1624 alternative. This particular parent model depends on the later weaver identity; the 1624 decedent would be an implausibly early direct father of this 1713–1722 household.

**30 October 2026 — a new maternal connection.** Agnes Glasgow-4133’s 1720 baptism names Katherine Wilson and Robert Glasgow, matching John Glasgow-2870’s separate 1722 Libberton parental couple. Select [Katherine Wilson-127539](/people/wilson-127539.html) as [Agnes’s mother](/people/glasgow-4133.html#research-findings), 95% confident. This extends the specific Wilson household from held transcripts, without merging the two Robert accounts or changing their paternal ancestry. Agnes’s existing father and all vital fields remain unchanged; it is not a father-confidence gain.

The Carnwath marriage citation gives Robert and Katherine Wilson in 1713; the captured 1722 Libberton baptism citation names Robert and Katharin Wilson as John’s parents. Those index citations define the proposed Wilson household but supply no paternal ancestry or age for Robert. The neighbouring Glasgow-4168 account combines Katherin Gibson in 1718 and Katherine Wilson in the corrected 1720 reading, and Katherine Watson in 1726. The 1720 and 1722 entries now agree on Wilson: the older Watson–Wilson–Watson argument is superseded. The 1718 Gibson and 1726 Watson entries still require their own identity comparison. Transcription differences, record misassignment, overlapping families, or one man across some entries remain possible. The 30 October reconciliation selects Wilson-127539 as Agnes’s mother at 95% from her named baptism and the matching 1722 parental couple. Wilson is not equated with Gibson or Watson, and the two Robert accounts are retained separately. These child records do not identify Robert’s father.

Glasgow-3093 remains an unselected alternative father for the Carnwath Robert, particularly if Glasgow-3407 is eventually identified with the Gibson/Watson Glasgow-4168, whose selected father is already Johne. Johne’s birth around 1648 could fit fatherhood around 1690; however, no later record follows him from the Mid Calder child entry to Libberton. Giving him both Roberts would otherwise require two living sons with the same forename or an unproved identity between the accounts. The present choice avoids building that assumption into the default model. If Glasgow-3332’s two father assignments and the Glasgow-3093 to Glasgow-4168 choice are right, Glasgow-3407 would be the latter Robert’s paternal uncle. That is a consequence of the conditional model, not independent evidence of kinship. Another unrecorded local father and a younger Lindsaylands generation remain possible. Captain Glasgow-2867 also remains a surviving identity comparison; his unsupported imported family is not a concrete exclusion, and no maritime or probate bridge identifies the Carnwath man with him.

Original 16 October father-hypothesis scope: One new uncertain father is selected from existing index and family reviews. The 1680 weaver identity and an earlier Robert birth are required conditions; no new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics are unchanged. The two Robert accounts remain separate retained profiles, and no genealogical certainty is inferred from their inclusion in one working family.

chapters.title: West Kilbride and Maryland: a conditional Ayrshire family
body: John Glasgow-3375 is the selected uncertain working father of the West Kilbride parent John Glasgow-3161, through possible identity with his son Jon Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679. The West Kilbride account already names Glasgow-1434 as an identity comparison. A child born near the 1679 baptism could have been about twenty at the January 1700 Patrick event, followed by the John/Margaret Cowan children at nearby Stevenston in 1701 and 1706 if that further adult identity is right. This supplies a specific neighbouring-parish household and ordinary generation, preferred provisionally to leaving the 1700 father without a named family. It does not prove that the Kilwinning child, Stevenston father and West Kilbride father were one person.

The West Kilbride John Glasgow-3161 is the selected uncertain working father of Rev. Patrick Glasgow-635, through possible identity with the indexed child Patrick Glasgow-3160 of 1700. The minister’s church-history account calls him Patrick, and the previously reviewed biography of his son calls the father a native of Scotland. If the 1700 child became the minister, he would have been about thirty-five when son James was born in 1735, thirty-six when ordained at Manokin in 1736, and fifty-three at his death in 1753. That is a coherent adult career and family sequence. The recorded Scottish childhood and compatible dates make this a useful low-confidence choice; no ministerial, marriage or migration record identifies that child as the Maryland man.

The supplied Scotland’s People entry reads PATRICK GLASGOW, 03/01/1700, West Kilbride, parish 620, reference 10 / 27, with JOHN GLASGOW/ as the parent field. The prior source review interprets that as 3 January; the structured child field instead says 1 March. Both readings remain visible, and neither an exact birthday nor original-image inspection is claimed. The minister’s inherited circa-1680 Irish birth is unsupported by his cited career records. Taken literally, 1680 would conflict with this childhood hypothesis and with a father represented by the 1679 Kilwinning child. It remains a conflicting profile estimate, not evidence that the proposed generations fit that year. No date or birthplace is silently changed to make the route work. Scottish origin rests on a later biographical statement, not a contemporary birthplace record. Ford’s church history, printed p.16, PDF p.22, records the 1736–1741 ministry and a 23 March 1753 death date (superseded by the contemporary notice below), but names no parent and supplies no age or birthplace.

John Glasgow-551, associated with County Tyrone in the William Melanchthon Glasgow family account, remains an alternative identity already named on the West Kilbride profile. His estimated birth and the absence of a West Kilbride event do not exclude him. The Ayrshire comparison is preferred for its specific neighbouring parishes and independently indexed 1679 child, not because an Irish route has been disproved. Another local John, a brother or cousin of the Kilwinning family, or a different father remains possible. The Kilwinning-child/Stevenston-adult identity is itself uncertain. No occupation, later residence or marriage connects John-3161 to either adult. Barbara Alason/Allason is named with the 1679 child; no mother is selected for the West Kilbride account, and Margaret Cowan is not assigned as Patrick’s mother from the later Stevenston events. John-3375’s earlier family scaffold retains its existing uncertainty.

The Gordon Patrick Glasgow-1440, indexed in 1667 and associated with Helen Fairburn and a later Scottish family, remains an alternative childhood/adult comparison. He would have been about sixty-eight at James’s 1735 birth and sixty-nine at the 1736 ordination if baptised near birth: less economical than the 1700 route, but not an exclusion. The Maryland-linked Patrick Glasgow-3002 is another unresolved account; its unsupported 1720 birth estimate does not identify or exclude him as the minister, and its cited Treasury entry has not been newly interpreted here. Other unrecorded Scottish or Irish childhoods remain possible. The 1700 child’s later life and the minister’s pre-1736 life are untraced. Shared forename, surname and plausible ages are indirect evidence, not a parent clause. Mary Jones remains the minister’s recorded wife; no new marriage, mother, migration date or Scottish parish of birth is asserted.

Two uncertain father hypotheses are selected; both depend on unproved child/adult identities. Their combination is a conditional model, not two independent confirmations of an Ayrshire-to-Maryland descent. The corresponding child and adult accounts are retained separately without a merge; connectivity counts retained profile accounts rather than proved distinct people. No original parish image, new kinship clause, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment or live WikiTree save is claimed. Current vital fields and confidently marked relationships are preserved, with the conflicting estimates explicitly explained.

Patrick-635](/people/glasgow-635.html) → [Secretary James-634](/people/glasgow-634.html) rises 47% → 95%, and James → [son James-2492](/people/glasgow-2492.html) rises 65% → 94%, following inspection of Holloman’s named family passages. The original 1819 will remains unread, and the Mary/Martha Jones maternal label is unresolved. The minister’s West Kilbride ancestry stays uncertain at 26%; these stronger later links do not prove that origin. The older Smith County James is now the selected possible father of [Wesley Guynn-2476](/people/glasgow-2476.html), 35%, from county and generation alone. No record names Wesley as his son; another father or collateral relationship remains possible. These are two strengthened existing links and one weak new working connection, not three confident genealogical discoveries.

The complete held accounts of daughters [Nancy-370](/people/glasgow-370.html) and [Elizabeth-2055](/people/glasgow-2055.html) are now reconciled with Holloman’s specific family passages. Their existing father links rise **73% → 96%** and **66% → 93%**, respectively. Nancy’s two husbands and reported pension father declaration identify the adult; Elizabeth’s Martin–Donelson sequence and two sons identify her. These are confidence improvements to existing relatives. The original pension, settlement and probate remain uninspected; birth and subsidiary marriage/death discrepancies stay open. The earlier 95% father and 94% son assessments remain unchanged.

Mr. Patrick Glasgow, rector of Allhallows Parish, died in Worcester County on “Thursday last”. This supports the date in the [held Findmypast derivative](https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=US%2FGPC%2F00191354&tab=this) for the same death event. chapters.period: 1639–1689 · two very uncertain fathers through possible identity
chapters.title: William Glasgow: a conditional Polwarth–Cavers–Ulster family
body: Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man.

The Polwarth child was baptised on 4 April 1658. If baptised near birth, he would have been about 21 at the examination of the Cavers servant in June 1679, 26 at the Ormistoun servant list in 1684 and 31 in 1689. Those are compatible ages for the recorded adult and the later military tradition. The Ulster profile’s circa 1656 birth is explicitly a rough grandson-based estimate, not an age stated by a record; its guessed Glasgow-city origin cannot exclude a Borders childhood. The exact forename and surname, compatible sequence and existing Borders candidate make this a usable provisional life model. Polwarth and Cavers are distinct parishes in different counties, and the chronology supplies compatibility rather than an identifying age match. The Cavers setting is recorded residence/association, not a proved birthplace.

The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

The weakest stage is the proposed father’s identity. Glasgow-2462 was born at Inveresk on 20 August 1639 and baptised the next day. He would have been only 18 at the 1658 Polwarth baptism and 16, nearly 17, at the associated Elizabeth baptism in August 1656. Young fatherhood is possible, but there is no marriage, residence or occupation connecting him with the named Polwarth father. An older, otherwise unidentified William is a substantial competing explanation. The named-child clause does not prove Glasgow-2462’s identity. The regional Polwarth/Gordon household of Glasgow-3107 is a stronger local kinship lead than Inveresk alone, but supplies no father clause for William; no exact brother, uncle or father relationship with James is selected. This inherited father remains a very low-confidence default and would fall away on both new adult accounts if the child/father identification fails. No mother is selected for either adult, and no wife or mother is transferred from the Inveresk ancestry.

The Polwarth child could be a different man from the Cavers Covenanter, and the Covenanter could be different from the late family history’s William. The Hawick father Glasgow-2731 in 1692 and Cavers groom Glasgow-3587 in 1708/09 remain competing later identities for the Covenanter; neither is newly equated with him. The attached Glasgow-3370 entry in 1694 does not independently establish the Polwarth man as her father. If later Scottish records identify the Covenanter continuously there, the family history’s permanent Irish settlement would need reconsideration. Other Scottish William candidates and the possibility that the late ancestor account is mistaken remain open. A missing contemporary Irish bridge is not an exclusion, but the combined identification is especially uncertain. No surname or Y-DNA grouping supplies these missing generations.

Two very uncertain local father hypotheses are selected from existing research; no new original inspection, certain relationship, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing child/adult records, vital fields, attached relatives and their grades remain unchanged. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates, and describes the selected model rather than a proved pedigree.

chapters.title: Calder and Irvine: selected uncertain parent families
body: Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. This adopts possible identity with John Glasgow-1544, the child indexed at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. The same name and parish and a normal adult generation favour this concrete child account over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1702, he would be about 28 in 1730 and 53 at the 1755 child. Those ages are conditional examples, not ages stated in the registers. The old circa 1710 birth was inferred from assumed age at the 1730 fatherhood and cannot exclude the 1702 child. The child’s existing father identity as William-1026 is itself qualified; no record explicitly identifies the later Meek husband as his son.

John-1544 and John-3481 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selection does not establish two distinct John sons. The 1702 date remains unreconciled: the child’s field uses a before 11 November boundary while its biography cites a 29 November baptism. Neither date is newly corrected. The later account combines the 1730 father of Jean, whose mother is omitted, with the 1751 and 1755 Meek household. That earlier adult identification remains a preferred working combination, not a continuous household proved by occupation, land or witnesses. John-81, estimated born 1709, remains a specific competing identity for the 1730 father. His Guthrie household is indexed with children in West Calder in 1751 and 1753 while the Meek household appears in Kirknewton in 1751 and Leith in 1755. That concrete overlap makes a simple succession of wives less persuasive; do not combine the full Guthrie and Meek families without resolving the entries. No birth estimate alone excludes John-81. Other local John origins remain possible. Ann McCook is not selected as John-3481’s mother: the reviewed 1702 child citation names William, and the attached Ann field does not supply an independently verified maternal clause. William’s existing uncertain John-3610 father and older family alternatives retain their grades; no date or family field is changed to force the new route.

Select John Glasgow-1057 and Agnes Spark-330 as the uncertain working parents of George Glasgow-4165, father with Margt at Irvine in 1741–1745. The preferred model uses possible identity with their son George Glasgow-1058, baptised at Kilwinning on 20 November 1687 and already associated with the George/Margaret Martain couple indexed marrying there on 11 June 1728. That couple’s son George-3312 is indexed at Kilwinning in 1729. The nearby Irvine household later repeats George and Margt, with no maternal surname or father’s age stated. This offers a specific existing couple and a compatible continuation across neighbouring parishes. On an infant-baptism assumption, the elder George would be about 54–58 at the Irvine children; late fatherhood remains possible. Margaret’s circa 1704 estimate would fit an adult mother in 1741–1745, but it is only a marriage-derived estimate. Neither calculation proves the identities or a move.

Agnes Spark’s proposed maternity is assessed independently from the same positive child evidence: the 1687 baptism index explicitly names John Glasgow and Agnes Spark as George’s parents. Their already confident parentage for the recorded child is not newly upgraded. Transferring either parent to the Irvine adult depends on the uncertain child/groom/Irvine identity chain, so both new adult links remain uncertain. They share that premise and are correlated, not independent confirmations. Margt in the 1741–1745 entries is George’s co-parent, not evidence for his own mother; Margaret Martin is not assigned a new mother or merged with any other Margaret.

The 1687 child, 1728 groom and Irvine father may be different men. The match of Margt to Margaret Martin is compatible, not a full recorded maternal surname match, and no age, occupation or property bridges the two parishes. The existing 1687-child/1728-adult family account also needs its identity assessment kept separate from the child’s explicit parent clause. A younger George from the Irvine Hugh/Service, James/Rae or another local family remains possible. The proposed father James-4158 would give a normal generation if George was born around 1720, but no record names him as George’s father; the specific older George/Margaret household is preferred provisionally. Keep the merchant son George-3312 distinct. If his 1729 entry represents infant baptism, he would be only about 12 at the 1741 fatherhood, a strong objection to assigning those children directly to that son. The index event type and adult-child identities still require their own review; an unsupported older birth estimate must not decide them. No merchant trade, Nethermains ownership, Manchester patent or artillery career is transferred to the Irvine father. No identity merge, duplicate removal or live relationship save is performed.

Two selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother using existing parish and profile research. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. John’s new mother remains unknown. Existing dates, recorded couples, earlier uncertain routes and possible duplicate accounts are retained; connectivity measures profile accounts, not proved distinct individuals.

chapters.title: Dublin watchmakers and Irvine: two uncertain fathers
body: **23 October 2026 review:** Assess the existing Thomas Glasgow-1242 → Philip Glasgow-1241 father pair at 72%, previously 52%. The inspected 1711 entries name Philip and the specific Thomas/Jean Duncan couple; the 1701 Linlithgow banns and marriage now independently establish that named adult household. Philip’s maintained 3 June date and Uphall place match exactly. The Mary label that depressed the earlier review is not supported by these entries. Thomas-1242’s retained 1675 Linlithgow child identity gives a plausible age of 26 at the 1701 marriage and 36 at Philip’s baptism, and the same local family route is preferable to an otherwise unidentified Thomas. 72% is a subjective probable assessment of the complete existing father-profile pair, including the unproved identification of the 1675 child with the 1701 adult. It is not 99% merely because a transcript names a father Thomas. The alternative 21 October/Linlithgow citation remains unresolved. Philip’s Scottish child identity is the basis of this assessment; his later identification with the elder Dublin watchmaker remains uncertain and is not upgraded. No mother, parent selection, birth/death field or live WikiTree value changes. Original parish registers were not inspected.

The newly inspected Findmypast transcripts establish Thomas Glasgow and Jean Duncan’s Linlithgow banns on 30 March 1701 (groom a servant; witnesses James Craw and William Duncan) and marriage on 4 May 1701. The banns leave both residences as question marks. A third Linlithgow register index names the same couple in 1701 without a day. These are related register entries, not three independent family identifications. Kirkliston banns dated 22 June 1716 name Thomas Glasgon, resident at Uphall, and Catharine Clerkson, resident at Kirkliston. The named couple, Uphall residence and Margaret’s following 1717 Uphall child entry identify the existing Clarkson household. The FamilySearch-derived duplicate calls this a marriage date; retain the more specific banns label from OPR 667/1, item 5, rather than asserting a ceremony on that day. The 15 June 1715 Edinburgh child is already represented by Thomas Glasgow-1243, whose selected father is the Edinburgh baxter Thomas Glasgow-3285. His transcript explicitly calls the father a baxter and indweller. This citation must not be used as another Uphall/Duncan birth or evidence for the proposed Duncan-to-Clarkson succession. The recorded Edinburgh father is retained as a separately identified household; no record establishes its identity with the Uphall father.

Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. The preferred model uses Glasco-146 as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241 as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The Glasco-146 account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The fresh Glasco-146 biography itself mixes the 1752 watchmaker with junior notices of 1765,1768 and 1770. Its c.1715 birth and the c.1740 birth of Glasco-147 are tree estimates, not evidence selecting a generation. If Glasco-146 instead represents the junior, the elder Philip is an alternative father-generation placement and the Thomas link would need revision; no competing father is attached alongside it. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. The junior’s 1765 unnamed-wife death,1768 Teresa Plunkett marriage and reported 1770 death remain with the younger documentary account Glasgow-3932. Glasco-147 is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called Glasco-146’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for Glasco-146. The father Thomas is common to the retained 1711 child records, while the 3 June Uphall versus 21 October Linlithgow Philip entries and their maternal readings remain unreconciled; Jean Duncan is not transferred as Glasco-146’s mother. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison.

Select Hugh Glasgow-3109, father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James Glasgow-4158, father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. This extends an actual local household across a compatible generation. A James born in the later 1690s could be a son of the 1696 household and an adult father by 1721; this is a compatibility example, not a new birth estimate. Hugh’s proposed identity with the 1676 Kilwinning child would make him a young father in the 1690s, which fits that example. The shared uncommon surname, same parish and two successive family generations favour this existing named parent model; no register entry names James’s father.

James could instead be a son of the Irvine John-2475/Isabell Kyle family, Michael-1406’s household, another Ayrshire family, or an unrecorded father. The named James child of John/Isabell indexed in 1711 would be only about ten at the 1721 fatherhood if baptised as an infant, so he is a weaker identity candidate unless an older-baptism explanation is established. James’s before 1702 boundary is an adult-status estimate, not an actual birth. If James were substantially older, Hugh’s proposed 1676 child identity would become less plausible; no date is changed to make either hypothesis fit. The older Hugh/Hew account, its existing uncertain parents, Jean Service/Mary Dean identity sequence and earlier alternatives remain as previously assessed. James’s merged Margaret/Marion Rae household remains a working combined father account; no remarriage or equivalence between the mothers is proved. The 1740 Prosperity of Irvine shipmaster is still a possible occupational identity only, with no transfer of occupation, voyage or trade to this father. Jean Service is not selected as James’s mother solely from Hugh’s co-parentage.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers, no new mother, identity merge, certainty upgrade or live WikiTree save. Existing newspaper/parish reviews supply the historical comparisons; three Open/non-living WikiTree profiles were read anonymously to reconcile their current wording. The elder’s 1772 death is conditional on the selected adult identity; no birth is changed. Possible duplicate profile accounts and inherited uncertain routes remain explicit limitations of the working connectivity score.

The anonymous Open-profile capture of Glasgow-3932 on 16 October 2026 contains Robert Glasgow’s Kilrea 1827 biography, not the Dublin watchmaker. The entire misplaced text is also preserved in the captured biography of the correct Robert Glasgow-3897. A complete sourced Dublin replacement is prepared locally; the real current biography remains available in the comparison, with its hash retained. No Robert birth, relatives or life events are transferred to Philip. The structured Dublin profile and the current Glasco-147/Teresa Plunkett family support retaining the earlier strong same-person match between the two younger-Philip profiles, without a live merge or duplicate spouse attachment.

chapters.period: 1648–1735 · two uncertain fathers and one uncertain mother
chapters.title: Libberton and Uphall: selected uncertain parent families
body: **23 October 2026 review:** Assess John Glasgow-1105 as Thomas Glasgow-1226’s possible father at 30%, previously 22%. The 1701 Thomas/Jean marriage is now anchored in Linlithgow, and the 1716 banns place the Clarkson groom specifically at Uphall before the 1717–1735 child sequence. Together with the Duncan household’s 1704 and 1711 Uphall entries, this makes a local succession more specific than a repeated surname alone. The proposed 1675 Linlithgow child would be about 26 at the 1701 marriage, 41 at the Clarkson banns and 60 at the last 1735 child. This is a coherent, if increasingly late, fatherhood sequence. The modest increase recognises the dated local fit; it does not assert remarriage or a proved identity. 30% is a subjective assessment of the complete Clarkson-adult → John-1105 proposition. Two identity bridges remain unproved: the 1675 child to the Duncan groom, and the Duncan father to the Clarkson groom. No widowhood, remarital status, age, trade or parent is given in the inspected marriage transcripts. Jean’s death is not established. An unrecorded younger local Thomas remains a serious alternative; Thomas-1311 (1666) and Thomas-3091 (1663) are older compatible rivals. The 1679 Carstairs/Spence groom is not an established identity for this adult. The unverified 1766 memorial contributes no weight. The 1715 Edinburgh citation is excluded from the supporting sequence. Both Thomas accounts remain separate and no biological or profile merge is made.

The newly inspected Findmypast transcripts establish Thomas Glasgow and Jean Duncan’s Linlithgow banns on 30 March 1701 (groom a servant; witnesses James Craw and William Duncan) and marriage on 4 May 1701. The banns leave both residences as question marks. A third Linlithgow register index names the same couple in 1701 without a day. These are related register entries, not three independent family identifications. Kirkliston banns dated 22 June 1716 name Thomas Glasgon, resident at Uphall, and Catharine Clerkson, resident at Kirkliston. The named couple, Uphall residence and Margaret’s following 1717 Uphall child entry identify the existing Clarkson household. The FamilySearch-derived duplicate calls this a marriage date; retain the more specific banns label from OPR 667/1, item 5, rather than asserting a ceremony on that day. The 15 June 1715 Edinburgh child is already represented by Thomas Glasgow-1243, whose selected father is the Edinburgh baxter Thomas Glasgow-3285. His transcript explicitly calls the father a baxter and indweller. This citation must not be used as another Uphall/Duncan birth or evidence for the proposed Duncan-to-Clarkson succession. The recorded Edinburgh father is retained as a separately identified household; no record establishes its identity with the Uphall father.

Select Johne Glasgow-3093, indexed at Mid Calder in 1648 as son of Jamis Glasgow, as the very low-confidence working father of Robert Glasgow-4168, father at Libberton in 1718–1726. The preferred local route runs through Johne’s existing uncertain James-3332 father identity and that James’s possible identification with the Lindsaylands weaver indexed in 1680. Lindsaylands and Quothquan/Libberton supply the adjacent Lanarkshire family setting; Mid Calder is a separate parish and no migration is proved. A Johne born around 1648 could father Robert in the 1680s–1690s, allowing ordinary adult fatherhood at the 1718 baptism. This generation is preferred over assigning Robert directly to the older weaver, who was dead by 1680 if that identity is correct. It is a specific family hypothesis using recorded men, not a father clause in Robert’s records.

Johne’s only reviewed record is the 1648 child entry; no later occupation, residence, spouse or death identifies him with Libberton. The Jamis-to-Glasgow-3332 identity and the latter’s Lindsaylands identity are both uncertain. Its inherited circa 1634 birth would make him only about fourteen at Johne’s 1648 event if literal; that unsourced estimate must not establish or exclude parentage. The 1648 source names Jamis, not John-1084. The known parish association therefore belongs to a conditional family chain, not to an independently followed migration. James-3332 himself remains an alternative father if Robert was born before 1680 and fathered the later children at an older age. The son James apprenticed in Edinburgh in 1690, explicitly son of deceased James the Lindsaylands weaver, is a genuine alternative intermediate father or uncle; his existing held draft is retained, and no unrecorded generation is invented. The 1624 Quothquan weaver is a separate death account; its early death makes direct paternity of a 1718–1726 father much less plausible. Robert’s merged Gibson/Watson household remains a working combined account, not proof of remarriage or identity between the two women. No mother is selected for Robert, and no vital date is changed to fit the route.

Select John Glasgow-1105 and Agnes Eastone-3 as the uncertain working parents of Thomas Glasgow-1226, the father with Catherine Clarkson/Classon at Uphall from 1717 and Livingston by 1730. This selects possible identity with their named Linlithgow child Thomas Glasgow-1242 of 1675, while retaining both profile accounts. That child would be about 42 at the 1717 Margaret entry and about 60 at the 1735 Hellen entry: later fatherhood, but chronologically possible. The existing Glasgow-1242 account also represents a Thomas/Jean Duncan household at Uphall in 1704. Recurring Thomas name, the same Uphall parish and a plausible succession of households provide a more specific route than the removed Kilbirnie-minister parents. The 1675 parent clause belongs directly to the child account; transferring it to the Clarkson adult depends wholly on the uncertain identity.

Agnes’s maternity is assessed separately: the 1675 FamilySearch parent index explicitly identifies Agnes Eastone in Thomas Glesgow’s entry, while John is named as father in the paired child citation. This is a positive maternal source for that child, not merely John’s spouse field. Agnes’s attachment to the Clarkson adult remains uncertain because the child/adult identity is uncertain. Eastone/Daston readings, her estimated birth and John’s own child/adult identification remain qualified. These two new parent links share one identity premise and are correlated, not independent confirmations of the adult’s ancestry.

The 1675 child, the Duncan adult and the Clarkson adult may represent one, two or three men. There is no inspected age, widowhood or probate bridge between the Duncan and Clarkson adults; the 1701 groom is indexed as a servant, and the 1716 groom as resident at Uphall. The 1701 marriage is now supported by inspected Findmypast banns/marriage transcripts; the original registers remain uninspected. No death of Jean, remarriage to Catherine or overlap resolution is invented. The differing Philip 1711 dates in the Thomas research compilation and the Glasgow-1242 biography, and the omission of a mother in the latter’s indexed child, do not establish a continuous Duncan household or certain maternity. They are not two independent confirmations. Catherine’s indexed surname variants remain as recorded. The before 1700 boundary for the Clarkson adult and the 2/21 February 1675 date discrepancy in the child account remain unchanged. The 1666 St Cuthbert’s Thomas-1311, child of Alexander and Issobell Anderson, remains a compatible identity alternative, albeit with fatherhood at about 51–69 in 1717–1735. His possible identification with the Edinburgh writer whose testament was indexed in 1691 is unproved and cannot be used to exclude him. The retained 1766 grave link is an unverified namesake comparison, not an established death for the Clarkson adult. The 1663 Thomas-3091 and an otherwise unrecorded local Thomas also remain possible. No identity merge or live attachment is performed.

Two selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother, using existing parish, testament and apprenticeship reviews. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge, spouse change or vital-date alteration. Robert’s new mother remains unknown. The Thomas parent pair depends on possible child/adult identity; profile-based connectivity retains potentially duplicate accounts and is not a count of proved distinct ancestors.

chapters.title: Glenarm and Stevenston: two selected uncertain fathers
body: Select Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, as the very low-confidence working father of Elizabeth Glasgow-3961, the Eliz Glascho at Glenarm Town in 1669. Robert is an older recorded adult at Larne in 1653, and the existing uncertain paternal family already includes John Glasgow-3913 and James Glasgow-1081, the adjacent Jo/James Glascho householders at Kilwaughter in the same 1669 roll. Elizabeth shares their unusual recorded Glascho form and the east-Antrim setting. Her assumed adult-householder generation in 1669 can be a daughter generation of the earlier Larne man. This extends an existing local family explanation rather than inventing an unnamed father; no record calls Elizabeth his daughter or John’s sister.

Glenarm Town and Kilwaughter Demesne are distinct places in neighbouring lower and upper Glenarm baronies, not one household or consecutive entries. Elizabeth’s forename, surname form and regional date pattern support a family comparison but do not distinguish daughter from sister, niece, cousin or unrelated namesake. The tax entry does not state whether Glasgow was her birth or married surname, whether she was a widow, or her age. A wife/widow identity within another Glasgow household therefore remains possible. Her circa-1650 birth and the competing before-about-1648 adult estimate are inferences, not ages that establish a generation. The Larne man’s possible identity with the 1618 Scottish child remains uncertain, as do his existing Kilwaughter sons and his own selected Scottish parents. No mother is selected for Elizabeth; neither the elder Jonet Cunningham nor the younger Janet Cunningham is transferred to her as mother. Existing chronology, the possible James identities and the hearsay status of the Larne allegations remain unchanged.

Select John Glasgow-3375, the father associated with Barbara Alason/Allason at Kilwinning in 1679 and 1689, as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-4170, father with Mary Auld at Stevenston in 1717–1718. This is a low/very low-confidence regional household placement. The recorded couple supplies a compatible parent generation, and their son John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning in 1679, is already a possible identity for the John who had children with Margaret Cowan at Stevenston in 1701 and 1706. That existing route gives a specific neighbouring-parish family comparison for James’s later Stevenston household. The preferred provisional model places James alongside that John as a possible paternal brother. It does not identify a baptism for James or claim that the 1717–1718 entries name his parents.

James’s before-1698 birth is an existing estimated adult boundary from his 1717 fatherhood, not a baptism or an age. His actual birth could fit a child of the Kilwinning couple, but the route also depends on the unproved identification of their 1679 son with the Stevenston adult. The John-3375 and Rev. John-1073 profiles remain possible accounts of one man; no merge, duplicate resolution, ministry or new son of the minister is established here. The shared John-1604 parent and older family scaffold remain uncertain. The already selected uncertain son James-3105, father at Kilwinning in 1689 with Margaret Park, is a serious surviving identity alternative for James-4170: an earlier Park household followed by a later Auld household is possible, but no occupation, age or marriage bridge identifies them. Retain both accounts without counting the father selection as proof of two distinct James sons. Other local fathers, including the older Matthew of Pyperheugh as a possible father or earlier kinsman, remain alternatives; his 1665 spouse entry alone supplies no James child, and the long interval to 1717 requires caution. No mother is selected for James: Barbara’s known maternity of the 1679 child does not establish James’s mother, and no marriage to Mary Auld is invented beyond the recorded parent pair.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers using existing records and household comparisons; no new mother, original-source inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing vital dates, age assumptions, source readings and earlier pending amendments remain intact. The two suggested paternal-sibling relationships depend on the selected fathers and the older uncertain identity/parent links; they are not independent sibling attestations. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, so possible duplicates remain a limitation of the working score.

chapters.title: Stevenston and South Leith: selected uncertain families
body: Select John Glasgow-1030 as the very low-confidence working father of Matthew Glasgow-3538 of Pyperheugh, Stevenston. John and Jonet Mathie married in Glasgow on 25 January 1618 and have recorded children in the following decade. A son of that household, born in the 1620s, could be an adult spouse in the 1665 testament index that names Matthew. This is a compatible generation, not a new birth estimate. The existing Mathie–Glasgow network supplies a positive social route between Glasgow and Stevenston: David Mathy and Robert Glasgow were co-witnesses in 1554, while Matthew Glasgow and John Mathie were together at Ardeer Nether in 1559–60. The later marriage joins those surname networks. The recurrence of Matthew in the same parish makes this existing household a useful selected descent hypothesis; it does not identify a father in a record.

No inspected record names Matthew’s parents or connects his Pyperheugh household directly to the Glasgow couple. The route depends on Jonet’s unproved place in the older Mathie network and on the probable identification of the 1618 husband with Ninian’s brother John represented by Glasgow-1030. John’s confident Robert Glasgow-1096 father assessment remains conditional on that adult identification and is not newly upgraded. Other Stevenston fathers, collateral descent from the 1559–60 Matthew, and an unrelated same-name family remain possible. The 106-year interval rules out identity with that earlier adult; no missing generation is invented and no direct father edge to him is selected. The Saltcoats sailor John, spouse of Isobell Gray, remains a separate record-defined household; this model does not merge them. The 1619 baptismal witness Mathew Will is not Matthew Mathie or proof of a Glasgow relative.

Assess Jonet Mathie-159 separately as Matthew’s uncertain working mother. Her recorded 1618 marriage and maternity in the following decade provide an actual couple and a compatible childbearing generation; her circa-1597 birth is an estimate. The Mathie associations in Stevenston are the proposed route for this household’s connection to Pyperheugh. Selecting her is a conditional couple hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of attaching John. It has very low confidence: no record calls Matthew her son, no Mathie ancestor is newly attached, and another mother remains possible. The paternal and maternal selections share the same network argument and are correlated, not two independent confirmations.

Select William Glasgow-3075, the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret Glasgow-3186, indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her circa-1610 birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity.

Retain the strongest specific alternative: Betham’s pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names Margaret as his only daughter, wife of an unnamed Cairns and mother of Thomas Cairns. The documentary father–daughter relationship is explicit, but identifying that Margaret with Glasgow-3186 remains unproved. A first Lyell marriage in 1633 permits a later Cairns marriage. The preferred William placement avoids requiring that unproved Scottish–Irish identity and remarriage. It also avoids tension with the probable identification of Archibald Glasgow-1101 as the child baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and the 1635 graduate: that child would be an implausible father of a 1633 bride. This is a ranking consideration, not an exclusion: the Scottish identity is unproved, and a baptism is not necessarily an infant’s birth. The new uncertain William field must not be used as a concrete father conflict to reject the Rathmalton candidate. A different South Leith Glasgow father also remains possible. No mother is selected: Catherine Fraith/Fraser’s 1610 bride identity and Christian Scot’s separate Glasgow household remain qualified. William’s testament names Archibald as lawful son and sole executor, not only child; omission of Margaret neither excludes her nor proves kinship.

Margaret’s copied source string records the 28 November 1633 South Leith marriage, OPR 692/2, 90/264, FR3038. Its truncated surname string ASGOWE is retained in the profile comparison, not silently expanded as an original-image reading. The old exact-looking birth year is displayed as circa 1610, an inherited estimate with no age record. South Leith is the marriage place, not an evidenced death place; death date and place remain unknown. Matthew’s before-1650 birth remains uncertain, and his inherited Stevenson birthplace is not proved by the Stevenston residence. The 24 April 1665 date belongs to Jonet Cowan’s testament-index entry, not Matthew’s birth, marriage or death. No original source was newly inspected.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother; no live WikiTree save, identity merge, new original inspection or certainty upgrade. Matthew’s two proposed parents form a correlated household hypothesis; Margaret’s Rathmalton identity alternative remains open. Margaret’s copied source string records the 28 November 1633 South Leith marriage, OPR 692/2, 90/264, FR3038. Its truncated surname string ASGOWE is retained in the profile comparison, not silently expanded as an original-image reading. The old exact-looking birth year is displayed as circa 1610, an inherited estimate with no age record. South Leith is the marriage place, not an evidenced death place; death date and place remain unknown. Matthew’s before-1650 birth remains uncertain, and his inherited Stevenson birthplace is not proved by the Stevenston residence. The 24 April 1665 date belongs to Jonet Cowan’s testament-index entry, not Matthew’s birth, marriage or death. No original source was newly inspected.

chapters.title: Quothquan and Thankerton: two uncertain fathers
body: Select Stephen Glasgow-1029 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3910. James’s weaver occupation and Quothquan locality favour using the 1612 court defender and the 1624 testator as one working adult account. Stephen is documented as an adult in Glasgow in 1575 and with wife Margaret Grahame in 1582; his approximate 1550 birth is an estimate, not a birth record. The existing tree already places John Glasgow-3296, the 1650 Quothquan testator, under Stephen, uncertain. The preferred model treats the two early Quothquan men as paternal brothers rather than making the later John James’s father. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. This uses a named family already connected to Quothquan, at very low confidence, rather than inventing a missing parent. No record names Stephen as James’s father or James and John as brothers.

The route depends both on the proposed James–John brotherhood and on John’s already uncertain Stephen parentage. The Glasgow–Montfoid–Mid Calder–Quothquan identities are not proved migrations. John’s 1650 testament names his sister Bessie and no child or parent; omission of James, already dead by 1624, does not disprove brotherhood. John himself could instead be James’s father if older than his inherited estimate, or the men could be uncle/nephew, cousins or unrelated local namesakes. The older John and Thomas tenants in the 1520s–1530s remain possible ancestral relatives with unproved intervening generations; no direct father edge to them is selected. Margaret Grahame is Stephen’s documented spouse in 1582, not a documented mother of James, so no mother is attached. John’s existing mother field and all earlier parent and identity alternatives remain unchanged.

The firmer family anchor is [Bessie Glasgow, the Lanark testament subject](/people/record-bessie-lanark-1650.html). The checked selected clauses of NRS CC14/5/5, images 65–66, confirmed 27 May 1650, call her the lawful sister and executrix of [John of Quothquan](/people/glasgow-3296.html). Their record-defined sibling relationship is documented at 99%. Extend John’s existing uncertain Stephen Glasgow-1029 father model to Bessie at the same 22%, conditional on John’s unproved paternity. This follows the proved sibling relationship without pretending the testament names Stephen. It supplies no independent support for John’s father hypothesis; Bessie’s mother remains unknown.

Bessie’s existing-profile identity remains on HOLD: eight compatible candidates survive and none is selected. Keep the complete evidence account and candidate comparison together under the existing record-bessie-lanark-1650 catalogue ID. The 99% sibling and 22% father assessments concern the woman named in the testament, not every candidate baptism profile. No merge, candidate-parent transfer or fixed-cohort population gain follows. This review reuses the checked original-image reading; no new image inspection is claimed.

Select the Quothquan weaver James Glasgow-3910 as the uncertain working father of Helen Glasgow-3909, the married Thankerton woman whose testament was indexed in January 1627. The shared uncommon surname, neighbouring Quothquan/Thankerton locality and an adult weaver recorded at the 1612 hearing followed by a married woman dead by 1627 give a coherent father/daughter generation. Helen’s circa-1605 birth is an inherited estimate, not her stated age; it is compatible with a James born before the mid-1590s but is not independent proof of that generation. This is a low-confidence local family selection. No inspected record calls Helen James’s daughter.

Helen could instead be James’s sister or niece, a daughter of the later John or another local Glasgow. Neither testament index supplies her age, children or parents. Thankerton is her household’s stated residence, not a proved birthplace or death place. Margaret Threipland’s 1626 Quothquan widow entry remains a possible wife for James, not a selected spouse identity and not a mother for Helen. Both newly considered mothers remain unknown. The original 1624 and 1627 testaments are discriminating follow-up evidence, not a prerequisite for displaying these qualified working links.

The circa-1605 birth estimate is replaced locally by an explicitly conditional adult-role estimate, before 1595: this assumes an age of at least 18 at the 1612 hearing and the preferred same-weaver identification. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history.

Two selected uncertain local fathers; no new mother, original-source inspection, live WikiTree edit, identity merge or certainty upgrade. The family placements use existing record reviews, named local accounts and checked chronology; paternal/full sibling status remains conditional. The circa-1605 birth estimate is replaced locally by an explicitly conditional adult-role estimate, before 1595: this assumes an age of at least 18 at the 1612 hearing and the preferred same-weaver identification. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history.

James Glasgow-3332 remains a surviving cross-profile identity alternative for the 1624 Quothquan weaver. Its circa-1634 birth is an unsupported estimate and cannot by itself exclude that earlier man. Identification with the distinct weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680 would exclude a death before 1624 if established, but that later identity is itself only possible. Retain Glasgow-3910 as the record-defined 1624 account for the selected uncertain family; do not merge the profiles or transfer Glasgow-3332’s unproved parent and child attachments. Those existing family fields remain unchanged, and the proposed Stephen placement is an alternative to that account’s current pedigree.

chapters.title: Michael of Irvine and James of Kirknewton: two working fathers
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1512 as Michael Glasgow-1406’s uncertain working father. This activates a parent comparison already recorded in Michael’s profile. Robert is a record-defined Ayr father with Margaret Donald in 1670 and 1671; Michael is recorded as an Irvine skinner in 1679 and is already treated locally as the later saddler/councillor. Robert’s before 1652 birth is an upper-bound estimate from his later children, not evidence that he was born in 1652. Michael’s before 1679 boundary likewise does not date his birth. An older Robert and a Michael born well before the summons could fit a father/son generation; their ages are not recorded. The regional family setting and existing candidate justify a very low-confidence working choice. No record names Michael’s father, and no shared occupation, holding, witness or household identifies this Robert as his parent.

John Glasgow-1604 is another viable older father generation, rather than a disproved alternative. Robert’s own attachment to that John is unproved, and taking John’s approximate 1626 date narrowly could press the generation spacing if Robert had Michael early. Those older dates and attachments remain hypotheses; no date is adjusted to repair the pedigree. Another Ayrshire father, or a sibling/collateral relationship to Robert, remains possible. Margaret Donald-1722 is named in Robert’s 1670–1671 children’s records, not in a record naming Michael’s mother. She is not selected as Michael’s mother. The existing 1679 skinner/later saddler/councillor identification is inherited from the completed merge, not newly proved; keep the 1679 summons,1686/1702 civic records and 1699/1701 leather-work references distinct in their evidence roles. Elizabeth Garven and Catharine Baird remain the recorded mothers in Michael’s later child group. The 1700 Elizabeth entry has an assumed year and no proved 1 January birthday. No mother, marriage or death date is newly inferred for Michael, and the 1700–1715 household chronology does not itself identify his parents. The earlier proof-level hold on Robert is retained as history, not treated as a disproof of this qualified local model.

Select the older William Glasgow-1026 as James Glasgow-3526’s uncertain working father. William’s Kirknewton household is documented by Bessie in 1682 and William in 1705. James is the father-name account behind John’s 1717 Kirknewton/East Calder entry, with a Helen 1714 association held in a collaborative tree. James’s 1688 birth is an unsupported profile estimate. If the rough 1660/1688 generations are close, William would have been about 28 at his birth, and the proposed son falls between William’s already recorded children. This same-area, compatible household generation is preferred provisionally, at low confidence. The combined Kirknewton/East Calder label does not establish the exact historic parish or continuous residence, and no record names William as James’s father.

John-3525’s earlier biography links its father to James Glasgow-1547, whereas the maintained local family uses James-3526. The 1717 index names James, not either modern profile ID. James-1547, associated with Andrew Glasgow-1546 and a 1702 entry, remains a surviving alternative childhood identity for the adult father. If baptised as an infant in 1702 he would be about 15 in 1717 and about 12 at Helen’s tree-held 1714 date. That makes the ordinary older-William model more straightforward, but neither a later childhood baptism nor an erroneous Helen association is excluded. No merge or categorical biological exclusion is selected. Andrew-1546 therefore remains an alternative father through that identity, not a newly attached parent. Andrew-1319 or another older Calder father remains possible. William-3974, the separate 1671 child of Andro, would imply younger fatherhood at a literal 1688 birth; the date estimates alone do not exclude him. Do not undo the split between that child and the older William-1026. The already attached Irish James-1025 may be another account of this James, a relative or an unrelated namesake. Sharing a proposed father does not prove two distinct James sons, and no Scottish-to-Tyrone identity or migration is established. Ann McCook is not selected as James’s mother, and Christian Cook’s attachment to James-1547 is not transferred. James’s wife and the two children’s mothers remain unknown. Helen’s exact 1714 date and father association are tree-held, not an inspected baptism. John’s 1717 record supplies a father name but not a birth or parents for the adult James. The existing child-parent grades, James’s estimated 1688 field, William’s selected uncertain John-3610 father and all older alternatives are preserved.

Both are selected uncertain local father models using existing material. Neither adult receives a mother. No original newly inspected, source-record discovery, identity merge, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Existing dates, places and attached relatives are retained; connectivity counts profile accounts, including possible duplicates and older uncertain links.

chapters.period: 1676–1699 · two uncertain fathers and one mother
chapters.title: Kilwinning and Irvine: the remaining early family heads
body: John Glasgow-3375 is the selected uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3105. James is the combined working father account behind the two 1689 Kilwinning child entries, one naming Margaret Park. John is a record-defined father in that same parish in 1679 and 1689, associated with Barbara Alason/Allason. The rough 1650 and 1670 family generations would put John at about twenty when James was born, and both generations could have children recorded during 1689. Neither year is a recorded birth; John’s captured before-about 1661 boundary is an adult-status estimate and permits an earlier birth. No date is changed to fit this placement. Prefer this recorded local adult as a provisional parent-generation anchor over assigning James directly to the older John-1604 scaffold or to an otherwise unidentified father. The shared parish and compatible generational spacing supply the logic, at very low confidence; no source names James as John’s son.

John-1604 remains a possible older father rather than a rejected alternative. His approximate 1626 birth and 1664 death are unsourced; a literal 1670 James birth would conflict with that death estimate, requiring at least one estimate to be wrong. Neither is silently adjusted. Hew-1066 or another local Glasgow remains possible; the current shortlist is not exhaustive. John-3375 may be the same man as the minister John-1073. If so, the minister’s approximate 1653 generation would imply younger parenthood around 1670, still dependent on James’s unrecorded birth. No merge, proved brotherhood, ministerial occupation for John-3375 or new father for the minister is inferred. John’s own attachment to John-1604 and the older Hugh-1603 scaffold retain their existing uncertainty. Barbara Alason is the recorded/probable mother of John’s known children, not a newly selected mother of James. James’s mother stays unknown. Margaret Park is recorded for the July 1689 child; Anne’s May 1689 index omits a mother. The combined James father account and the two children’s sibling status remain provisional. Two index/baptism dates two months apart do not prove two births to one mother. No witness, occupation, property or inheritance bridge ties James to John.

Select Hew Glasgow-1066 and Margaret Lachland-2 as the uncertain working father and mother of Hugh Glasgow-3109, the Irvine father with Jean Service in 1696, through the existing strong possible identity with their 1676 Kilwinning child Hew Glasgow-1067. If baptised near birth, the child would have been about twenty in 1696. The name variant Hew/Hugh, compatible generation and neighbouring Ayrshire parish setting make this a practical preferred childhood comparison. This activates a comparison already explicitly retained in both profiles, rather than treating the 1696 child’s entry as the adult father’s birth. Maternity is assessed independently from the 1676 child clause: the supplied Scotland’s People index explicitly names Margaret Lachland with Hew Glasgow. The Findmypast transcript abbreviates/queries her name as Mt Lach?. Margaret is not selected merely because she is Hew’s spouse. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain childhood identity and remain uncertain; the child’s recorded parentage is not proof of the adult’s origins.

Keep Glasgow-1067 and Glasgow-3109 as separate profile accounts of a possible single man. The shared parents do not establish two distinct sons called Hew/Hugh. No record joins the 1676 child to the 1696 Irvine father or proves the proposed sequence from Jean Service to Mary Dean from 1699; no death, remarriage or continuous personal identifier has been supplied. The Mary Dean family retains its own unproved childhood-to-adult identification. The older Hew-1066 himself is a possible alternative identity of the 1696 father, rather than simultaneously being his proved father. That alternative would invalidate the selected child identity and the maternal transfer; it is not materialised alongside them. A different unrecorded Hugh remains possible. The 1677 preacher has no inspected residence or kin bridge here; the selected 1676 child could not have been that adult preacher a year later. The 1751 Irvine/London sailor remains an unselected occupational identity, not an event newly assigned to either account. Retain the literal source discrepancies: the official supplied index and Findmypast give24 May 1676, while the older father biography reports5 May from FamilySearch. A24 May marriage is also reported in that family biography; the original page and event type were not re-read. No baptism, birthday or ceremony date is newly corrected or proved. Hugh-3109’s before-about 1676 boundary remains an estimate, not a birth record or a hard exclusion of the 1676 child. Existing Jean Service co-parentage, both 1696 children, Mary Dean associations and the child’s parent-field grades are retained. No relationship-certainty change is counted. Margaret is not assigned to any other child whose record does not name her.

These are selected uncertain working relationships using existing material, not new original-record discoveries. No vital date, location, existing spouse or attached relative is cleared, and no identity merge, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is claimed. Counts concern retained profile accounts and inherit uncertainty and possible duplicates in older links.
