chapters.title: Two Lothian family heads: the Duffe and Kirknewton households
body: The fresh public WikiTree capture marks Ann McCook’s motherhood confident(flag 20). The local review explicitly downgrades that inherited certainty to an unselected uncertain alternative: the child sources cited for it name only William. This is a reassessment of a tree flag, not proof that Ann could not be Bessie’s mother; no live flag or relationship is changed. William’s existing confident father role for Bessie is individually rated 98%, without counting it as new certainty.

Select William Glasgow-1026 and Marion Glasgow-3025 as the probable intended couple of the 1681 banns, at 69% subjective confidence for the combined profile identification. William’s record-defined Kirknewton father account is established by Bessie’s 21 April 1682 baptism, about ten months later. The same uncommon full paternal name, parish and close sequence favour identifying that father with the groom. Marion-3025 is the existing local child account indexed in 1655, whose name, parish and ordinary mid-twenties adult generation make her the leading bride comparison. Prefer this qualified reuse of two compatible existing accounts to leaving the recorded couple unconnected or creating another William and Marion. This selects the intended couple; it does not prove a completed wedding or a ceremony date. Select Marion Glasgow-3025 as Bessie Glasgow-1545’s possible working mother, at 54% subjective confidence, replacing Ann McCook-217 locally while retaining Ann as an unselected alternative. The 1681 named couple followed by the same-parish William’s child in April 1682 supplies positive contemporary household evidence that Ann’s inherited attachment lacks. The mother is omitted in Bessie’s inspected indexes. The lower 54% includes the bride/profile identity, groom/father identity, completion or continuation of the union, and maternity; it is not direct record wording. This is a new preferred maternal hypothesis, not a documented maternity upgrade. Ann is not biologically disproved, and her other attached children and spouse hypothesis retain their prior status. [Current Bessie and maternal comparison](/people/glasgow-1545.html#research-findings).

Findmypast’s transcript names William Glasgow and Marion Glasgow in banns dated 10 June 1681 at Kirknewton and East Calder, OPR 689/20, item 1, p.39. It gives marriage year 1681, without a separate wedding date, ages, parents, occupations or residence within the parish. This transcript was inspected on 20 October 2026. Marion’s existing findings already contained the same couple/date from the supplied ScotlandsPeople index, OPR 690/10/82, FR51; these are derivatives of one event, not independent corroboration. The original remains uninspected and the archive-reference discrepancy unresolved. The alternative explanations remain: another William could be the groom or Bessie’s father; the bride could be another Marion, including the compatible Inveresk Marion-1429/Marione-3049 or Edinburgh Marion-3143 accounts. The earlier 1664 William banns item supplies another adult-couple comparison, not proof of one man’s remarriage. The older William-1087 remains a possible groom comparison if the bride is a different Marion; Marion-3025’s own William-1087 father identification is ungraded and cannot be used circularly to exclude that possibility. William-3974’s recorded 1671 childhood makes him a poor ordinary groom comparison for 1681, without validating the older man’s estimated 1660 birth. Marion’s 11 October/4 November 1655 date discrepancy is retained. Neither a shared surname nor a presumed cousin marriage proves the couple’s ancestry. The pair and maternity share identity premises and are correlated assessments, not independent proofs or mechanically multiplied probabilities. William’s John-3610 father remains 24%; no mother is transferred to his later children, no biological father is changed, and all vital fields remain unchanged. Earlier Ann-associated wording below is inherited family reconstruction, not evidence that an inspected record names Ann.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: Select Johnne Glasgow-1151 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2682, husband of Isobell Duffe. James’s captured biography already proposes Johnne as a possible father. The Inveresk and Musselburgh index records Johnne on25 November 1632 with father Alexander Glasgow. James and Isobell’s Edinburgh children begin with Jean on13 April 1677. If Johnne was baptised near birth and James’s approximate 1655 birth is close, Johnne would have been about 23 at James’s birth and 44 at the first known grandchild’s baptism. This is an ordinary father/son generation within the wider Lothian setting. Select that already recorded comparison provisionally, at very low confidence. Neither James’s own birth nor Johnne’s adult life is established; this is a parent-generation model, not a source naming James’s father. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

James Glasgow-3076, recorded at St Cuthbert’s in 1661 with father James Glasgow-3077 and mother Annapill Glessie, remains an alternative childhood identity explicitly suggested in that child’s profile. If baptised as an infant he would have been about 16 at Jean’s 1677 baptism; that younger parenthood makes it less straightforward than the selected ordinary-generation model, but does not exclude him. An older-child baptism also remains possible. John Glasgow-1084 is another previously proposed father. His Gordon/Berwickshire household and separate James Glasgow-3107 account remain viable comparisons; no missing death or marriage is treated as an exclusion. A different unrecorded father remains possible, and the shortlist is not exhaustive. No source joins Johnne’s 1632 child record to an adult father of James, supplies James’s age, or connects their households by craft, witness, property or inheritance. The preference is weak, based on the existing candidate, chronology and regional fit; the component gain supplies no identity evidence. No mother is selected for James. Johnne’s index names Alexander but no mother; his existing Clerk attachment does not establish a mother for James. Keep the Duffe household distinct from the Edinburgh weaver Glasgow-1150 and the unresolved Whitecastle James Glasgow-1376. The old 1657 event on1376 names James as father of Marione, not as the child. That role error does not supply a birth or parentage for the Duffe husband. The old reference to “James-1168,about1540” also mislabels the Corsankell elder; the selected route instead uses Johnne’s actual recorded father Alexander Glasgow-1148. The 1679 and 1680 sons called James remain separate child accounts; no infant death or survivor marrying Jean Dobie is newly established. The 1679 mother’s indexed Elizabeth/Isobell Duffe difference remains an existing household-identity qualification. All six children, spouse, dates and previous assessments are preserved.

Select John Glasgow-3610 as the uncertain working father of William Glasgow-1026, the older Kirknewton householder associated with Ann McCook by 1682. This activates the same-parish candidate already retained in William’s research. A 1649 Kirknewton/East Calder index names Johne Glasgow as the father of the child Johne; the adult account also carries a Margaret comparison with unresolved 1646/1649 dates. A father active in 1649 could have another son around William’s estimated 1660 birth. If the adult John is the 1608 Mid Calder child used in his own selected family model, he would have been about 52 in 1660, chronologically possible for a father. That childhood identity is itself uncertain and is not required for the local parent generation to remain possible. The common parish setting and compatible parent generation favour this existing John comparison over restoring the younger Walter-1554 as William’s father or importing the weak Kilwinning John-1604 comparison. Select John at low confidence. No inspected baptism, marriage, testament or property record names William as this John’s son.

Earlier argument retained, superseded for the father selection on 18 October: William Glasgow-1026 is the older father in the 1682 household, not William Glasgow-3974, the child born/baptised in 1671 with father Andro Glasgow. Do not restore the 1671 child’s father to the older man. Walter Glasgow-1554 was indexed in 1649 and would be only about eleven at a literal 1660 birth; retain him as a non-selected former proposal, not a restored father. William’s 1660 date is an estimate, so that subtraction is not a newly proved biological exclusion. Other older Calder Glasgows, including William-1087 or Robert-4006, remain possible father-generation alternatives without a parent clause. John-1604’s Ayrshire route is retained as a weaker geographic comparison. John-3610’s own selected father John-3296 remains uncertain at 28%; the possible 1608 childhood identity is separate. The secure adult entry is the 1649 father record, not a proved 1646–1650 baptism sequence. The uncertain adult Alexander-3118 attachment is not a proved 1650 baptism and supplies no independent sibling evidence. No mother is selected for William. The 1649 source names only the father in this review; Ann McCook is William’s existing co-parent/spouse account, not evidence of his mother. Preserve the current wives, children and their individual evidence grades. The new father route does not validate the unsupported Captain Robert-2867 or Irish James-1025 parentage, a Tyrone migration, the legacy Tyrone death-place field, or the unsourced Walter middle name. The 1682–1705 same-father household reconstruction and the wider descendant accounts keep their existing uncertainty. A large working component is not a proved pedigree. No vital date, location, spouse or current attachment is cleared to force the new parent. Current selection: James-991, possible40%; John-3296 remains alternative28%. See the current Easter Newtoun working-ancestry comparison.

Both father selections are expressly uncertain local hypotheses using existing material. No new mother, original inspection, live WikiTree edit, identity merge or confidence upgrade is claimed. The fixed cohort and all confidently marked connectivity measurements must remain unchanged. Counts describe retained profile accounts and inherit uncertainty in older links, including possible duplicates.

Killycurragh generation comparison,20October2026: the full family-letter transcription distinguishes the older William of Killycurragh from his son William, the Cunningham husband. Select the1705 child [William Glasgow-1318](/people/glasgow-1318.html) as the possible older adult,36%; his adult identity and migration remain unproved. The named father and three-son cluster also raise James-1025’s existing William-1026 father assessment from12% to32%, possible. The minister John’s94% father is the younger Irish William; that high rating does not cross the Scottish identity gap. [Family sequence, complete drafts and source limits](/free-space/glasgow-of-killycurragh-early-c19-aa9477/).

chapters.title: Issobell: a Mid Calder childhood for the McCaskie bride
body: Select David Glasgow-1028 as the uncertain working father of Issobell Glasgow-3185, the bride indexed with Robert McCaskie at St Cuthbert’s on 19 July 1632, through possible identity with David’s Mid Calder daughter Issobell Glasgow-1085, baptised on 3 May 1612. This adopts an existing comparison in the captured child profile, rather than inventing a new named parent from the marriage alone. Exact forename and surname, the compatible Lothian setting and an age of about twenty in 1632 if baptised near birth favour this childhood as a practical working choice. The child’s baptism names David, but neither it nor the marriage supplies the bridge between child and adult. Shared name and compatible chronology do not prove the identity. Prefer this young-adult explanation provisionally over an older widow or an unrecorded childhood, at low confidence.

Retain Glasgow-1085 and Glasgow-3185 as separate profile accounts of a possible single woman; the selected parent does not establish two distinct daughters called Issobell. The father–daughter link is already confidently marked for the record-defined 1612 child; only the transfer to the 1632 bride is newly selected and uncertain. The marriage index names no father, age, birthplace, prior marital status or children. The 19 July date belongs to a combined banns/marriages index and is not newly verified as the ceremony date. The bride’s before-1612 birth boundary is an inferred profile estimate, not a birth record or an independently established exclusion of the May 1612 child. It is retained unchanged; no new birth date is entered to force the connection. The child’s 1642 Hardington, Somerset death fields remain an unsourced tree-held later-life lead in this review, not a verified fate or proof of migration. Even if correct, that later date alone would not exclude the 1632 marriage. The older Isobel Glasgow-3336, who represents Andrew’s testament-named daughter and is probably the William Symountoun bride of 1619 and mother of the 1620 child, remains a possible remarriage alternative. No death of Symountoun, remarriage record or continuing incompatible household was inspected; do not exclude her merely because she already has a spouse. An unrecorded Isobel remains possible and the candidate list is not exhaustive. No mother is named in the 1612 baptism review, so none is selected for the bride. David’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and supplies no independent corroboration. Existing relatives, dates and all confidently marked links are preserved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Working connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: The 1652 Edinburgh cordiner: a working Glasgow childhood
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 as the uncertain working father of the Edinburgh cordiner Robert Glasgow-3938 through possible identity with the indexed Glasgow child Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised on 17 November 1618. The published Edinburgh marriage register names Robert as a cordiner with Janet Thomsone on 1 July 1652. The older Robert is the probable identity of the Glasgow cordiner admitted burgess on 22 April 1613 and is the named father of the 1618 child. If baptised near birth, that child would have been about 33 at the July 1652 marriage. The matching name, compatible adult generation and same craft make this a useful preferred family comparison over an otherwise unidentified parent or a more distant cordiner kinsman. The trade association supplies a reason to select the family, but neither hereditary training nor a Glasgow-to-Edinburgh move is documented. The father selection is low confidence; it does not identify the child with the adult as an established fact.

Select Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the independently assessed uncertain mother of the Edinburgh adult only through the same possible childhood identity. The 1618 baptism explicitly names Jonet Conynghame as mother of Robert Glasgow-1078. This is an explicit maternal clause for the child, not an inference from the older Robert’s marriage alone or from a Cunningham surname elsewhere. Its transfer to Glasgow-3938 depends entirely on the uncertain identity and therefore remains uncertain. The father’s craft provides no independent evidence of maternity.

Keep Robert Glasgow-1078, Glasgow-3938 and the Larne Robert Glasgow-3970 as separate profile accounts. Both adult accounts are now provisionally placed in the 1618 child’s family; this does not establish two distinct sons named Robert. The 1652 Edinburgh event and the 1653 Larne account are not simultaneous incompatible events on the available evidence: they could concern one mobile man or different namesakes. Neither a migration nor that combined identity is selected as proved. Robert Glasgow-1149 remains the separate existing candidate for the Euphame Lorimer household. Her indexed children in 1651, 1659, 1662 and 1664 bracket the Thomsone marriage, favouring two Edinburgh men. The reported 1 March 1644 West Port sasine also names Eupham Lorimer and belongs to that household comparison; it does not give a West Port residence or wife to the 1652 bridegroom. The original sasine is uninspected. The 1618 child’s attached younger Cunningham spouse and 1645 James association do not prove his adult identity. A later Thomsone marriage could be a remarriage if that association is correct, but no death or remarriage sequence is supplied. Preserve the existing attachments and all namesake alternatives. Glasgow-3938’s before-1634 birth boundary is an age-derived profile estimate, not a recorded birth. It remains unchanged, as do the child’s baptism, the Larne estimate and all existing spouses, children and confidently marked links. The Edinburgh marriage gives no parents, age or children. No apprentice, burgess, witness, property or migration record joins these accounts. An unrelated cordiner or another son, nephew or cousin in the wider family remains possible. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or relationship-confidence upgrade is claimed. Connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Campbeltown: a provisional Linlithgow origin and Agnes’s placement
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. A child baptised in 1622 could have been about 37 at Alexander’s 1659 Campbeltown event and about 28 in the approximate 1650 generation assigned to James and Agnes. This is a workable adult generation for the household. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

Select George Glasgow-3100 as Agnes Glasgow-1562’s uncertain working father. This activates the existing geographic family suggestion: Agnes’s captured profile places her Longwill household in Campbeltown, with a 1670 marriage-year field and a son’s 1683 birth field, while George is the named father in the 1659 Campbeltown event. Their approximate parent/child generations permit an older daughter in that household. The same locality and generation make daughter a useful provisional placement alongside George’s attached James and recorded Alexander. The marriage year, child details and Agnes’s circa-1650 birth are profile-held leads, not a newly inspected parish entry. No source names Agnes’s father; a sister, cousin, other local family or unrecorded father remains possible.

George-1560 and George-3100 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; shared proposed parentage does not prove two distinct sons called George or an identity merge. The 1605 and 1627 childhood candidates remain viable, and the list is not exhaustive. A separate unrecorded childhood is possible. The illustrative ages assume baptism near birth. George-3100’s 1630 structured and 1640 narrative births are unsupported estimates; neither is silently replaced by a proved 1622 birth. The existing John review cites X1RN-XV7 whereas the child profile cites X1RN-XVQ; retain that reference difference for original-register comparison, without treating the citations as independent events. James-1496’s father link to George is inherited and unproved; its name pattern supplies no independent corroboration for the chosen childhood. Agnes’s 1670 marriage field does not establish her age. No birth year is altered to force a generation. Assess mothers separately. No mother is supplied for the 1622 child in this review and none is selected for the Campbeltown adult. Grizel Dunlop-3562 is already the confidently marked mother of Alexander-3101 in the 1659 event, but that does not establish her maternity of Agnes or James. Her circa-1640 birth is also an unsupported estimate. Neither James nor Agnes receives a mother. The FMP 13 April 1659 birth-date field and Scotland’s People 12 April index date remain literal alternatives; the original entry and reference conventions are unresolved. The Auchinhork residence reading is not assigned a guessed modern place. John-1561’s own Andrew-of-Calder father and his other childhood-to-adult comparisons remain uncertain. No new original inspection, confident relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and retains the possible duplicate.

chapters.title: A provisional Glasgow–Larne–Belfast family
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Robert-1078 and Robert-3970 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct Robert sons or an identity merge. No record joins the 1618 baptism to Larne, supplies the Larne man’s Scottish origin, or rules out another Robert. The 1666 John of Portrush shipmaster is a further possible identity, not an occupation proved for either Robert; the later Robert/Rachel household remains separate. James-3172, the Scottish child James-3971 of 1645, and the Kilwaughter James-1081 may be one, two or three men. All accounts remain; no identity among those James groups is selected. A child baptised in 1645 could have been a shipmaster aged about 22 in 1667, assuming infant baptism, but that is compatibility only. The father named in that 1645 record is not independently identified with the 1618 child. John-3913’s circa-1630 and Captain James’s circa-1640 births are inherited estimates, not dates that establish or exclude a generation. If John’s 1630 were literal and the Larne man were born in 1618, fatherhood at about twelve would be an important chronological objection; both the age estimate and John’s uncertain paternal attachment require testing. No birth year is changed to force the selected route. Captain James could instead be a nephew, other relative, unrelated namesake, or a member of the Saltcoats sailor John-4152’s family; the named Saltcoats vessel makes that a real competing route, not evidence that John was his father. The two women Cunningham-20923 and Cunningham-22604 are distinct: the elder is the named 1618 mother, the younger the named mother in the 1645 James record. Neither that younger maternity nor a marriage to her is transferred to the Larne adult or captain through these selections. The existing uncertain Kilwaughter father links remain uncertain; none becomes proved by joining their supposed ancestor to Scotland. The Larne allegations are hearsay, not a judicial finding of guilt, and the 1686 will reference is not a proved death date. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and does not resolve the possible duplicates.

Later Larne–Inishrush comparison, reviewed 17 October 2026: select [James Glasgow, the older Larne ropemaker](/people/glasgow-1509.html) as [John Glasgow-822](/people/glasgow-822.html)’s very uncertain working father at 18%. John and [Adam of Inishrush](/people/glasgow-3902.html) were nine years apart and headed the only two Glasgow households in the 1831 parish return. John’s 1847 letter and the family-news and naming network support a brother or close-collateral comparison. The selected James-to-Adam father model is 27%; extending it to John depends on both that unproved paternity and unproved Adam–John brotherhood. These are correlated inferences, not independent parent records. No source establishes a Larne-to-Inishrush migration or names John as James’s son.

An older Adam and Maria remain the stronger unnamed parent alternative; no placeholder people are created and no mother is selected for John. Adam-3902 himself was about nine when John was born and cannot be John’s father. The identity of John-822 with [the 1831 Inishrush householder, John-3927](/people/glasgow-3927.html), is separately assessed at 94% from the Bible household, Inishrush and Drimbolg associations, 1847 letter and compatible emigration chronology. The disputed census denomination remains unresolved. That identity assessment does not prove ancestry, merge the accounts or alter John-3927’s captured placeholder father.

The nearby Cross family has a separate reviewed father identity: [John Glasgow-2407](/people/glasgow-2407.html)’s existing father [John Glasgow-1657](/people/glasgow-1657.html) is probable at 84%. The 11 September 1865 marriage names the groom’s father John, farmer; the precise Cross locality, compatible generation, older John’s 1836 death notice and a Glasgow holding in the 1862 valuation favour the attached man. The certificate’s parental role is explicit, while identifying its father with John-1657 is inferred. Glenleslie John-1022 remains an alternative; the holding is not proved inherited. The nephew married since 1839 is excluded as the 1865 bachelor groom, which does not disprove his uncle’s paternity. This is a confidence review of an existing attachment, with no new mother or upstream father.

These later comparisons use maintained source readings, not fresh original inspection. The new James-to-John edge remains uncertain; the Cross father review and John-822/3927 identity are separate assessments. None strengthens the earlier Robert-of-Larne or captain hypotheses above.

chapters.title: Jean of Linlithgow: connect the childhood and mother accounts tentatively
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of Jean Glasgow-3083, the mother named in the 1654 Issobell Glen baptism citation. The existing Linlithgow father study places an indexed daughter Jean in John’s household in 1613, represented by Glasgow-3055. The later mother’s profile also places her in Linlithgow. A child baptised in 1613 could have been a mother in 1654, about 41 years later if baptised in infancy. The 1626 birth stated for the later mother has no identified birth source and is not a concrete conflict with that identity. Prefer the possible same-woman explanation and carry the existing father comparison to the adult account, at low confidence. This is a selected inference from the existing local family and chronology, not a parent named in the 1654 citation.

The profiles Glasgow-3055 and Glasgow-3083 remain separate accounts of a possible single woman. The selection establishes neither two distinct daughters called Jean nor a completed identity merge. The 1613 daughter’s later whereabouts are not established. Another Jean in another Glasgow household remains possible; a later daughter in John’s wider family is another explanation. The 1654 citation identifies Jean Glasgow as Issobell Glen’s mother, but its full event fields and original page have not been re-read here. body: The 1637 testament identifies Glasgow-4152 as sailor in Saltcoats, dead December 1636, father of Glasgow-4151 and Glasgow-4153. These father links were already confident; his omitted catalogue page separated the visible family.

Select John Glasgow-3193, the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John Glasgow-4152’s uncertain working father. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns.

No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. chapters.title: Agnes Glasgow: a working daughter of James younger
body: Select James Glasgow younger (Glasgow-3921), the Corsankell tenant, as Agnes’s uncertain working father. Her probable 1601 and compatible 1606 Milneburne sasines and her 1628 Stevenston testament place her in the same small parish as the documented Corsankell family of 1559–1571. James younger’s approximate 1540 generation is a natural fit for the father of a woman already married by 1601. His existing plausible daughters Katherine Glasgow-1495 and Geillis Glasgow-3179 belong to the neighbouring Stevenston–Ardrossan women’s network; Geillis’s 1603 estate also names a James Glasgow in Stevenston in its debts. These are local family comparisons, not proved sisters or identification of the creditor. The earlier James-1168/Margaret Smith placement mixed two generations: Margaret is associated with the younger James, not the elder. Selecting the younger James gives the leading generational placement without inheriting that unsupported mother.

No record names Agnes’s father. Parish, generation and the existing family comparisons support only a low-confidence choice. The 1601 entry is a land-record registration, not a marriage date or an age statement; Agnes may already have been married for many years. As an illustration only, a married woman aged about 20–35 in 1601 would have been born about 1566–1581, making James younger about 26–41 and James elder about 51–66 at her birth. These are comparison assumptions, not birth estimates or exclusions. James elder remains an alternative father if Agnes was older. Edward Glasgow-1557 or another local Glasgow remains an alternative, especially if the unproved sisterhood with Jonet Glasgow-1494 is established. Edward’s own approximate 1570 birth makes that father generation less comfortable for a woman already married in 1601, but the estimate is not a hard conflict.

Neither the two women’s sisterhood nor the two Logan husbands’ brotherhood is documented. Under the selected James-younger father and the existing uncertain James → Edward → Jonet chain, Agnes could instead be Jonet’s aunt; that is a conditional model consequence, not a new proved kinship. Margaret Smith is not selected as Agnes’s mother, and her 1632 husband is not proved identical to the Corsankell man. The unnamed Stevenston elder is printed under 1613, probably in error for 1616; the inspected printed page leaves his forename blank. No identity merge or live relationship edit is made.

Agnes’s captured WikiTree birth field is blank. The public c.1610 display was an unsupported inherited estimate and cannot date a woman probably already married in 1601. Her actual birth remains unknown; “before 1601” is a conditional outer boundary from the probable sasine identity. The 1628 testament date is not an exact death date. Stevenston is in Ayrshire; the corrected death locality is an uncertain inference from her stated residence, not a recorded place of death.

One uncertain father joins an existing family. The 1601 year denotes a probable record identity, not a birthday. Measured cohort memberships, the fixed baseline and confident links are preserved; only working connectivity gains the selected edge.

Printed-page check, 18 October 2026. The printed page leaves a visible blank before “Glasgow elderis”; it supplies no forename. Page 191 prints 28 January 1613 but also says Sunday and gives regnal years xlix and xiij. The immediately preceding instrument is dated 3 January 1616 and the following one 31 January 1616. The printed year is therefore internally suspect: 28 January 1616 was Sunday in the Julian calendar, whereas 28 January 1613 was Thursday. Prefer 1616 provisionally, retaining 1613 as the printed reading until the manuscript is checked. This is an unidentified male elder, not an occupation or event assigned to Agnes. The printed-page check cannot recover his forename or identify him as Hugh Glasgow-1603, James, John or Edward. An original manuscript or an independently dated account of the institution is needed; the manuscript has not been inspected. No kinship percentage or parent selection changes.

chapters.title: Three more early family placements, explicitly uncertain
body: The local working tree now selects William of Saltmarket as Michael of Stevenston’s possible father, Andrew of Calder as Jonat Menzeis’s possible father, and Ninian as Barbara Wilson’s possible father. These choices use the existing brother/cousin, same-parish remarriage and daughter/niece comparisons.

Michael Glasgow of Stevenston: The existing Stevenston study places Michael as a probable brother or cousin of James elder of Corsankell, rather than his son. Michael was an adult witness in the Glencairn estate network in 1549; both appear in the same small estate landscape in the 1559–60 teind list. Their approximate 1525 and 1515 generations fit brothers. Select the brother option provisionally and extend James’s already uncertain father William to Michael. This uses an existing older household without inventing an intervening person. The Mathie–Glencairn network supplies a credible route between the burgh family and these estates. Limits: The brother-versus-cousin choice is unresolved, and James’s own father William is uncertain. No record calls Michael William’s son. A cousin through another burgh household, an older generation than the estimated 1525 birth, or a separate family remains possible. Brakpleuch and Dubbs may represent one Michael or two. No mother, exact birth or death is inferred.

Jonat Glasgow, wife of David Menzeis: Jonat is the mother in a Mid Calder baptism in 1609. The existing comparison prefers her possible identity with Jonet Glasgow who married Martin Ramsy in the same parish in 1624, fifteen years later. That Jonet is already placed as Andrew’s testament daughter. Select Andrew as Jonat’s uncertain father through this local identity reconstruction. Her estimated 1585 generation fits Andrew’s household; the same name, parish and feasible remarriage sequence favour this model over the more distant Ninian household. Limits: This combines two uncertain identity steps: the 1609 mother with the 1624 bride, and the bride with Andrew’s testament daughter. David Menzeis’s death and the bride’s widowhood are not recorded in the material reviewed. Jonat and Jonet may be different women; retain both profiles and do not count an identity merge. Ninian Glasgow remains a competing father hypothesis. No mother is attached.

Barbara Glasgow, wife of Johne Wilsoune: The existing branch assessment already favours Barbara as a daughter or niece of Ninian. Her 1611 South Leith marriage entry fits the Leith setting of Ninian’s possible son William and the adjoining Edinburgh craft households; Ninian’s documented son Robert was a cordiner. The estimated 1590 daughter generation fits Ninian’s estimated 1550 generation. Select daughter as the simpler working placement within this already identified household, while retaining niece as an alternative. This is a combined locality, generation and family-network inference. Limits: Neither the marriage entry nor Ninian’s testament names Barbara as his daughter. The proposed Leith brother William is himself uncertain, and shared craft geography is suggestive rather than individual proof. Barbara may instead be Ninian’s niece or belong to another local family. If she is Barbara-567, the existing William-3522 father claim becomes a rival explanation. The adult Barbara identities remain separate, the 1611 date discrepancy stays open, and no mother is assigned.

Each is low confidence and counts only as a selected uncertain parent in the working graph. Keep possible duplicate profiles separate, mothers independent, and the confident graph unchanged. No new source reading is claimed.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

Earlier argument retained, superseded for the father selection on 18 October: John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: retain the selected uncertain father at 28%. The 26 June 1608 Mid Calder child would have been about 40–41 when the 22 April 1649 Kirknewton/East Calder entry named Johne as father. Name, adjacent parish and chronology favour the comparison, without a shared holding, trade, spouse, witness or proved sibling to identify the adult. John-1086 primarily represents the 1685 Quothquan decedent, only possibly the 1608 child; John-3296 primarily represents the 1650 Quothquan decedent, only possibly the Mid Calder father. The 1609 William baptism supplies local context, not independent identity proof. Margaret-3112 has disputed 1646/1649 readings; Alexander-3118 has an estimated circa-1650 birth from a 1667 marriage, not a baptism. Use the secure 1649 occurrence rather than a claimed 1646–1650 series. John-1084, the 1616 child of James-991, is a compatible adult-identity alternative through the 1642 Porteous marriage, 1643 Edinburgh child and 1652 Kirknewton child, now supported by a supplied index and inspected transcript; the matching Easter Newtoun residence links its father to the 1649 household, without proving the Porteous mother or the 1616 identity. James-991 remains an unselected father alternative conditional on that identity, without percentage, merger or maternity assignment. Robert-4006 remains a father-generation alternative and John-3056 a compatible childhood comparison. The 1650 testament’s omission of children is not an exclusion. William-1087 remains an unsupported removed father, not biologically excluded merely by his 1609 baptism; 1629 is not a recorded birthday. Current selection: James-991, possible40%; John-3296 remains alternative28%. See the current Easter Newtoun working-ancestry comparison.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.

chapters.title: Murieston: probable older George identity beside James’s household
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

The witness’s own residence is unstated, and another George in the district remains possible. The residence reading Muirestoun and its identification as Murieston remain probable. Shared spelling and locality are related observations; McCall repeats Maidment’s 1586 act and is not a second muster occurrence. Naming the child George is supporting context, not proof of a naming rule. The 1586 act records an obligation, not attendance. Neither source gives George’s age or states a relationship to James. Father, uncle, brother, other kinsman and neighbour remain alternatives. No father is changed: Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains James’s selected uncertain father, while George is an important competing paternal or collateral explanation. George Glasgow-1099, the merchant, remains compatible but unselected; the 1586 minor’s curatorship and the 1598 marriage contract do not identify him at Murieston. No mother, birth date, identity merge or confidently marked paternal edge is added.

This improves a specific identity assessment within the 216-profile James branch, rather than raising Andrew’s father grade. The earlier possible assessment is retained as history. The working tree, confident paternal graph and fixed cohort are unchanged. body: Medieval officeholders, messengers, clerics and burgh entries preserve name occurrences across several places and roles.

The official description of the 8 August 1475 Stirling charter, B66/25/43, groups John Glesgw among the burgess witnesses. Three Stirling occurrences are now assigned to the same working identity. chapters.title: Govan nailers: father 78%, new mother 86%, probable couple 82%
body: The Barony banns transcript names Samuel Glasgow and Lillias Stewart on 24 February 1790, OPR 622/7, item 1, p 42, register 1778–1819. It gives marriage year 1790 but no separate wedding date, ages, parents, occupation or residence field. The transcript was inspected on 21 October 2026; the original register was not inspected.

Select the record-defined Lillias Stewart as the probable mother of James Glasgow-1483 at 86% subjective confidence. The 1790 Govan baptism explicitly names Samuel Glasgow and Lilias Stewart; the independently recorded Barony banns name that same distinctive full parent pair shortly before either disputed baptism date. This supports one local household across the two registers. James’s adult account has a Govan nailer burial in 1833, aged 42, and children Samuel and Lillias with Jean Cunningham. Parish, approximate age and the paired family names favour identification with the 1790 child. The granddaughter’s Lillias name is supporting naming evidence, not proof.

Prefer the 1790 banns couple as Samuel Glasgow-3063 and the record-defined Lillias at 82% subjective confidence, including the groom’s identification with the older nailer. The same full parent pair in the Govan baptism and a chronologically compatible local adult household support the match. Samuel’s 1818 burial at 65 fits a father in 1790, but the banns and baptism supply no trade or age to distinguish him from another Samuel. This rates an intended couple in banns, not a proved completed wedding.

The 86% assesses the complete maternity proposition for the adult James, including the child-to-adult identity. It is not the near-certain named maternal role for the indexed 1790 child alone. The baptism dates 22 March and 25 April remain unresolved versions of one underlying event; no original was inspected. The banns identify neither man as a nailer. James’s burial age suggests about 1790–1791 and is not an exact match to the indexed child. A different James or Samuel remains possible. No birth, death, parents or childhood identity is assigned to Lillias from the contributed 1766 estimate.

Samuel Glasgow-3063 remains James’s probable father at 78%. The new banns strengthen the documentary household, but do not resolve the older-nailer identity. No father grade, paternal component, vital field or existing spouse/child is changed. The proposed mother and couple share identity premises and are not independent confirmations.

Inspect the original Govan baptism for its date, residence and paternal occupation, then the 1814 James–Jean Cunningham marriage and children’s entries for an occupation, witness or lair link. Test the older Samuel’s identity separately. A 1797 Barony Samuel banns entry (OPR 622/7, item 1, p 88) remains unassigned: do not infer a remarriage, Lillias’s death or a second household for this nailer from the shared name alone.
Earlier 20 October 2026 source account follows; its no-selected-mother statement is superseded by the current 86% selection.
Research rationale: connect James’s unattached seven-child Govan family to an existing older nailer, testing the competing Partick sibling suggestion against named baptism parents.

Two Findmypast baptism transcripts name James Glasgow’s parents as Samuel Glasgow and Lilias Stewart at Govan in 1790. SCOT/OPR/BAP/3976076 gives 22 March 1790, OPR 646/2, item 2, page 69, register range 1756–1819; R_688515992 gives 25 April 1790. Treat them as versions of one baptism lead, not two independent witnesses or two children. The date disagreement remains unresolved. Separate inspected burial transcripts record James, nailer, resident Glasgow, buried at Govan on 8 September 1833 aged 42, and Samuel, nailer, resident Glasgow, buried at Govan on 7 December 1818 aged 65. These are burial dates, not established death dates. All four transcripts were inspected on 20 October 2026; no original register image was inspected.

Select Samuel Glasgow-3063 as James Glasgow-1483’s probable working father at 78% subjective confidence. The 1790 Govan child has a named father Samuel. The existing adult James account represents the Govan nailer buried in 1833, while Samuel-3063 represents the older Govan nailer buried in 1818. The same surname, parish, Glasgow residence and specific trade favour a father–son occupational family. Samuel would have been about 37 at the baptism; James’s burial age implies about 1790–1791, close to the indexed child. James and Jean Cunningham’s existing children include Samuel and Lillias, matching the baptism parent pair. Naming supports the combined argument but is not proof. This identifies an existing father candidate for James’s seven-child family instead of creating another Samuel.

The 78% assesses the whole proposed father-profile link, including both identifications: the 1790 child as the adult nailer, and the named father as the nailer buried in 1818. Neither burial names a parent or child, and the baptism transcripts give no paternal occupation. Age 42 in September 1833 is approximately a year younger than the 1790 child; the circa-1790 birth on James’s profile is not an exact independent record. Another Samuel or another James remains possible. A contributed Ancestry tree links this same Jane Cunningham family to Samuel and Lilias, but gives an incompatible circa-1850 death for James; it is a comparison lead, not independent confirmation or authority to replace the 1833 burial. FamilySearch’s contributed Lilias account estimates her partner Samuel at 1763, whereas the buried nailer’s age implies about 1753; no underlying birth record was checked for that estimate. Do not merge those accounts on that basis. Lilias is the named mother of the indexed child, but no maternal attachment or new mother profile is selected here. All existing vital fields, spouses and children are preserved.

John Glasgow-2721’s biography suggests the Govan James as a possible brother and names its own father John Glasgow-3034. The cited Samuel Glasgow journal’s machine text at viewer image 28 (printed page 22), under “Other information in this book”, lists a James born 1793 but does not itself establish that he is James-1483 or explicitly call him John’s brother. The page image was not successfully inspected, so that text remains a lead. The John route is retained as an unselected identity alternative; the independently indexed Govan child and the two nailer burials currently favour Samuel. Do not alter John-2721’s attached father or join the two James identities as proved.

Check the original Govan baptism, especially the date and any occupation or residence, then the 1814 James–Jean Cunningham marriage and children’s baptisms for kin or trade identifiers. Seek a nailer apprenticeship or burial-lair relationship connecting Samuel and James. Inspect the journal’s final page before treating its compressed family list as a pedigree.

chapters.title: Dundonald: William’s recorded mother and possible father
body: Research rationale: join the disconnected 1733 child to an existing recorded mother and test the nearby weaver household, keeping direct maternity separate from inferred paternity.

Barbara Stevenson-14560 is the confidently identified mother of William Glasgow-4101, assessed at 99% subjective confidence. His retained Findmypast transcript records a Dundonald baptism on 12 June 1733 and explicitly names Barbara Stevenson as mother (OPR 590/1, item 3, p.82; SCOT/OPR/BAP/3536725). Barbara’s existing WikiTree account identifies which modern profile represents this recorded mother: its sole citation is the FamilySearch presentation of this same 1733 child, XYZB-Z9Z. The two indexes represent one underlying register, not independent historical corroboration. This is a new outstanding mother attachment to an already existing profile, not a newly discovered baptism or a new person.

Select William Glasgow-3586, the weaver at Achenyeards named as Jean’s father in the 1 October 1732 Dundonald baptism, as William Glasgow-4101’s possible father at 52% subjective confidence. The specific existing local household offers a more useful working placement than leaving the 1733 child isolated: the children share the uncommon surname and parish, their entries occur on nearby pages of the same register, and the boy’s William name agrees with the proposed father. The existing father account is already paired with Barbara Stevenson, the boy’s named mother, but that tree pairing has not been traced to an independent marriage or full-parent entry and is not counted as additional proof. The whole father proposition remains an indirect household reconstruction.

Upstream review21October2026: John-1057 now selected as possible father46%, through Irvine identity56%. Earlier no-upstream-selection statements below are superseded; the1733 father52% and mother99% assessments remain. The 1733 transcript has no father field or residence; absence from a transcript does not establish what the manuscript contains or prove illegitimacy. The 1732 transcript names William, weaver at Achenyeards, but no mother. Their baptisms are only 254 days apart, about eight and a half months: close spacing weakens a routine successive-infant-birth interpretation, while unknown birth dates and possible delayed baptism leave the proposed siblings compatible. Do not manufacture birth dates to resolve it. Another Glasgow father, a different Barbara Stevenson, and two separate local families remain alternatives. Barbara’s identification with her own 1733 citation is strong; the adult couple and cross-child father assignment are separate inferences. No mother is assigned to Jean, no full-sibling claim is made, and the existing ungraded Jean-to-William father relationship is unchanged. The earlier Ayrshire William accounts Glasgow-1055, Glasgow-3288 and Glasgow-1061 remain compatible wider comparisons; estimated ages or missing family details do not exclude them. No record links this father to any of their birth families, so no upstream father is selected. No later newspaper, maritime or American identity is inferred for the child. Exact percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies. Original register images were not newly inspected and no live WikiTree edit is made.

chapters.title: Kilmarnock: Hugh the glover’s family
body: Research rationale: test an existing family with a specific repeated trade, resolve the literal maternal surname variants, and restore an omitted local parent link without counting it as new genealogy.

The Kilmarnock baptism transcripts for Mary in 1732, Margaret in 1738 and Hugh in 1742 each name their father as Hugh Glasgow, a glover, resident at Kilmk (Kilmarnock). Repeated name, specific trade, locality and compatible child sequence identify one paternal household much more strongly than surname and chronology alone. The adult glover is represented by Glasgow-1929. Each of these three father–child roles is assessed separately at 99% subjective confidence. This concerns the recorded glover as father; his further identification with the 1710 Kilwinning child is an independent inferred step, not newly proved by these baptisms.

The retained transcripts actually give three maternal surname readings: McEachan for Mary in 1732, McGlashan for Margaret in 1738, and McGechan for Hugh in 1742. Earlier summaries normalized all three to McGechan. The 1732 marriage names Margaret McEachin. The same father, glover trade, parish and repeated Margaret given name support one family, but the McGlashan reading deserves separate treatment. Assess McEachin-120 as Mary’s mother at 98%, Hugh’s mother at 98%, and Margaret’s probable mother at 84%. McEachan and McGechan are compatible renderings in this specific household; McGlashan is not silently declared an equivalent surname. The original may confirm another reading or distinguish another mother.

The evidence reviewed is the retained Findmypast transcript text captured 3 September 2026 and quoted in the public child biographies, checked against fresh anonymous WikiTree captures 21 October 2026; original register images were not inspected. The three baptisms are separate events; copied summaries of one entry are not independent evidence. All three parent pairs are already attached on WikiTree with unmarked certainty fields. Restoring Hugh-4104’s omitted local parents is a publication repair, not a newly discovered father or a new WikiTree attachment. Individual percentages are subjective judgments, not frequencies or a probability that the whole ancestry is correct. The 1744 Mary entry names Margaret Giffen and remains separately unresolved; no mother is reassigned, no second marriage or maternal death inferred. No change is made to the upstream ancestry, births, deaths, spouses or other children.

chapters.title: Findmypast: birth-surname review through 1799
body: Research rationale: the earlier audit searched events only through 1750. The current review concerns people born with the surname Glasgow before 1800, including their later marriages, burials and other records. No birth cutoff is inferred from an archive collection’s title or coverage range. New-person suggestions require concrete conflicts with existing candidates; missing fields or an empty search are insufficient.

Current coverage, 26 October 2026: the exact Glasgow birth 1759 ±40 query (1719–1799) displays 5,872 BMD rows. Pages 1–28 have 560 saved result rows; 545 have reviewed dispositions (9.3% of this query only), with pages 1–27 fully reviewed and 15 page-28 transcript gaps remaining after browser control failed. The literal ledger has 612 indexed receipts plus 19 supporting indexed IDs retained at original pointers (631 bounded indexed IDs). These count provider IDs, not people or independent events. Page 28 is only partially reviewed: three new transcripts form two source-only documentary groups; one receipt reuse and one saved access hold complete its five dispositions. Resume the 15 saved page-28 gaps before advancing. Earlier births, variants, other categories, later-life records without indexed birth and unresolved identity/access holds remain. Whole-provider completeness is unknown and INCOMPLETE. Earlier dated batch accounts below remain history.

Abigail Glasgow’s three compatible indexes describe one Midcalder baptism on 18 June 1769. The OPR transcript adds birth 5 June 1769 and names Alexr Glasgow and Emilia Glending; companion indexes give Alexander and Emilia Glendining. A complete new-person draft is in the People catalogue. Abigail Glasgow-1655 is concretely excluded by her 1759 marriage, ten years before this birth. Her named parents have no established modern profile identities. Alexander Glasgow-1309 is a regional comparison only; no parent attachment is proposed.

HOLD — no new person is proposed. The companion Glasgow indexes report birth year 1786 but supply no separate birth date or age; only R_687411873 gives baptism, 7 April 1786. An original register has not been inspected, so the indexed birth year may be baptism-derived. Earlier Abraham Glasgow-1227 and Glasgow-1235 remain compatible, unproved adult-baptism comparisons: their earlier lives contradict an actual 1786 birth, but that premise is unestablished. Glasgow-750 is excluded because his nineteenth-century birth follows the baptism. Retain one documentary group with identity unassigned, birth on or before 7 April 1786, birthplace unresolved and no parents invented.

Two further indexes describe one Abraham Glasgow burial, 16 July 1818, aged 89, at St Mary, Birmingham; one adds Hill Street. The displayed 1729 birth is derived from age. Abraham Glasgow-1227 and Glasgow-1235 remain candidate identities because neither has a documented death or a life-course exclusion. The latter’s birth is BEFORE 18 August 1745, not an exact birthday. No Birmingham death, residence or 1729 birth is assigned to either, and no third Abraham is proposed for the burial.

Agnes Glasgow is indexed as born 1784 at Glasgow, without a baptism date or parents. Agnes Glasgow-32 has no recorded birth, a Scottish death in 1801 and an undated Weir marriage; it remains compatible. All 132 live Agnes Glasgow results were checked. The index remains candidate evidence under Glasgow-32, with no new-person suggestion or vital-field replacement.

Unnamed children remain anonymous: Kilmarnock boys born 1792 and 1797 name John Glasgow but no mother; John Glasgow-3298 is a compatible local father lead, whereas John-3051, born 1791, is too young. A Kirkliston boy born 1797 names the exact existing couple John Glasgow-159 and Agnes Gray-6937 and supports their already recorded family, without establishing a new distinct son or a forename.

The unnamed Leith North child born 11 December and baptized 17 December 1734 names William Glasgow, soldier, and Jean Lore (OPR 692/3, item 2, p.17). William Glasgow-1318 is a regional adult comparison; William-3013 and the older William-3080 remain alternatives. The unnamed Knowhill, Cambusnethan child born 10 May and baptized 5 June 1756 names James Glasgow and Mary Cowie (OPR 628/1, item 1, p.66); James-3523 is a compatible local comparison. No soldier occupation or spouse is assigned to these candidates as a proved fact.

The unnamed Midcalder 1757 child names Andrew Glasgow and Janet Young, with baptism literally “17 ? 1757” (OPR 694/2, item 4). Andrew-1239 and Andrew-3052 remain compatible; a different known spouse alone is not an exclusion. The unnamed Midcalder 1767 entry names only Alexr Glasgow (OPR 694/2, item 4, p.64). Alexander-1309, Alexander-1342 and Alexander-1321 are compatible regional adults. Do not transfer Emilia from Abigail’s 1769 record into this unnamed child’s mother field.

Five burial rows concern unnamed “Mrs Glasgow”, not a proved Glasgow birth surname. For 26 December 1821, two indexes agree on age 25 but label the date differently as death or burial; one notes childbed. For 3 July 1823, the OPR index gives age 30 while the companion Calton index gives 70. They are retained as a comparison, not forced into one person or split into two. Another Calton entry, 11 August 1832, gives age 57 and dropsy. Their calculated birth years are not independent birth records. No named person, exact birth or natal surname is invented from these rows.

The sources below are inspected provider transcripts; original register images were not inspected except the Crossle abstract image on page 23. Companion indexes of one event are not independent corroboration. The People accounts retain named-profile identifications separately from documentary parent roles and unproved comparisons. Next: reconcile the candidate families against original registers, review page 8 and earlier birth windows, and verify unresolved identities against concrete conflicts rather than treating no-match as a new person.

Page 2 review: twenty Agnes transcripts comprise seventeen baptism entries for eleven birth/baptism events, plus three later burial entries. Eight birth events match existing people by the recorded date, parish and family. Three other source-defined childhoods retain compatible alternatives, and no new person is proposed. The age-25 Paisley/Abbey burial entries may concern one woman, but their relation is not established.

The same Libberton baptism on 21 August 1720 names Robert Glasgow and Katharin/Katherine Wilson. The OPR transcript adds Gladhaimb and OPR 650/1 item 3 p.11. Watson in the current biography is not the recorded maternal surname; Watson-53558 remains an unresolved modern identity, and the live child has no attached mother. The R indexes report birth year 1720, but the OPR transcript supplies no birth date or age; retain birth before baptism rather than an invented exact birthday.

One Irvine baptism on 7 December 1725 names William Glasgow and Margaret Montford, matching the existing daughter of William and Margaret Montfort. Montford is the recorded spelling, not a second mother. The supplied day is a baptism date, not proof of an exact birthday.

Agnes was born 15 December and baptized 18 December 1726, Hugh Glasgow and Janet Kilpatrick, residence Byres, Kilwinning, OPR 599/1 item 1 p.208. This is a reinspection of the already assigned event, with exact dates retained; no new child or relationship is proposed.

One Covington and Thankerton baptism on 23 December 1744 names George Glasgow and Agnes Williamson, matching the existing child. The reported birth year 1744 does not turn the baptism day into an exact birthday.

One Midcalder baptism on 22 March 1767 names Alexander Glasgow and Emilia Glendinning. The same parent names and parish support a probable sibling connection to Abigail baptized there in 1769, whose mother appears as Glending/Glendining. Modern parental identities remain unresolved. Agnes Glasgow-32 has no recorded birth or parents in the checked live data and remains a compatible child comparison; her local circa-1783 estimate is not a concrete exclusion. Do not assign this and the competing 1780/1785 births as three facts about her. No new person is proposed.

One West Calder baptism on 15 July 1770 names John Glasgow and Margaret Mill, matching the existing child. These transcripts give 15 July as baptism, not an explicit birth date. The catalogue currently displays an exact 15 July birthday; its independent birth-date basis still needs checking before that precision is retained or corrected.

The Edinburgh entry explicitly records birth 15 July and baptism 30 July 1774, Alexander Glasgow, Brewers Servt, and Agness Cunninghame, residence Cross Causeway, OPR 685_2/9 item 1 p.172. It refines the existing before-30-July birth boundary. This secure child identification does not establish the later Geo Smart wife comparison.

One Wandell and Lamington baptism on 29 July 1780 names father James Glasgow; the mother field is a dash. James Glasgow-1120 is a local father comparison, not an identification. Agnes Glasgow-32 remains a compatible child alternative because her circa-1783 birth is an unsupported local estimate. Do not transfer one of James’s known spouses into the blank mother field or combine all competing Agnes birth events. No new person is proposed.

Agnes was born 22 October and baptized 15 November 1785 at Irvine, father James Glasgow, occupation Shipmr, mother Janet McMillan, OPR 595/1 item 1. No modern parent-couple identification is established. Agnes Glasgow-32 remains a compatible comparison, not an assigned identity; the local circa-1783 estimate does not exclude her. This is an alternative to other source-defined childhoods, not an additional birth of the same woman. No new person is proposed.

The Barony baptism on 20 March 1791 names Agnes Glasgow, John Glasgow and Helen Smith, matching the existing child. The transcript explicitly labels Sex Male. Preserve that conflicting field for original-register review; do not silently change the subject’s sex or create another Agnes. The reported 1791 birth year and a baptism boundary are separate claims.

The Bathgate entry names Peter Glasgow and Elisabeth Dick and explicitly reports birth 5 March and baptism 22 March 1795, OPR 662/2 item 1. The current profile/catalogue birthday is 3 March 1795. The parents and event identify the existing child, but the 3-versus-5 March reading is unresolved without comparing the underlying source. Keep both readings visible and do not silently overwrite the birthday or create a second child.

Agnes Glasgow was buried 6 November 1810 at Edinburgh, age 32, described as Spouse of Geo Smart, residence literal Hossier Niccolson, OPR 685_2/31 item 2 p.86. Birth circa 1778 is calculated from age. The Edinburgh child Glasgow-1482, born 15 July 1774, is a candidate but would be 36, four years older than the burial age; Glasgow-3406 would be 40. Age error is possible, but no spouse or household bridge identifies either. Do not assign the death or Geo Smart marriage. clusters.title: Medieval and early-burgh occurrences
clusters.summary: Entries establish recorded bearers and roles in multiple places before a continuous pedigree can be demonstrated.
clusters.boundary: They do not establish a shared medieval founder or identify same-named people across records.

clusters.title: Glasgow burgh property and fishers
clusters.summary: Property records directly identify some parent–child links and testaments define a fisher family core.
clusters.boundary: The older title succession and unresolved John identities do not prove every attached descendant.

clusters.title: Ayrshire estate and parish records
clusters.summary: Tenancy, charter and church sources preserve households and careers in the Ayrshire corridor.
clusters.boundary: Neighbourhood, later tradition and a common surname do not supply the missing connections.

clusters.title: Calder and Lothian testament and register records
clusters.place: Calder district, Mid Calder and Inveresk
clusters.summary: Two testaments identify separate rural households; baptism indexes frame a carefully bounded James question.
clusters.boundary: Neither testament proves a burgh bridge or resolves all later-profile identities.
